article.content: By Staff Writer , ITWeb Johannesburg, 09 Nov 2026 An indicative map showing the maritime route of the deployment to resolve the regional WACS circuit disruption (Image source: Congo Telecom). Repair operations on the West Africa Cable System (WACS) submarine fibre-optic network have entered a critical phase, with the designated repair vessel sailing towards the fault location. The deployment follows a 29 October circuit disruption that affected Congo Telecom’s redundancy mechanisms. Technical teams isolated the suspected fault to the cable segment linking the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Republic of Congo. Although the exact coordinates of the damage have not been publicly disclosed, an official update from Congo Telecom confirmed that the repair vessel is scheduled to reach the affected area on Wednesday, 11 November, to begin physical restoration of the undersea link. The Gulf of Guinea and Central African coastal waters are known locations for submarine cable faults. Disruptions along this Atlantic seabed corridor can result from deep-sea seismic activity, maritime incidents such as anchor dragging, or underwater landslides in geographical features such as the Congo Canyon. The latest disruption follows previous WACS outages, including underwater landslides that affected the network in 2020 and August 2023, as well as a separate outage in January this year that disrupted internet traffic across the region. Despite the loss of the primary circuits, Congo Telecom reported no service disruption for its customers. The operator said its automated failover and redundancy mechanisms were activated when the fault occurred, switching traffic to alternative backup links and maintaining internet capacity across its subscriber base. “Congo Telecom is closely monitoring the evolution of the situation and remains attentive to the progress of operations,” the operator said. “We will continue to keep customers informed of further developments as new information becomes available.” Spanning 14,500 kilometres, the WACS network connects South Africa with Portugal and the UK. With landing stations in 14 countries, including the Republic of Congo, Gabon, Cameroon, Nigeria, Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, the infrastructure serves as an international backbone for regional data transit and internet connectivity across Central and West Africa. article.content: 1.9 min read SUBCO Weighs Australian Cable Ship and Survey USV Ry Crozier, iTnews October 7, 2026 SUBCO is evaluating two prospective additions to Australia’s subsea infrastructure capabilities: an uncrewed surface vessel for cable-route surveys and a dedicated cable-laying ship. Founder and co-CEO Bevan Slattery outlined the concepts at the AusNOG conference in Brisbane, according to iTnews. Neither asset has been ordered, and the company is still assessing whether to proceed. The smaller proposal is a survey USV that SUBCO could own or control under a lease while using a specialist operator for maintenance and day-to-day operations. A December 2027 delivery target is being considered. SUBCO’s presentation indicated that the vessel could support route surveys for submarine cable projects, alongside marine biology and ecological work, giving the company access to survey capacity when project schedules require it. The larger proposal is a new cable-laying vessel that could cost about US$165 million, including remotely operated vehicles and ploughs for trenching and burying cable. Slattery said he would prefer a newbuild for reliability and fuel efficiency and would want a trusted partner to operate it. SUBCO does not expect to carry the cost alone and would seek contributions from the United States and Australian governments, but no public funding commitment has been announced. For the regional industry, the concept addresses both installation capacity and long-term repair resilience. Australia does not currently have its own dedicated cable-laying vessel, while existing operators rely on the South Pacific Marine Maintenance Agreement for regional repairs. Slattery warned that the mix of systems and operators supporting that arrangement may shrink after 2030 as older cables retire and newer networks are concentrated among fewer owners. A locally based vessel could provide more certainty for laying and repair availability as SUBCO advances multiple international routes under its APX program. The next confirmed decision point is the end of 2026, when Slattery said he expects to decide whether to buy the cable ship. If SUBCO proceeds on that timetable, a new vessel could be built and delivered by the end of 2029. The survey USV remains on a separate, earlier potential schedule. Until purchase, operating, and funding decisions are completed, both initiatives should be treated as capacity plans under evaluation rather than committed fleet additions. article.content: Photo courtesy of Converge / FB Text size A− Reset A+ Save Converge ICT Solutions Inc. limited the impact of a submarine cable disruption between the Philippines and Singapore after shifting traffic to alternative international routes, preventing a wider interruption for its residential and enterprise customers. The fiber internet provider reported on Monday that it rerouted traffic following the disruption on Friday, with most of the affected traffic shifted through the Bifrost international cable system. “This allowed minimal disruption in our services to both our residential and enterprise customers due to the cable issue between Singapore and the Philippines,” Converge CEO Dennis Anthony Uy said. Cable disruption Some customers experienced difficulties accessing applications and websites hosted in Singapore following the cable disruption. Converge said its investments in additional international cable systems gave it alternative routes to handle traffic during outages, reducing its reliance on individual connections between the Philippines and overseas destinations. “We have planned our investments in these international cable systems as early as five years ago precisely in anticipation of these incidents. Investment in Bifrost Our investments in Bifrost along with SEA-H2X (Southeast Asia — Hainan — Hong Kong Express Cable) have allowed us to achieve international network redundancy that’s most important at a time like this,” Uy said. The Trans-Pacific Bifrost Cable System spans more than 20,000 kilometers and connects the Philippines to Singapore, Indonesia, Guam and the United States. It has a total design capacity of more than 240 terabits per second. Converge serves as the Philippine landing party for Bifrost through its landing station in Davao and owns one fiber pair in the cable's trunk. Consortium owning SEA-H2X submarine cable The company is also part of the consortium that owns the 6,000-kilometer SEA-H2X submarine cable, which links Hong Kong, Hainan, the Philippines, Thailand, and Singapore. The system has a design capacity of more than 200 Tbps and lands in La Union.

title: Submarine cable outage disrupts internet across PH providers

original_text: Internet users in the Philippines experienced slower and intermittent connections on Friday, October 2, after an undersea cable segment linking the Philippines and Singapore went offline, affecting several telecommunications providers and internet service providers.

article.content: MANILA, Philippines – Internet users in the Philippines experienced slower and intermittent connections on Friday, October 2, after an undersea cable segment linking the Philippines and Singapore went offline, affecting several telecommunications providers and internet service providers. PLDT said the submarine cable cut affected services nationwide. The telco said it had successfully rerouted most of the affected traffic and expected service to normalize shortly. Converge ICT Solutions likewise said it had rerouted internet and data traffic going to and coming from Singapore through other submarine cables. Its technical teams were continuing to monitor connections to apps and websites hosted in Singapore. Globe, meanwhile, advised customers that they could experience slow internet access on both mobile and broadband services because of a technical issue, saying it was working to restore normal access as soon as possible. The UP Diliman Network Helpdesk also issued an advisory saying one of the undersea cable segments between the Philippines and Singapore was offline. The university said many of its upstream internet providers connect through these major international data routes, which could result in “increased latencies and intermittent performance,” particularly when users access websites and services hosted overseas. What the cable cut means for consumers For ordinary internet users, a submarine cable outage does not necessarily mean losing internet access entirely. Telecommunications companies can redirect, or reroute, data through other submarine cables and international connections. But with traffic moved away from its usual route, data may have to travel farther or share capacity with more users. Consumers may therefore notice slower website loading, higher latency or “ping,” video buffering, sluggish downloads and intermittent connections, particularly when accessing apps, websites, cloud services or game servers hosted outside the Philippines. Services hosted locally may be less affected, while connections that normally pass through Singapore or other affected international routes could experience more noticeable slowdowns. Submarine cables carry much of the internet traffic moving between countries. Having multiple cable routes allows telecommunications companies to keep users connected when one link fails, although performance can temporarily suffer while traffic is being rerouted. PLDT and Converge said they had already rerouted affected traffic as of October 2, while Globe said restoration efforts were underway. – Rappler.com

article.content: Skip to content Converge: No major interruption after PH-SG cable break — thanks to Bifrost By PNN Admin October 6, 2026 12:19 pm No Comments No major brownout for Converge users! Leading fiber provider Converge ICT Solutions Inc. says its services remained stable after a submarine cable disruption between the Philippines and Singapore last Friday — the same break that affected some users trying to access Singapore-based apps and websites. While some customers reported slow access to SG-hosted sites, Converge said it immediately rerouted traffic to alternative international paths, mostly through its new Bifrost cable system. “This allowed none to minimal disruption in our services to both our residential and enterprise customers due to the cable issue between Singapore and the Philippines,” said Converge CEO Dennis Anthony Uy. According to Uy, Converge was able to recover quickly because it invested early in two new international cables — Bifrost and SEA-H2X — for exactly this kind of emergency. Bifrost is a 20,000-km trans-Pacific cable linking PH to Singapore, Indonesia, Guam, and the US. Converge owns one fiber pair and is the PH landing party in Davao. Design capacity: 240 Tbps. SEA-H2X is a 6,000-km cable connecting Hong Kong, Hainan, La Union (PH), Thailand, and Singapore. Design capacity: 200 Tbps. Uy said with these two, Converge now has one of the most redundant international networks in the country — crucial as demand for AI and cloud services surges. article.content: Subsea cables entered the Philippine news twice in the span of a week, for different reasons. The first involved a research vessel holding position in waters that host cable corridors connecting the country to Northeast Asia. On September 28, the Philippine Coast Guard reported that the vessel did not answer radio challenges and had displayed a physically impossible Automatic Identification System trail. It later deployed a ship and aircraft, disrupted what it described as unauthorized marine scientific research, and compelled the vessel to leave its position. The second was a network disruption. On October 2, the C2C Philippines-Singapore link went down while its Hong Kong link was under maintenance. Providers rerouted traffic, but the disruption coincided with reports of slow or intermittent connections. The Singapore link was restored the following day. Its cause had not been made public as of writing. No public reporting has established a connection between the incidents. They should not be treated as one chain of events. But each exposes a different part of the same problem: what can the country detect and protect, what disruption can the network absorb? They also raise a third question that becomes critical when redundancy is no longer enough: how quickly can the system recover? Taken together, this is a question of resilience. Archipelagic governance For the Philippines, subsea cable resilience is a question of archipelagic governance. This is the approach being explored by The Asia Foundation through its Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables (AGOS) initiative, which brings government and industry together to look at subsea cable resilience beyond the infrastructure itself. The cable is only one part of a wider system of infrastructure, institutions, policies, and capabilities. The system connects what happens at sea with what happens on land. For an archipelago, these connections are shaped by geography. Connectivity crosses maritime spaces, lands in different communities and jurisdictions, and depends on institutions and infrastructure spread across islands. Must Read Subsea cable cut between Philippines and Singapore disrupts internet services A disruption at sea can affect banking, government services, businesses, and emergency communications. Suspicious activity near a cable route may force government to respond before it fully understands the risk. Delays in maritime access can also delay repair and restoration. The connection works both ways. Decisions on permits, power supply, security arrangements, and coordination with local governments affect whether the system can expand, remain operational, and recover from disruption. The system stretches from cables on the seabed to landing stations and land-based networks. It also includes power, network operations, repair capacity, government policies, emergency arrangements, and the institutions responsible for them. This makes protecting cables and building cable resilience related but different tasks. Protecting a cable is about reducing the risk of damage or interference. Resilience is about whether the larger system can continue to function when disruption happens. Across AGOS consultations with government and industryparticipants spoke about resilience in different ways: protecting the system, keeping services running during a disruption, and restoring connectivity quickly. Taken together, their inputs pointed to three qualities describing a resilient system: protected, adaptable, and recoverable. These qualities do not come from infrastructure alone. They also depend on the policies, capabilities, and coordination that allow the system to function. A protected system can identify and manage risks. An adaptable system can reroute traffic and keep essential services running. A recoverable system can quickly mobilize maritime access, repair permits, security, technical teams, and local support. The cable alone can do none of these things. The question, then, is not only whether the Philippines can prevent something from happening to a cable. Not every cable fault, anchor drag, natural hazard, technical failure, or deliberate act can be prevented. The question is also whether the system around the cables can continue functioning when something does happen. This is why keeping the system resilient cannot be treated as the work of the Coast Guard or Navy alone. Maritime authorities have distinct responsibilities at sea. But building a resilient subsea cables system also requires action from telecommunications regulators, economic and security agencies, emergency authorities, and operators. Uncertainty over the cause of disruption further complicates the response. An incident may be accidental or deliberate, and establishing which takes time. But the response cannot wait for attribution. If services on land are already affected, continuity measures, repairs, and coordination have to kick in. Attribution and resilience therefore operate on different clocks. Authorities may still be determining what happened while operators and government already need to keep services running and preparing for recovery. Building a response before it’s needed The Philippines already has laws, mandates, and mechanisms that cover parts of the system. Telecommunications and data-transmission rules govern networks. Maritime authorities operate under their respective mandates at sea. Disaster-response mechanisms can support continuity. The Konektadong Pinoy Act provides an open-access framework for data transmission, while Executive Order No. 32 streamlines permitting process for telecommunications and internet infrastructure. The challenge is not always the lack of a policy. It is whether existing mandates can be brought together quickly enough when an incident crosses institutional boundaries. Which agency receives the first report? What threshold triggers interagency coordination? Who verifies the incident, secures the area, prioritizes essential services, authorizes emergency access, and communicates with affected communities? Which approvals can be expedited, and under whose authority? What information should operators share with government, and what information should remain protected? An incident protocol is one way to answer those questions before a disruption. It should connect detection to assessment, protection, continuity, repair, and public communication. This is where an archipelagic approach becomes operational rather than conceptual. The task is not necessarily to create another institution. The task is to make sure the institutions that already hold different parts of the system know when and how to act together. The Philippines is not starting from scratch. PCG detected and acted on unusual vessel activity. Operators shifted traffic when an international route became unavailable. Companies already invest in additional capacity, route diversity, and repair arrangements. At the September 29 AGOS Forum, PLDT Global Corporation President and CEO, Albert Villa-Real put the industry case plainly: “Capacity without diversity is not resilience.” He also pointed to exploratory discussions among Philippine operators on shared or complementary infrastructure that could provide greater redundancy. Route diversity makes the network more adaptable, but redundancy does not address the whole resilience problem.When redundancy is no longer enough, or when physical repair is required, maritime access, government processes, security, information sharing, and repair capacity become part of the system’s ability to recover. Those efforts show that competition and cooperation can coexist. No single operator or government agency controls all the elements needed for resilience. Some forms of cooperation are therefore necessary, and possible, even within a competitive industry. What is needed is a clearer way for the different parts of the system to work together. That means having a common operating picture that protects sensitive information, clear rules on when to share it, an agreed response protocol, and a process for settling government requirements before a repair vessel is ready to move. International experience shows a growing recognition that protecting undersea infrastructure requires cooperation between government and industry. After several incidents involving damaged cables in the Baltic Sea, NATO launched Baltic Sentry to strengthen surveillance and support national authorities. NATO also works with industry through its Critical Undersea Infrastructure Network. But the Philippines cannot simply copy the Baltic model. Archipelagic governance must respond to the country’s own geography, institutions, communities, and risks. It does not require placing every decision under one institution. Nor does it mean treating subsea cables primarily as a military or security problem. It requires each institution to understand how its authority connects with others, what actions should follow when an incident occurs, and how consequences at sea will be managed on land. The recent incidents point to a broader lesson. A country can patrol the waters above a cable and still lack resilience. It can add cable capacity and still lack resilience. It can have repair arrangements, permits, emergency authorities, and capable institutions, but still find that these pieces do not connect quickly enough when disruption occurs. For an archipelago, the weakest link may therefore not be the cable itself. It may be the system around it. – Rappler.com Kat Tolosa is director of The Asia Foundation’s Governance and Resilience unit in the Philippines. Taj Basman is a program officer in the same unit and leads the Foundation’s Archipelagic Governance for Subsea Cables initiative. The views expressed are their own.

article.content: A submarine cable disruption between the Philippines and Singapore affected internet services nationwide, forcing major telecommunications companies Globe Telecom Inc., PLDT Inc. and Converge ICT Solutions Inc. to reroute international data traffic as available bandwidth was reduced. Globe and PLDT said Sunday their network services had fully normalized following the Oct. 2 cable disruption, while telecommunications companies continued to monitor their networks and international connections. In an advisory issued at 4:30 p.m. on Oct. 4, PLDT said it had fully restored network services nationwide. “Services have fully normalized nationwide following the submarine cable cut between the Philippines and Singapore on Oct. 2,” PLDT said. Globe earlier said it had also fully restored internet services, with mobile and broadband customers who experienced intermittent connectivity and slower browsing expected to have normal service. Globe said traffic was restored after the Philippine cable landing station reactivated the system and normalized fiber connections. The company said it was coordinating with international network partners to determine the exact nature and location of the fault. PLDT had advised customers on Oct. 2 that a submarine cable cut was affecting services nationwide, although most traffic had been rerouted through alternative paths as the company worked to normalize connectivity. Converge ICT Solutions Inc. likewise said traffic to and from Singapore had been rerouted through other submarine cable systems. The company said it was monitoring its network as well as applications and websites hosted in Singapore. The disruption reduced available international bandwidth and underscored the importance of alternative submarine cable routes in maintaining connectivity when faults occur on major international links. article.content: 1.8 min read Ireland, UK Test Joint Subsea Cable Response Publication Staff, BreakingNews.ie September 30, 2026 Ireland and the United Kingdom staged their first bilateral readiness exercise for undersea communications infrastructure on September 30, 2026. Officials worked through a simulated attack that disrupted several cable links in the Irish Sea, testing how the two governments would coordinate their response. Communications Minister Patrick O'Donovan called the event a key step in preparing the neighboring countries for failures affecting shared critical infrastructure. The exercise put into practice the Subsea Infrastructure Bilateral Collaboration Framework announced by both governments on March 13. The framework is intended to move information between national authorities and organize a coordinated reaction when a major subsea communications incident affects either country. Its published plan called for multiple readiness exercises, beginning in September, so this week's event marks delivery of the first planned test. The choice of a multi-cable scenario matters for operators because a broad regional incident could require more than repair coordination on one system. Government agencies may also need to share situational data, establish priorities and maintain cross-border communications while owners and maintenance providers assess physical damage. The public sources did not disclose operational results, response times or specific systems, and those details should not be inferred. This work sits inside a wider shared-seas agenda that covers maritime awareness, joint defense planning, closer contact between naval and defense organizations, and cooperation on cyber defense. Ireland has also applied to join the North Sea Joint Declaration alongside Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. The governments have said that channel could extend infrastructure-protection coordination toward the Irish and Celtic seas, giving the bilateral exercise a broader regional context. The immediate milestone is complete: the first joint exercise has taken place in the month designated by the framework. The standing commitment is for a series of additional exercises, but neither public source gives a date for the next one. For the cable sector, the practical signal is that Ireland and the United Kingdom are testing their incident-response arrangements before a real disruption requires governments, network owners and maritime authorities to act together. STAR / File MANILA, Philippines — Broadband provider Converge ICT Solutions Inc. found an immediate return on investment in its new subsea cable to Singapore when it spared subscribers from internet disruption over the weekend. Converge CEO and co-founder Dennis Anthony Uy yesterday said the provider immediately brought back internet services when a submarine link to Singapore was cut last Friday. Uy said Converge rerouted data traffic through its Bifrost Cable System, a project that goes to Guam, Indonesia, Singapore and the US through the Celebes Sea and Java Sea. Bifrost extends for around 20,000 kilometers across the Pacific Ocean. It is designed to transmit data among parties by about 240 terabits per second, landing in the Philippines via Davao. Apart from this, Uy said Converge relied on the Southeast Asia-Hainan-Hong Kong Express Cable System for redundancy. SEA-H2X lands in the country via La Union. SEA-H2X crosses more than 6,000 kilometers of waters between China and Southeast Asia, with the capacity to transfer over 200 Tbps across China, Hong Kong, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. “We planned our investments in these international cable systems as early as five years ago precisely in anticipation of these incidents,” Uy said. “Our investments in Bifrost, along with the SEA-H2X, allowed us to achieve international network redundancy that’s most important at a time like this,” he added. Last week, the University of the Philippines Diliman Network Helpdesk flagged erratic access to its information pipelines. The desk attributed the downtime to a fiber cut in one of the submarine cables to Singapore, where its data are hosted. Afterward, leading Philippine telcos PLDT Inc. and Globe Telecom Inc. confirmed that they are also subscribed to the disrupted subsea cable. In response, they rerouted their data traffic to other lines, knowing that fiber cuts, especially underwater, take weeks to repair. Subsea links like Bifrost act as passageways for data transmission between and among countries, so telcos invest on them to expedite internet traffic and strengthen infrastructure redundancy. Mostly, telcos subscribe to submarine cables that plug into countries where tech giants host their data offices, such as Japan, Singapore and the US. article.content: 1.9 min read PNG DataCo Reports Kumul Cable Fault and Repairs John Tanner, Developing Telecoms September 28, 2026 PNG DataCo is preparing to repair a fault on the Kumul Domestic Submarine Cable System branch serving Vanimo, according to a September 28 report by John Tanner in Developing Telecoms. The state-owned Papua New Guinea network wholesaler detected the fault on August 25. It affected point-to-point services, IEPL services and wholesale internet services in Sandaun Province. The company set October 23 as its target for bringing Vanimo's subsea connectivity services back; it has not reported the repair complete. The Kumul branch fault is one of several separate disruptions PNG DataCo reported during the preceding month. Its effect on both dedicated connections and wholesale internet services makes the Vanimo restoration target relevant to multiple service types in Sandaun Province. For now, the confirmed status is repair preparation, not a return to normal subsea service on that branch. article.content: 1.8 min read ESA Funds Automated Cable Backup Project Publication Staff, Advanced Television September 15, 2026 The European Space Agency has selected multi-orbit satellite operations specialist neXat to lead CableShield, a €1.5 million project intended to automate backup connectivity when submarine fiber routes fail. The project brings neXat together with Telesat and Colt Technology Services Belgium. Their demonstration will monitor for cable failures, then transfer selected traffic to satellite links automatically. ESA is funding the work through its Space Systems for Safety and Security initiative within the Advanced Research in Telecommunications Systems program. CableShield is designed as an orchestration layer across separate communications domains instead of a single-vendor backup network. Its architecture links detection and decision functions with terrestrial-network controls and satellite-network controls. Those layers will communicate through application programming interfaces from ESA's Pooling and Sharing Interface Definitions work, allowing multi-vendor and multi-orbit satellite systems to exchange operational data, request capacity and manage shared resources as one service environment. When a fault occurs, the platform is expected to select available satellite resources and reroute a controllable, scalable portion of affected traffic with defined routing and prioritization. For submarine cable owners and network operators, the project addresses the difficult interval between a fault and physical restoration. Satellite capacity cannot replace the full throughput of a major fiber system, but automated allocation and traffic prioritization could preserve selected critical services while repair work proceeds. The multi-provider pooling approach also tests whether operators can obtain resilient capacity across satellite fleets without building a separate manual process for every provider. Colt supplies the terrestrial-network perspective, while Telesat brings the satellite-operator role to the field demonstration. The current award begins an 18-month effort devoted to development and validation, not an immediate commercial deployment. The partners must still integrate the detection, control and traffic-shifting functions and then prove them under field conditions. neXat aims to offer the backup service commercially in 2028, timed to Telesat's planned Lightspeed service entry. The demonstration and its validation results are therefore the next confirmed milestones for determining whether CableShield can progress from an ESA-backed resilience project into an operational continuity option for submarine cable networks. article.content: 1.8 min read Fitburg Trial Opens Over Baltic Cable Damage AFP, ET Telecom September 8, 2026 A Russian captain and an Azerbaijani bosun from the cargo ship Fitburg went on trial in Helsinki District Court on September 8 over alleged damage to two subsea telecommunications cables linking Finland and Estonia. AFP, reporting through ET Telecom, said prosecutors charged the two seafarers with aggravated criminal mischief and aggravated interference with telecommunications. Both defendants deny the charges. Prosecutors are seeking prison terms of at least two years and six months. The case centers on the 132-meter Fitburg, which was sailing from Russia to Israel under the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines when Finnish authorities stopped it on December 31, 2025. Prosecutors allege the vessel dragged a damaged anchor for at least 130 kilometers across the Gulf of Finland seabed, cutting two telecom cables and attempting to damage eight additional subsea connections. They say the incident caused significant immediate damage and created a serious risk for telecommunications, electricity and gas networks in Finland. Jurisdiction is a central issue because prosecutors say most of the alleged dragging occurred in Estonia's exclusive economic zone, although some damage was sustained in Finnish territorial waters. The defendants argue that Finland lacks authority to hear the case because the cables were damaged outside Finnish territory. That question also arose in the separate Eagle S cable-damage prosecution: Helsinki District Court dismissed that case on jurisdictional grounds in 2025, before the Helsinki Court of Appeal overturned the ruling in August 2026 and returned it to the district court. For submarine cable owners and operators, the Fitburg proceedings are a practical test of how national courts address alleged vessel activity affecting cross-border infrastructure beyond territorial waters. The prosecution's case focuses not only on the two damaged telecom cables but also on the claimed risk to eight other subsea connections and to Finland's wider critical-network environment. Two other officers were investigated but were not charged. The Fitburg trial is now underway, and the next confirmed step is the court's consideration of the evidence and competing jurisdiction arguments. The cited report did not provide a verdict date. Jurisdiction is a central issue because prosecutors say most of the alleged dragging occurred in Estonia's exclusive economic zone, although some damage was sustained in Finnish territorial waters. The defendants argue that Finland lacks authority to hear the case because the cables were damaged outside Finnish territory. That question also arose in the separate Eagle S cable-damage prosecution: Helsinki District Court dismissed that case on jurisdictional grounds in 2025, before the Helsinki Court of Appeal overturned the ruling in August 2026 and returned it to the district court. For submarine cable owners and operators, the Fitburg proceedings are a practical test of how national courts address alleged vessel activity affecting cross-border infrastructure beyond territorial waters. The prosecution's case focuses not only on the two damaged telecom cables but also on the claimed risk to eight other subsea connections and to Finland's wider critical-network environment. Two other officers were investigated but were not charged. The Fitburg trial is now underway, and the next confirmed step is the court's consideration of the evidence and competing jurisdiction arguments. The cited report did not provide a verdict date. "Vocus is working closely with its marine repair partner to progress repair readiness activities. article.content: Four of Vietnam's subsea cables suffer faults, leading to fresh connectivity outages for country Not for the first time in recent years September 01, 2026 By Paul Lipscombe Have your say Vietnam has once again been plagued by multiple subsea cable outages. As reported by VN Express , four of the six subsea cables that connect the country have suffered from disruption due to multiple simultaneous faults within these cables, though the specifics about these faults have not been revealed. 26 Aug 2021 What is a submarine cable? Subsea fiber explained Our wireless world depends on a few hundred fiber cables laid on the ocean floor Vietnam is connected by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2, with the last two being the newest cables. The cables impacted include parts of the SJC2 cable, which connects the country to other parts of Asia, the AAE-1 cable, which has seen issues since February, while the Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the US, and the Intra Asia (IA) cable have also seen issues. Repairs on the AAG and IA cables are expected to start this month. The SJC2 cable is the latest to suffer disruption, notes VN Express, which reports that the cable developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, last week. These faults have led to mobile network operators in the country reporting network disruption, including VNPT and Viettel, while around 30 percent of Vietnam's international Internet traffic. In order to navigate these challenges, Viettel has added 800Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable on Wednesday, and is also adding 300Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway. It's not the first time the country's subsea cables have suffered severe disruption. In 2024, three cables connecting Vietnam (IA, APG, and AAE-1) were all hit by outages, while a year earlier all five cables that connected the nation at the time were down simultaneously. Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results A fourth undersea fiber-optic cable serving Vietnam has developed a fault, further disrupting international Internet connectivity with three other cables remaining out of service. The SJC2 cable, which connects Vietnam with other parts of Asia, developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, on Tuesday, according to an international undersea cable operator. The simultaneous problem with four undersea cables has badly affected Vietnam's international Internet traffic, the operator said. The AAE-1 cable has been experiencing problems in its S1.H2 segment since February and has yet to be repaired. The Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the U.S., and the Intra Asia (IA) cable are also experiencing problems, with repairs expected to begin in early September. Undersea fiber-optic cables carry the bulk of Vietnam's international Internet traffic, and so its international bandwidth has been substantially reduced. Internet service providers have been balancing loads, rerouting traffic and adding capacity through other connections to minimize the impact on users. Ethernet cables connected to the LAN ports of a Wi-Fi modem/router. Photo by VnExpress/Luu Quy Network provider VNPT said it rerouted traffic through available connections immediately after the problems emerged to make the best use of its remaining capacity. But Internet access would "be affected to some extent" during peak hours, it said. Users might experience slower connections when browsing websites, streaming videos, or playing games hosted on overseas servers, though Internet services generally remain stable because of backup infrastructure, it said. The company described the incident as a force majeure event that affects all Internet service providers in Vietnam. A Viettel spokesperson told VnExpress that the company has been affected by the problems with the IA and AAE-1 cables. Its AAE-1 connection has been completely disrupted, sharply reducing the company's international capacity though its backup systems have not recorded any overload. To compensate for the lost capacity, Viettel added 800 Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable Wednesday. It is also adding 300 Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway, with the additional capacity expected to be available by Aug. 31. It has also rerouted some international traffic through a terrestrial cable running via Laos to Singapore and plans to add another 1.5 Tbps of capacity on that route by the end of the month. It said it could increase capacity on its Asia Direct Cable (ADC) to 50 Tbps if needed to "handle all international Internet traffic." The ADC, which was installed in 2025, links Vietnam with three major Asian connectivity hubs Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan. Vietnam is linked by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems, AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC and SJC2, the last two being the newest. The systems have suffered some 10 incidents a year since 2022. Repairs to undersea cables typically take several months to half a year and can sometimes take as long as a year. To reduce its dependence on undersea cables, Vietnam launched its first VSTN terrestrial fiber-optic cable in 2025 and has also approved trials of satellite Internet services. Earlier this month, Elon Musk's Starlink became the first company to be licensed to provide such services. Get VnExpress first in Google Search See more of the news you trust. article.content: Thursday, August 27, 2026 Sign in Hello, Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Vietnam News Ho Chi Minh City Travel Economy Education Expat Life World Video Photo Vietnam News Thursday, August 27, 2026, 14:49 GMT+7 Vietnam’s international Internet connection affected by faults on three undersea cables Three undersea cable systems serving Vietnam have encountered problems, cutting the country’s international Internet capacity by an estimated 30 percent and potentially causing slower connections during peak hours. Undersea cable disruptions may affect some Internet services, particularly online gaming, in Vietnam. Photo: Duc Thien / Tuoi Tre The SJC2 and AAE-1 cables recently suffered outages while repairs to the AAG system have yet to be completed, according to domestic telecom operators and international cable management units. AAE-1, which links Vietnam with Hong Kong and Singapore, experienced an incident at 6:22 pm on Tuesday. Repair work is expected to begin in late September, depending on the availability of specialized vessels and weather conditions at sea. Starlink satellite Internet launches in Vietnam Vietnam’s Internet infrastructure ready to power low-altitude economy With AAG still under repair following an earlier fault, three of Vietnam’s major international undersea cable systems are now affected. According to preliminary estimates from several telecom operators, the outages have reduced Vietnam’s total international Internet capacity by about 30 percent. Internet service providers have activated contingency measures, rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Vietnam’s telecommunications provider VNPT said it had balanced and redirected traffic across alternative routes to optimize available capacity, helping keep its network generally stable. However, users may experience slower speeds and higher latency during peak hours when accessing overseas-hosted services, including websites, high-definition video streaming, and online games. Some operators said the impact on customers remained limited thanks to backup capacity across multiple independent routes. Vietnam currently relies mainly on six undersea cable systems for international Internet connectivity: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2. SJC2 spans about 10,500 kilometers across the Asia-Pacific region, with an initial investment of US$439 million and a designed capacity of up to 126 Tbps. article.content: Thursday, August 27, 2026 Sign in Hello, Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Vietnam News Ho Chi Minh City Travel Economy Education Expat Life World Video Photo Vietnam News Thursday, August 27, 2026, 14:49 GMT+7 Vietnam’s international Internet connection affected by faults on three undersea cables Three undersea cable systems serving Vietnam have encountered problems, cutting the country’s international Internet capacity by an estimated 30 percent and potentially causing slower connections during peak hours. Undersea cable disruptions may affect some Internet services, particularly online gaming, in Vietnam. Photo: Duc Thien / Tuoi Tre The SJC2 and AAE-1 cables recently suffered outages while repairs to the AAG system have yet to be completed, according to domestic telecom operators and international cable management units. AAE-1, which links Vietnam with Hong Kong and Singapore, experienced an incident at 6:22 pm on Tuesday. Repair work is expected to begin in late September, depending on the availability of specialized vessels and weather conditions at sea. Starlink satellite Internet launches in Vietnam Vietnam’s Internet infrastructure ready to power low-altitude economy With AAG still under repair following an earlier fault, three of Vietnam’s major international undersea cable systems are now affected. According to preliminary estimates from several telecom operators, the outages have reduced Vietnam’s total international Internet capacity by about 30 percent. Internet service providers have activated contingency measures, rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Vietnam’s telecommunications provider VNPT said it had balanced and redirected traffic across alternative routes to optimize available capacity, helping keep its network generally stable. However, users may experience slower speeds and higher latency during peak hours when accessing overseas-hosted services, including websites, high-definition video streaming, and online games. Some operators said the impact on customers remained limited thanks to backup capacity across multiple independent routes. Vietnam currently relies mainly on six undersea cable systems for international Internet connectivity: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2. SJC2 spans about 10,500 kilometers across the Asia-Pacific region, with an initial investment of US$439 million and a designed capacity of up to 126 Tbps. article.content: 1.3 min read India Plans Faster Subsea Cable Repair Clearances Danish Khan, Moneycontrol August 25, 2026 India’s Department of Telecommunications is developing a single-window portal intended to reduce delays in approvals for submarine cable repairs. The proposed platform would bring agencies involved in the clearance process onto one system, including shipping authorities, the Coast Guard and the Ministry of Home Affairs. Telecom operators are affected by cable faults, but many repair permissions currently sit with other government bodies. The department expects to complete a proposal for the portal in about two months. After that, the plan would move through approvals, procurement, tendering and implementation. An information technology agency under the Centre for Development of Telematics is expected to participate, with March 2027 identified as a tentative implementation target. DoT is also discussing the development of domestic repair capability with industry and the Directorate General of Shipping. India does not currently have a dedicated submarine cable repair vessel and relies on foreign resources, which can increase costs and extend restoration times when suitable vessels are unavailable or operating elsewhere. Building a domestic ecosystem would require investment in a specialized vessel and supporting infrastructure. The initiative comes as international cable routes face operational and geopolitical risks. Multiple Red Sea cable faults in 2024 affected systems between Asia and Europe, although Indian operators largely mitigated the impact by rerouting traffic. A faster domestic clearance process and locally based repair resources could reduce the time needed to respond when future faults affect cables serving India. article.content: 1.3 min read Four Cable Faults Disrupt Vietnam International Traffic Publication Staff, VOV.VN August 28, 2026 Four of Vietnam’s eight international submarine cable systems are facing technical problems, creating pressure on overseas internet connectivity, according to VOV. The affected routes are SJC2, AAE-1, AAG and Intra-Asia, or IA. The latest status makes IA the fourth system currently listed as impaired. Cable operators said SJC2 and AAE-1 developed faults nearly at the same time on August 25, 2026. AAG was already affected by an unresolved issue, while IA has also been hit. Repair activity for IA is expected to start in early September, but no repair timetable has been released for SJC2, AAE-1 or AAG. SJC2 and AAE-1 are significant links for Vietnam’s international internet capacity. SJC2 is designed for up to 126 Tbps and includes investment from VNPT, with a landing point in Quy Nhon. AAE-1 has about 40 Tbps of design capacity and extends from Asia toward networks in the Middle East, Africa and Europe. Viettel is the cable’s only partner in Vietnam and manages the local landing facilities. AAG connects Southeast Asia with the United States and has been operating for many years. Users may see localized slowdowns at busy times when accessing overseas social media, streaming platforms and online games. Services and websites hosted inside Vietnam are not expected to be affected. Internet providers in Vietnam have responded with contingency steps, including traffic rerouting and load balancing through working submarine systems and land-based networks. original_text_zh: 根据约翰·坦纳于9月28日在《发展中电信》中的报道，PNG DataCo正准备修复为瓦尼莫服务的库穆尔国内海底电缆系统分支的故障。这位巴布亚新几内亚国有网络批发商于8月25日检测到故障。它影响了桑道恩省的点对点服务、IEPL服务和批发互联网服务。公司设定的目标是在10月23日前恢复瓦尼莫的海底连接服务，但尚未报告修复完成。

article.content: 1.9 min read PNG DataCo Reports Kumul Cable Fault and Repairs John Tanner, Developing Telecoms September 28, 2026 PNG DataCo is preparing to repair a fault on the Kumul Domestic Submarine Cable System branch serving Vanimo, according to a September 28 report by John Tanner in Developing Telecoms. The state-owned Papua New Guinea network wholesaler detected the fault on August 25. It affected point-to-point services, IEPL services and wholesale internet services in Sandaun Province. The company set October 23 as its target for bringing Vanimo's subsea connectivity services back; it has not reported the repair complete. The Kumul branch fault is one of several separate disruptions PNG DataCo reported during the preceding month. Its effect on both dedicated connections and wholesale internet services makes the Vanimo restoration target relevant to multiple service types in Sandaun Province. For now, the confirmed status is repair preparation, not a return to normal subsea service on that branch. The October 23 date is a company target rather than confirmation that connectivity has already been restored. In a separate incident beginning September 19, commercial power problems affected the Gerehu Earth Station, a nearby data center, and cable landing stations at Kerema and Daru. PNG DataCo attributed the problem to abnormal phase rotation following PNG Power maintenance. Power at Gerehu was restored September 21, while services at Kerema and Daru were restored September 23. Those restorations concern the power-related disruption, not the outstanding Kumul branch repair. Also on September 19, vandalism damaged a terrestrial fiber cable on the Madang–Yonki corridor, disrupting services in Lae, Yonki and the Highlands Region. The cable was repaired and services were restored September 21, according to the report. This was a land-based cable incident distinct from both the Vanimo-serving subsea fault and the power problems at PNG DataCo facilities. The Developing Telecoms report also identified a separate break on the Australia–Singapore Cable between Indonesia and Singapore. Although that cable does not directly connect to Papua New Guinea, the break contributed to degraded performance, latency and intermittent access for some Asia-hosted services. The report said Vocus rerouted Australia–Singapore Cable traffic over alternative paths pending repair. Taken together, the reported incidents affected different infrastructure and services; among them, the Kumul branch fault remains the one with repair preparations underway and an October 23 restoration target. article.content: Saturday, August 29, 2026 Sign in Hello, Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Vietnam News Ho Chi Minh City Travel Economy Education Expat Life World Video Photo Vietnam News Thursday, August 27, 2026, 14:49 GMT+7 Vietnam’s international Internet connection affected by faults on three undersea cables Three undersea cable systems serving Vietnam have encountered problems, cutting the country’s international Internet capacity by an estimated 30 percent and potentially causing slower connections during peak hours. Undersea cable disruptions may affect some Internet services, particularly online gaming, in Vietnam. Photo: Duc Thien / Tuoi Tre The SJC2 and AAE-1 cables recently suffered outages while repairs to the AAG system have yet to be completed, according to domestic telecom operators and international cable management units. AAE-1, which links Vietnam with Hong Kong and Singapore, experienced an incident at 6:22 pm on Tuesday. Repair work is expected to begin in late September, depending on the availability of specialized vessels and weather conditions at sea. Starlink satellite Internet launches in Vietnam Vietnam’s Internet infrastructure ready to power low-altitude economy With AAG still under repair following an earlier fault, three of Vietnam’s major international undersea cable systems are now affected. According to preliminary estimates from several telecom operators, the outages have reduced Vietnam’s total international Internet capacity by about 30 percent. Internet service providers have activated contingency measures, rerouting traffic through unaffected submarine cables and terrestrial networks. Vietnam’s telecommunications provider VNPT said it had balanced and redirected traffic across alternative routes to optimize available capacity, helping keep its network generally stable. However, users may experience slower speeds and higher latency during peak hours when accessing overseas-hosted services, including websites, high-definition video streaming, and online games. Some operators said the impact on customers remained limited thanks to backup capacity across multiple independent routes. Vietnam currently relies mainly on six undersea cable systems for international Internet connectivity: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2. SJC2 spans about 10,500 kilometers across the Asia-Pacific region, with an initial investment of US$439 million and a designed capacity of up to 126 Tbps. affected_area: Kamchatka, parts of Chukotka and Severo-Kurilsk on Sakhalin
original_text: Rostelecom says it has completed repairs to the Kamchatka-Sakhalin submarine fiber line and restored full telecommunications service on August 14, 2026. The work took place in the Ust-Bolsheretsky district under difficult marine and weather conditions. The project focused on improving the cable's shore-end route in the shallow coastal waters of the Sea of Okhotsk. Divers exposed the existing cable at depths of up to five meters, roughly one hundred fifty meters from shore, cut it on the seabed and transferred a section to a pontoon. Technicians then spliced in about four hundred meters of new cable installed from land by horizontal directional drilling. Divers subsequently buried the cable in the seabed. Onshore crews installed and buried another one hundred fifty meters of new cable and added a shore joint. Rostelecom said the revised route follows a safer coastal alignment intended to improve reliability and reduce the risk of future damage. Specialists from BULAT, including divers, supported the preventative work. Full service has resumed in Kamchatka, parts of Chukotka and Severo-Kurilsk on Sakhalin, with online services operating without speed restrictions.
original_text_zh: 俄罗斯电信公司Rostelecom宣布，已于2026年8月14日完成堪察加-萨哈林海底光纤线路的修复工作，全面恢复电信服务。修复工作位于乌斯季博利舍列茨基区，在恶劣的海洋和天气条件下进行。项目重点是改善电缆在鄂霍次克海浅海沿岸的登陆段路由。潜水员在距岸约150米、水深达5米处暴露出现有电缆，在海底将其切断并将一段转移到浮筒上。技术人员随后接入了约400米的新电缆，这些新电缆通过水平定向钻探从陆地安装。潜水员随后将电缆埋入海底。岸上工作人员安装并掩埋了另外150米的新电缆，并增加了一个岸上接续盒。Rostelecom表示，修订后的路由采用了更安全的沿岸路径，旨在提高可靠性并降低未来损坏的风险。来自BULAT的专家（包括潜水员）支持了这项预防性工作。服务已在堪察加半岛、楚科奇部分地区和萨哈林的北库里尔斯克全面恢复，在线服务运行无速度限制。

article.content: Technology Major Underwater Internet Cable Damage In Australia Raises Suspicions Of Targeted Attacks By Aaron Greenbaum Aug. 14, 2026 11:17 am EST Christoph Burgstedt/Getty Images Add BGR on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover While we rely increasingly on wireless accessories, wired gadgets are generally more reliable than wireless devices — or at the very least, they provide faster data communication speeds. This logic holds true for international communication: The majority of internet traffic between continents relies on undersea cables, so when one gets damaged, people start to worry. Earlier this week, two subsea cables that connect Australia to the rest of the world's internet experienced "shunt faults" (a short circuit caused by damaged cable insulation). The CEO of the company that manages these cables, Subco, posted on LinkedIn that the cables were "in close proximity to each other," and the faults happened within a short time span. Despite being a sovereign nation, Australia's economy is heavily dependent on its ability to connect to the rest of the internet — just like every other country in the world — and any disruption could prove catastrophic. While Australia's internet flows in and out of 16 underwater cables, the circumstances behind the damage were highly suspicious. Around the time of the shunt faults, Subco detected "some suspicious/coincidental activity from a vessel." This information has fueled the theory that the damage was intentional, possibly terroristically so. Dr. David Brewster, senior researcher at the National Security College at the Australian National University, has cited similar attacks over the past four years as credence for the claim. He doesn't know who sliced the cables, or if anyone did, but he did say that, like with the prior cable attacks, countries such as Russia or China would be the most likely suspects. Who owns Australia's subsea internet cables? Sybille Reuter /Getty Images In the spirit of fairness, shunt faults are a semi-common occurrence, as these underwater internet cables are easily cut . An errant ship's anchor can slice through the insulation, and sharks have been known to bite underwater cables and test whether they are edible (sharks hunt by following magnetic fields, and these cables are veritable roman candles of magnetic activity). However, once a cable is damaged, either due to an intentional attack or accident, bureaucracy can get in the way of repairs. While the shunted cables were situated in Australian waters — specifically, an area known as a "cable protection zone" — not all lines placed in this location belong to the Australian government. According to Dr. Brewster, many of these cables actually belong to U.S. tech giants, including Meta, Google, and Amazon. And even when a cable is 100% Australian property, ownership and responsibilities are never cut and dry. Even though Subco owns the damaged cables on paper, Dr. Brewster has clarified that no single governmental agency was responsible for them. These metaphorical monkey wrenches make it almost impossible to determine who needs to take responsibility or patch the physical damage. As of writing, people involved in the investigation are working under the assumption that the shunt fault was an act of deliberate sabotage. According to an email from the Australian Federal Police that Tom's Hardware received, officials are still examining all the information and will comment on the situation when they can.

article.content: Technology Major Underwater Internet Cable Damage In Australia Raises Suspicions Of Targeted Attacks By Aaron Greenbaum Aug. 14, 2026 11:17 am EST Christoph Burgstedt/Getty Images Add BGR on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover While we rely increasingly on wireless accessories, wired gadgets are generally more reliable than wireless devices — or at the very least, they provide faster data communication speeds. This logic holds true for international communication: The majority of internet traffic between continents relies on undersea cables, so when one gets damaged, people start to worry. Earlier this week, two subsea cables that connect Australia to the rest of the world's internet experienced "shunt faults" (a short circuit caused by damaged cable insulation). The CEO of the company that manages these cables, Subco, posted on LinkedIn that the cables were "in close proximity to each other," and the faults happened within a short time span. Despite being a sovereign nation, Australia's economy is heavily dependent on its ability to connect to the rest of the internet — just like every other country in the world — and any disruption could prove catastrophic. While Australia's internet flows in and out of 16 underwater cables, the circumstances behind the damage were highly suspicious. Around the time of the shunt faults, Subco detected "some suspicious/coincidental activity from a vessel." This information has fueled the theory that the damage was intentional, possibly terroristically so. Dr. David Brewster, senior researcher at the National Security College at the Australian National University, has cited similar attacks over the past four years as credence for the claim. He doesn't know who sliced the cables, or if anyone did, but he did say that, like with the prior cable attacks, countries such as Russia or China would be the most likely suspects. Who owns Australia's subsea internet cables? Sybille Reuter /Getty Images In the spirit of fairness, shunt faults are a semi-common occurrence, as these underwater internet cables are easily cut . An errant ship's anchor can slice through the insulation, and sharks have been known to bite underwater cables and test whether they are edible (sharks hunt by following magnetic fields, and these cables are veritable roman candles of magnetic activity). However, once a cable is damaged, either due to an intentional attack or accident, bureaucracy can get in the way of repairs. While the shunted cables were situated in Australian waters — specifically, an area known as a "cable protection zone" — not all lines placed in this location belong to the Australian government. According to Dr. Brewster, many of these cables actually belong to U.S. tech giants, including Meta, Google, and Amazon. And even when a cable is 100% Australian property, ownership and responsibilities are never cut and dry. Even though Subco owns the damaged cables on paper, Dr. Brewster has clarified that no single governmental agency was responsible for them. These metaphorical monkey wrenches make it almost impossible to determine who needs to take responsibility or patch the physical damage. As of writing, people involved in the investigation are working under the assumption that the shunt fault was an act of deliberate sabotage. According to an email from the Australian Federal Police that Tom's Hardware received, officials are still examining all the information and will comment on the situation when they can.

article.content: (Image credit: Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 6 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The founder and CEO of Subco, a company that owns several undersea cables servicing Australia, said that two of its cables — Indigo-West, connecting Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, and Indigo-Central, which has endpoints in Victoria, Tasmania, and New South Wales — reported shunt faults in close succession, with the detected problems also appearing to be in close proximity to each other. According to Bevan Slattery’s LinkedIn post , the errors occurred at around the same time that a vessel was traversing the area. In a statement, Australian Federal Police told Tom's Hardware that it had received a report of a crime and was investigating, strongly hinting the cables may have been cut in an act of sabotage. “Earlier tonight: Shunt faults on two systems (Indigo West and Indigo Central) straight after each other and in close proximity to each other. Remarkably this also happened in the Submarine Cable Protection Zone off Perth Australia. Coincidently some suspicious/coincidental activity from a vessel near the location and timing of the shunts occurring,” Slattery said in his post. “This is a concerning development. Partially because submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation, but also because this could very well turn out to be the second such incidence in a Federally declared cable protection zone. This maybe a coincidence, but it’s important for the Australian Federal Police (AFP) to investigate the issue urgently.” "The AFP has received a report of crime in relation to this matter," the force told Tom's Hardware . Further stating, "This report is currently being assessed based on the information provided. Further comment will be made at an appropriate time." Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: (Image credit: Bevan Slattery/LinkedIn ) Australia established the Cable Protection Zone in 2007, with the one near Perth extending 51 nautical miles from the shore at depths of over 6,500 feet (2,000 meters). Despite that, it seems that something has damaged the cables, as they reported shunt faults. A shunt fault is when the insulation of a conductor has been broken, allowing it to unintentionally contact another conductor or the ground, resulting in a short circuit. While there is no proof yet, Slattery shared the track of a marine vessel on his post, which was allegedly within the approximate area of the faults when they happened. Nation states have been cutting undersea infrastructure as part of gray zone warfare, with Russia and China suspected of sponsoring these activities. For example, Finland has been hit twice by undersea cable disruptions in the past couple of years, which has led to the prosecution of some of the crew members of the suspected vessels. Taiwan has also increased its naval patrols around its undersea cables, especially as a Chinese “research vessel” has been seen lurking above a cable that connects the island nation to the U.S. It’s unclear what caused the shunt faults in two of Australia’s undersea cables, but the incident happened at around the same time that the National Security College of the Australian National University released a report highlighting the growing threat that submarine cables face in the modern world. The regional government said timing remains weather-dependent. article.content: 1.2 min read Kamchatka Prepares for Subsea Cable Repairs The Moscow Times Staff, The Moscow Times August 10, 2026 Kamchatka authorities say maintenance on an undersea fiber-optic cable will cause a near-total internet interruption across Russia’s Far Eastern peninsula for as long as four days. The work is scheduled to begin at midnight local time on Wednesday and will be carried out by state telecommunications provider Rostelecom. The regional government said timing remains weather-dependent. Mobile and home internet services are expected to be unavailable during the maintenance window, affecting messaging apps, social platforms and other online services. Officials said conventional voice calls, SMS, television broadcasts and emergency services should continue operating. Hospitals, fuel stations, supermarkets, automated teller machines and other critical infrastructure are expected to switch to satellite backup connections while the main fiber link is offline. The government advised Kamchatka’s roughly 280,000 residents to prepare before the outage by obtaining cash and arranging offline resources. The announcement frames the disruption as planned maintenance rather than an unexpected cable fault. The work had previously been scheduled for September 2025 but was postponed, according to The Moscow Times. The latest notice establishes a new operational window and gives the region advance warning, though it does not identify the precise cable section, describe the technical repair scope or provide a guaranteed restoration time. Service duration will depend on repair progress and weather conditions. article.content: Submarine Cables: The Security Threat of Digital Chokepoints Image generated using artificial intelligence technology Executive Intelligence Snapshot The strategic vulnerability of global submarine cables networks is increasingly moving from a contingency scenario to an operational concern in hybrid warfare. Essential for over 99% of transoceanic data traffic, these seabed conduits face compounding risks of state-sponsored sabotage, signal interception, and collateral disruption within contested maritime choke points, most notably the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz. Consequently, the convergence of Sino-American competition over infrastructure deployment with asymmetric regional threats necessitates a re-evaluation of national digital resilience and maritime security frameworks. Background Between 8-9 August 2026 , two separate cables in the Submarine Cable Protection Zone off Perth , Australia, had both experienced faults straight after each other and in close proximity to each other. A vessel was reportedly observed nearby, with movements considered suspicious by some industry experts. On 9 August 2026 , a Chinese-flagged research vessel was observed loitering directly above an undersea cable system, the Pacific Light Cable Network , an 8,000-mile fiber-optic system linking Taiwan, the Philippines and the United States. Between 2024 and 2025, several Red Sea cables were damaged after a vessel struck by a Houthi missile dragged its anchor. In May 2026 , media outlets close to the IRGC claimed that undersea cables traversing Iranian-controlled Persian Gulf waters should be subject to Iranian regulation. The reported proposals include: licensing requirements for companies that own the cables; annual fees; mandates for major tech companies to operate in accordance with Iranian legislation; greater Iranian control over maintenance and repair activities. This does not establish an Iranian intention to physically sabotage the cables. It does, however, demonstrate Tehran’s recognition of subsea connectivity as a potential instrument of strategic leverage . Seventeen submarine cables pass through the Red Sea alone, carrying the majority of data traffic between Europe, Asia, and Africa. While, at least seven commercial submarine cable systems transit through the Strait of Hormuz . These include systems connecting Asia to Africa to Europe (AAE-1) and Southeast Asia to the Middle East to Western Europe (SEA-ME-WE 5) . Another two systems, FALCON , which connects India and Sri Lanka to Gulf states, Sudan, and Egypt, and the Gulf Bridge International Cable System (GBI) , which connects all Gulf countries, also run through Iranian territorial waters. Intercontinental data transmission relies almost entirely on approximately 500 active submarine fibre-optic cables, which carry over 95% of global communications, cloud traffic, and financial transfers. Historically financed by international telecom consortia, ownership has shifted significantly over the past decade, with major US technology firms (namely Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon), funding and controlling around 90% of new transatlantic capacity. Notably, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google spent years building data centres across the Gulf, betting the region would become the world’s next great hub for artificial intelligence. Concurrently, the United States government has systematically restricted Chinese infrastructure providers, such as HMN Tech, from landing cables on allied territories, prompting Beijing to establish alternative submarine routes connecting Asia, East Africa, and Europe via the Red Sea corridor . Why Does It Matter? Physical security risks have escalated as commercial and non-state vessels have repeatedly severed key subsea links in strategic maritime choke points. Recent incidents involving vessels dragging anchors over prolonged distances across seabed corridors, have disrupted high-capacity systems. These disruptions highlighted operational vulnerabilities stemming from limited global repair vessel capacity, complex maritime jurisdiction frameworks, and the challenge of distinguishing accidental maritime damage from deliberate infrastructure interference. In response, multilateral bodies including NATO and the European Union have introduced dedicated surveillance missions and regulatory frameworks aimed at hardening subsea network resilience. Subsea telecommunications cables can represent high-value, low-cost target for asymmetric warfare (shallow or relatively accessible waters, deep-sea sabotage is not necessarily cheap). From a tactical perspective, disrupting a fibre-optic bundle requires minimal kinetic expenditure, such as a commercial trawler or shadow-fleet tanker dragging a modified anchor along known seabed corridors. This method can create significant attribution ambiguity, particularly when the damage can plausibly be presented as accidental. Because international maritime law, primarily defined under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) , was framed around accidental civilian damage, it lacks robust mechanisms for attribution, jurisdiction, or pre-emptive interdiction against state-directed civil proxies in international waters. At the micro-tactical level, adversary tactics do not require the catastrophic physical destruction of entire cable spans . Targeted, localised severance within narrow, shallow waterways, such as the Bab el-Mandeb or the Strait of Hormuz, achieves disproportionate operational impact. The primary vulnerability lies not merely in the initial data blackout, but in the repair bottleneck . The global repair ecosystem is itself a strategic bottleneck, with limited repair-vessel availability and increasingly complex regulatory and security constraints capable of extending restoration times. In May 2026 , for instance, only one cable-repair vessel was operating in the Persian Gulf, owned by UAE-based e-Marine. In active military zones, high war-risk insurance premiums, naval escort demands, and protracted permit negotiations effectively can transform a temporary physical fault into a prolonged connectivity disruption. Submarine cable map (Credits: cable data by Greg Mahlknecht , map by Openstreetmap contributorsOpenStreetMap contributors, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons) The ongoing conflict in the Persian Gulf has once again laid bare the fragility of these digital superhighways. On one hand, US military pressure in the Gulf is simultaneously increasing the security exposure of infrastructure in which major US technology companies have invested heavily; on the other, it provides Iran with yet another form of asymmetric leverage, afforded by its favourable geographical position. Iran could exploit its control over portions of the territorial waters surrounding the Strait, its ability to restrict or complicate access to Iranian ports and coastal areas, and the broader security environment to delay or obstruct cable-repair operations. Beyond immediate economic disruption, the exposure of these maritime chokepoints accelerates the structural fragmentation of the global interne t. As the Red Sea and Gulf corridors become high-risk zones, sovereign states and private consortia are forced to re-route digital traffic overland (e.g., through terrestrial routes via Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Turkey) or seek alternative maritime paths. Such is the case with European actors currently backing the development of Arctic submarine connectivity designed to provide an alternative Europe–Asia route . The Polar Connect project , for instance, specifically aims to build a resilient connection between Europe and Asia via the Arctic Ocean. Nevertheless, this shift carries major geopolitical consequences. Terrestrial rerouting increases the importance of sovereign transit states, potentially exposing data flows to additional jurisdictional, regulatory and surveillance risks. Simultaneously, the heightened risk profile of Western-backed maritime routes incentivises developing nations across the Global South to adopt state-subsidised Chinese digital infrastructure, accelerating the emergence of two distinct, geopolitically aligned global data ecosystems. Outlook Cable geopolitics is increasingly coming to resemble that of pipelines: whoever controls the routes controls the chokepoints, and consequently dictates the overall resilience of the network. The Persian Gulf case is emblematic. Over the past decade, major US technology conglomerates ( hyperscalers ) have poured billions of dollars into subsea infrastructure and AI data hub expansion across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. Kinetic confrontation in the Gulf effectively weaponises the very geography these corporations rely upon. By destabilising the corridor, US geopolitical pressure risks undermining the asset security of its own corporate sector , creating a strategic friction between Washington’s defence posture and the global infrastructure architecture of US hyperscalers. The strategic consequence is that subsea connectivity can no longer be treated as a purely commercial infrastructure issue. As geopolitical competition increasingly extends into the seabed , the resilience of digital networks will depend not only on the number of cables deployed, but on the ability of states and private operators to protect, repair, and reroute them under conditions of conflict. In this environment, control over maritime corridors, repair access, landing stations, and alternative terrestrial routes will become an increasingly important component of national power. For the Gulf, this creates a paradox : the same geography that makes the region attractive as a global hub for energy, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence also concentrates its digital infrastructure around some of the world’s most contested maritime chokepoints. The strategic question is therefore no longer whether submarine cables can be disrupted, but whether the states and corporations that depend on them can maintain connectivity when the geography itself becomes contested. Still, modern networks are designed around redundancy and traffic rerouting. A cable being cut does not necessarily produce an outage. The real vulnerability is geographical concentration, insufficient route diversity, simultaneous faults and limited repair capacity. The strategic threat emerges when several apparently independent routes share the same chokepoint. Written by Silvia Boltuc SpecialEurasia Co-Founder & Managing Director. She is an international affairs specialist, business consultant, and political analyst who has supported private and public institutions in decision-making by providing reports, risk assessments, and consultancy. Because of her work and reporting activities, she has travelled in Europe, the Middle East, South-East Asia, and the post-Soviet space assessing domestic dynamics and situations and creating a network of local contacts. She is also the Director of the Energy & Engineering Department of CeSEM – Centro Studi Eurasia Mediterraneo and the Project Manager of Persian Files. Previously, she worked as an Associate Director at ASRIE Analytica. Suspicious undersea cable damage exposes Australia’s defence vulnerability 10/08/2026 Share this article Millsy & Karl Two subsea cables were severed off the coast of Western Australia over the weekend under suspicious circumstances, exposing a concerning vulnerability in Australia’s defence.
