article.content: In March 2026, the United Kingdom and Ireland held joint exercises to evaluate how they would respond to disruptions in undersea cables. The practice followed a series of cases in European waters in which cables were broken under unknown circumstances. These events are no longer viewed as accidents. Governments increasingly see them as potential acts of intentional interference. This move demonstrates a more fundamental shift in how infrastructure is understood. More than 95% of worldwide internet traffic is carried by undersea cables. They also facilitate financial transactions worth trillions of dollars per day. These wires are not only technological systems. They are currently involved in global power politics. Recent incidents show a definite pattern. Since 2022, cables in the Baltic Sea have been repeatedly damaged. In October 2023, the Balticconnector gas pipeline connecting Finland and Estonia was damaged. In December 2025, Finnish officials seized another vessel when a connection between Finland and Estonia was damaged. The ship was suspected of dragging its anchor down the seafloor. In both instances, these incidents fall below the level of open conflict . At the same time, they impose significant economic and political costs. The Indo-Pacific region now faces similar dangers. In February 2023, Taiwan captured a Chinese-manned vessel suspected of destroying a cable connecting Taiwan to the Matsu Islands. Many residents were unable to communicate because of the destruction. Taiwan had to rely on backup satellite systems for several weeks. In early 2024, numerous Red Sea subsea cables near Yemen were damaged. This occurred amid a period of increased attacks by Houthi forces on commercial ships in the Red Sea, an important route that transmits roughly 17% of worldwide internet traffic. When cables were cut, data had to be redirected via longer routes , increasing delays and hindering digital services. Private enterprises are already responding to these issues. New cable projects in the Red Sea were delayed in 2024 and 2025 by companies such as Google and Meta as increasing insurance prices and security concerns made them less practical. This shows how security risks influence infrastructure decisions. It also highlights how non-state actors can influence global systems. A few focused attacks can alter the flow of data between continents. These threats become considerably more acute at key chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is one such example. It handles around 20% of worldwide oil commerce. It is also an important route for subsea cables linking Europe and Asia. Tensions between Iran and Western countries have escalated in recent years drastically. There have been numerous incidences of maritime attacks and vessel seizures . If wires in this region are damaged, the impact will be severe. Financial systems rely on fast and consistent data flows. Interruption might hinder transactions, cause communication delays, and generate confusion in global markets. Control of cable infrastructure is also becoming more contested. China has taken on a larger role in the construction and maintenance of submarine cables. This extension is tied to the Digital Silk Road , which was established in 2015 as part of the Belt and Road Initiative. Chinese enterprises, such as HMN Technologies , have worked on projects across Asia, Africa, and the Pacific. These projects have raised concerns about data security and strategic dependency. In 2020, the United States vetoed the Pacific Light Cable Network proposal. The project would have connected California with Hong Kong. US officials emphasized national security threats associated with Chinese engagement. This move shows that cable projects are now seen from a strategic viewpoint. India is attempting to establish itself as an alternate hub. In 2023, firms led by Reliance Jio announced the India-Europe Xpress cable project . This project proposes to connect Mumbai straight to Europe via the Middle East. It is intended to increase speed and lessen reliance on older routes. In 2023, India launched deliberations on the Digital India Act . This policy is intended to promote data governance and digital infrastructure. India’s digital economy is expanding rapidly. This rise increases the demand for safe and dependable cable networks. It also opens up new potential for international investment. Canada is part of this system. Canada’s Indo-Pacific Strategy was launched in November 2022. The policy allocated 2.3 billion dollars to enhance trade, investment, and security partnerships in the region. Digital and infrastructure connectivity is an important aspect of this approach. At present, these risks are no longer theoretical. The ongoing United States–Iran conflict in 2026 has pushed some of the world’s most critical cable routes into active conflict zones. Since late February 2026, the Strait of Hormuz has seen a near halt in commercial shipping after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned vessels against transit and carried out drone and missile strikes in the region. At the same time, Houthi forces in the Red Sea have resumed attacks on maritime traffic, effectively placing two of the most important digital chokepoints under simultaneous stress. These corridors are not just energy routes. Around 17 major undersea cables pass through the Red Sea alone , carrying most of the data traffic between Europe, Asia, and Africa, while additional cables run through the Strait of Hormuz connecting Gulf economies to global networks. Military activity, sea mines, and drone strikes increase the risk of accidental cable cuts, and repair ships are often unable to safely access damaged areas. This has already begun to affect infrastructure planning . In March 2026, work on major cable projects in the Persian Gulf, including extensions of Meta-backed networks linking India, the Gulf, and Europe, was suspended because operators could not safely function in the region. These changes leave a gap in NATO’s policy. The alliance has mostly focused on traditional military domains. It has also invested in cyber defence. However, the physical infrastructure that enables digital communication has received less attention . In 2023, NATO established the Critical Undersea Infrastructure Coordination Cell . This was a step towards improved monitoring and protection . NATO has also strengthened its patrols in areas such as the Baltic Sea . These activities reveal rising awareness. However, they remain limited in comparison to the scope of the problem. Some governments have already taken steps to mitigate risk. Japan has invested in several cable lines and landing stations, decreasing its reliance on any one route. Australia has financed the Coral Sea Cable System . Finished in 2019, it connects Australia with Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands while reducing cable vulnerability. The European Union has likewise taken this approach. In 2023, it proposed the Secure Connectivity Programme to upgrade digital infrastructure and increase resilience. These cases provide clear lessons. Diversification lowers risk . Variety increases resilience. Public investment can help to shape a secure infrastructure. Canada can use these lessons in its Indo-Pacific policy. It may invest in new cable lines that avoid high-risk areas like the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz. It can collaborate with partners such as India, Japan, and Australia to establish reliable networks . It can also use its financial power to encourage improved security standards in infrastructure projects. For Canada, the stakes are rising as its economic ties to the Indo-Pacific strengthen after Prime Minister Carney’s diversification of partners. Protecting subsea infrastructure will require collaboration, investment, and long-term planning. What lies under the ocean floor now influences what occurs above it. article.content: ASC cable break causes connectivity disruption between Perth and Singapore Repairs are underway September 07, 2026 By Paul Lipscombe Have your say A major cable break in Vocus' Australia-Singapore Cable (ASC) subsea cable has caused disruption to connectivity between Perth, Australia, to Singapore. The break was first acknowledged by Vocus on Friday (September 4), though the break is still causing issues as of today (September 7), as confirmed via Vocus' outages page . 26 Aug 2021 What is a submarine cable? Subsea fiber explained Our wireless world depends on a few hundred fiber cables laid on the ocean floor Launched in 2018, the 4,600km (2,858 miles) ASC connects Australia to Christmas Island, Jakarta, and Singapore. Vocus noted that it was able to detect a fault condition on the ASC impacting traffic between Perth and Singapore last Friday. This led to Wavelength and Ethernet services becoming unavailable, while Internet traffic has been rerouted via other paths. "The fault appears to be a subsea cable fault in Indonesian waters," said the company. The cause of the fault has not been disclosed, though Vocus said it's working closely with its marine repair partner to progress repair readiness activities, while planning for the repair of the ASC is underway. "Vocus is working closely with its marine repair partner to progress repair readiness activities. This includes technical review of the latest diagnostic results, confirmation of the required spare materials, and coordination of the necessary permits and regulatory approvals," said Vocus today in its most recent update. The company added that it will provide its next update on September 11. It's not the first time the ASC cable has suffered a major break. Back in 2021 , a Maersk ship captain was arrested and charged after allegedly damaging the cable, though the case was later dropped against the captain. Select your language English (UK) 简体中文(中国) Search Home Systems Trans-Pacific AAG AAG Cable Down Offshore Vietnam on April 3 (repaired on April 21) AAG Cable Down Offshore Vietnam on April 3 (repaired on April 21) Details By Winston Qiu Winston Qiu Category: AAG 04 April 2020 According to The Saigon Times, the Asia America Gateway (AAG) undersea cable system encountered an incident on Friday, April 3,2020. This is the first submarine cable incident in Vietnam in 2020, it has affected Vietnam’s international internet traffic. Many Vietnamese Internet users on April 3 complained that access to international services, such as YouTube, Instagram and Facebook, was choppy. One of these providers sent an announcement to customers, saying that the AAG cable system was broken and warning that connections to services provided by Facebook and YouTube would slow down. Meanwhile, access to local websites remains normal, according to the announcement. According to Vietnami Isider, there are now six submarine cable systems connecting Vietnam , as well as a 120Gbps bandwidth that runs overland through China. The undersea cables have had a very high risk of interruption and been under frequent repair, affecting all service providers in Vietnam. It is said, Vietnam’s average broadband speed is 10 times slower than Singapore’s 70.86 Mbps, a third of Malaysia’s 23.86 Mbps and half that of Thailand’s (18.21 Mbps). It is expected to take more than two week to repair the AAG cable. Update 1: The repair of AAG cable system was completed on April 21, 2020. Update 2: The AAG cable system broke down for the second time this year on May 14. Repairs to this cable system are expected to be finished on June 2. Meanwhile, the APG cable system connecting Vietnam also broke down on May 23 . Select your language English (UK) 简体中文(中国) Search Home Systems Trans-Pacific AAG AAG Cable Cut Offshore Vietnam on Jan. 5 AAG Cable Cut Offshore Vietnam on Jan. 5 Details By Winston Qiu Winston Qiu Category: AAG 12 January 2015 According to Vietnamnet , the AAG submarine cable was cut at 8:04 am on January 5, at a point about 117km from the landing station in Vung Tau. It seems Vietnam ISPs have improved their network diversity and restoration of internet traffic. Vietnam internet was seriously disrupted by the frequent AAG cable cuts recently: On December 20, 2013 , the AAG broke at about 278km away from Vung Tau. It was repaired on January 4, 2014. On July 15, 2014, the cable broke at 18km off Vung Tau, and was repaired on July 27. On September 15, 2014 , a break occurred somewhere near the Vung Tau coast at 11:41 pm This has slowed down Internet services offered by Viettel and VNPT, FPT and STP On September 29, 2014 , a break was identified at about 68km from Hong Kong’s coast, while the repair of the above AAG cable cut occurred near the Vung Tau coast on September 15 was still going on. The frequent cuts of AAG cable in the past years, especially in its Vietnam branch, incurred blames on its poor design . So far, it seems Vietnam carriers have taken measures to mitigate the internet disruption due to AAG cable cut . It is said Vietnam carriers have acquired more than 100G capacity over the Vietnam-China land cable routes, via reciprocal deals in 2014. As a result, FPT Telecom has used land cables to forward traffic from the broken cable segment in order to minimize the impact of the incident. Viettel has adjusted interconnection capacity through the pan-Asian fiber-optic cable and the land cable to China Telecom and China Unicom. Besides, from January 10, Viettel included an additional 80Gbps for the route to Hong Kong and Singapore. With active measures, Vietnam internet has substantially restored from the AAG cable cut. original_text_zh: 发生了什么印度洋西部和印度洋中部这两个系统受到影响，服务于不同的路线：印度洋西部连接珀斯到印度尼西亚和新加坡，而印度洋中部则连接珀斯到悉尼、维多利亚和塔斯马尼亚。两者都发生了分流故障，即电缆外部绝缘层破裂，使海水接触到内部电源导体，导致沿其长度的光中继器电路短路。

article.content: This prompted an Australian Federal Police assessment and arriving days before a government-funded paper argued Australia should position itself as the region’s safest place to land a cable. What happened Indigo West and Indigo Central, the two systems affected, serve different routes: Indigo West connects Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, while Indigo Central links Perth to Sydney, Victoria and Tasmania. Both developed shunt faults, where a breach in a cable’s outer insulation allows seawater to reach the internal power conductor, shorting the circuit that powers the optical repeaters along its length. The faults occurred inside the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone, a corridor extending roughly 100-112km offshore where anchoring and seabed-contact activities are restricted. SUBCO founder and co-chief executive Bevan Slattery raised the issue publicly, describing the faults as occurring “straight after each other and in close proximity to each other.” He flagged what he called suspicious or coincidental vessel activity near the location and timing of the faults, but was careful not to assign cause: “This could be a coincidence or an external aggression event,” he said, adding that root cause won’t be confirmed until the cable is physically recovered, since neither Indigo system has FibreSense monitoring installed. The Australian Federal Police confirmed on 11 August that it had received a report of crime and was assessing the information provided. It has not characterised the incident as sabotage, named a vessel, or confirmed a cause. Repairs are being planned through Indigo’s marine maintenance operator, with an estimated completion date of 26 August, subject to clearance, logistics and weather. Why attribution remains genuinely uncertain The instinct to read deliberate action into two near-simultaneous faults inside a protected zone is understandable, but the base rate cuts against it. The International Cable Protection Committee estimates that roughly 70-80% of global cable faults are caused by fishing gear and ship anchors, ordinary accidents rather than sabotage. This same Perth protection zone has direct precedent for exactly that outcome: in 2021, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau found a vessel had damaged cables here after dragging its anchor, and the AFP later charged that ship’s master. Independent vessel-tracking analysis has added a layer of scrutiny without resolving the question. Maritime intelligence firm Windward ran a multi-sensor review combining AIS behavioural history, electro-optical imagery and synthetic aperture radar, and found a vessel whose movements aligned with the timing and location of the damage. No vessel has been named publicly, and alignment in time and space does not establish cause. Why the timing matters more than the incident itself The faults landed just days before the ANU National Security College published a government-funded paper making the case that Australia should market itself as the Indo-Pacific’s preferred, safest cable-landing hub. The paper, produced under a Department of Defence strategic policy grant, argues that Australia’s political stability, legal protections and distance from contested maritime chokepoints position it to capture landing stations, repair infrastructure and route diversity that hyperscalers are increasingly seeking as they route around less stable waters. That argument aligns with the 2024 New York Joint Statement, a commitment endorsed by the US, Australia, the EU and the UK to favour low-risk cable providers and coordinate repair and maintenance practices. The Perth incident functions, whether by coincidence or not, as an unplanned early test of whether that framework holds up in practice: a live investigation, a firm repair timeline, and a protection zone whose enforcement is now under fresh scrutiny, all playing out just as the policy case for Australia’s hub ambitions was published. Google, Meta and other hyperscalers are already redrawing Indo-Pacific cable routes to avoid geopolitical chokepoints, part of the broader shift toward hyperscaler-led cable investment reshaping the region’s connectivity logic . original_text: Earlier this week, Bevan Slattery, the chief executive of subsea cable company SubCo, announced that two cables had experienced faults over the weekend. He deemed it a 'concerning development' because these 'submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation'. Slattery called on federal police to investigate the issue urgently. The subsea cable damage occurred within the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone, an area specifically designed to keep these cables safe.
original_text_zh: 本周早些时候，海底电缆公司SubCo的首席执行官Bevan Slattery宣布，上周末两条电缆出现故障。他认为这是一个'令人担忧的发展'，因为这些'海底电缆是我们国家的数字命脉'。Slattery呼吁联邦警察紧急调查此事。海底电缆损坏发生在珀斯海底电缆保护区，这是一个专门为保护这些电缆安全而设计的区域。

article.content: JEAN-SEBASTIEN EVRARD/Stringer/Getty Earlier this week, Bevan Slattery, the chief executive of subsea cable company SubCo, announced that two cables had experienced faults over the weekend. He deemed it a “concerning development” because these “submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation”. Slattery called on federal police to investigate the issue urgently . The subsea cable damage occurred within the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone , an area specifically designed to keep these cables safe. However, this safe zone extends over 100 kilometers offshore with the cables on the seabed, making them difficult to monitor and access. But there is a way Australia can practically safeguard these cables. Connecting us to the rest of the world Australia is connected to the global internet by fewer than two dozen undersea fibre optic cables, which carry more than 95% of our international internet traffic. Each cable has multiple strands of optical fibre – structured glass about an eighth of a millimetre across – and can carry more than 20 terabits per second. In other words, two of these fibres could carry all of the National Broadband Network’s data . The Indigo West and Indigo Central cables that were affected connect Perth to Sydney, and Perth to Jakarta and Singapore. These are part of a web of fibre optic cables that connect Australia to the world. Australia’s access to the global internet depends on a surprisingly small number of undersea cables – just 22 are connected or currently being built . Satellites are valuable for connecting remote areas, but they cannot yet carry anything like the enormous amount of data that travels through these cables. This map shows the approximate location of international submarine cables presently landing in Australia. Australian Communications and Media Authority What could have caused the damage? Slattery called the issues a “ shunt fault ”. This is where the electrical part of the cable is damaged, degrading performance or stopping the cable from working entirely. Subsea optical cables are able to span thousands of kilometres due to the use of optical amplifiers which boost the signal every 50 to 100 kilometres. These optical amplifiers need electrical power to run, and so high-voltage direct current power is transmitted through metal wires alongside the glass optical fibres. There can be multiple causes of shunt faults that short out this power supply. There is increasing concern about deliberate interference. But most often these faults are accidental , caused by anchors or trawler nets dragging along the seafloor . Slattery said we “will not know the root cause” of the fault “until the cable is recovered during repair”. But how can we more effectively monitor these cables? Home-grown tech to keep us connected to the world Distributed acoustic sensing is a laser technology that can sense vibrations travelling across fibre optic cables. It is an evolving technology only recently adopted by fibre optic communications companies for monitoring their infrastructure. You can think of this technology a bit like shouting “coo-ee”: listening for the echoes can tell you something about what they reflected off. Similarly, distributed acoustic sensing measures light “echoing” off small changes along the length of a fibre. Crucially, it can sense the environment around the fibre to tell us things about vessel activity, seabed disturbances, and other physical interactions near the cable. The technology can also be used to map the structure of the soil and rock around the fibre, or to monitor and provide early warning of earthquakes and tsunamis. Slattery said that if distributed acoustic sensing had been installed on the affected cables, it would have been possible to identify the vessel responsible for the fault almost instantly. He also said that because the technology is installed on nearby unaffected cables in the same area, “we can confirm no seabed activity around or near” those other cables. Working towards more resilient national infrastructure Distributed acoustic sensing can provide both environmental monitoring of the world around us and a way to safeguard key national infrastructure. Our team’s work has also shown that this evolving technology and high speed data can simultaneously work right next to each other in the same fibre . This is important as telcos have stringent requirements on keeping data flowing through these cables, with heavy penalties for non-compliance. We think we can help get more distributed acoustic sensing into our fibres in two ways: by demonstrating it can live side-by-side in modern optical communications systems with data, and by leveraging optical microcomb technologies to make the technology smaller, better, and perhaps cheaper. Our research is showing that the existing fibres that connect Australia to the rest of the world could carry significantly more data than they are currently. They could also reveal new insights about the world around us. By making this technology affordable and deployable, we will make Australia’s future communications networks not only faster, but safer and more resilient. article.content: JEAN-SEBASTIEN EVRARD/Stringer/Getty Earlier this week, Bevan Slattery, the chief executive of subsea cable company SubCo, announced that two cables had experienced faults over the weekend. He deemed it a “concerning development” because these “submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation”. Slattery called on federal police to investigate the issue urgently . The subsea cable damage occurred within the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone , an area specifically designed to keep these cables safe. However, this safe zone extends over 100 kilometers offshore with the cables on the seabed, making them difficult to monitor and access. But there is a way Australia can practically safeguard these cables. Connecting us to the rest of the world Australia is connected to the global internet by fewer than two dozen undersea fibre optic cables, which carry more than 95% of our international internet traffic. Each cable has multiple strands of optical fibre – structured glass about an eighth of a millimetre across – and can carry more than 20 terabits per second. In other words, two of these fibres could carry all of the National Broadband Network’s data . The Indigo West and Indigo Central cables that were affected connect Perth to Sydney, and Perth to Jakarta and Singapore. These are part of a web of fibre optic cables that connect Australia to the world. Australia’s access to the global internet depends on a surprisingly small number of undersea cables – just 22 are connected or currently being built . Satellites are valuable for connecting remote areas, but they cannot yet carry anything like the enormous amount of data that travels through these cables. This map shows the approximate location of international submarine cables presently landing in Australia. Australian Communications and Media Authority What could have caused the damage? Slattery called the issues a “ shunt fault ”. This is where the electrical part of the cable is damaged, degrading performance or stopping the cable from working entirely. Subsea optical cables are able to span thousands of kilometres due to the use of optical amplifiers which boost the signal every 50 to 100 kilometres. These optical amplifiers need electrical power to run, and so high-voltage direct current power is transmitted through metal wires alongside the glass optical fibres. There can be multiple causes of shunt faults that short out this power supply. There is increasing concern about deliberate interference. But most often these faults are accidental , caused by anchors or trawler nets dragging along the seafloor . Slattery said we “will not know the root cause” of the fault “until the cable is recovered during repair”. But how can we more effectively monitor these cables? Home-grown tech to keep us connected to the world Distributed acoustic sensing is a laser technology that can sense vibrations travelling across fibre optic cables. It is an evolving technology only recently adopted by fibre optic communications companies for monitoring their infrastructure. You can think of this technology a bit like shouting “coo-ee”: listening for the echoes can tell you something about what they reflected off. Similarly, distributed acoustic sensing measures light “echoing” off small changes along the length of a fibre. Crucially, it can sense the environment around the fibre to tell us things about vessel activity, seabed disturbances, and other physical interactions near the cable. The technology can also be used to map the structure of the soil and rock around the fibre, or to monitor and provide early warning of earthquakes and tsunamis. Slattery said that if distributed acoustic sensing had been installed on the affected cables, it would have been possible to identify the vessel responsible for the fault almost instantly. He also said that because the technology is installed on nearby unaffected cables in the same area, “we can confirm no seabed activity around or near” those other cables. Working towards more resilient national infrastructure Distributed acoustic sensing can provide both environmental monitoring of the world around us and a way to safeguard key national infrastructure. Our team’s work has also shown that this evolving technology and high speed data can simultaneously work right next to each other in the same fibre . This is important as telcos have stringent requirements on keeping data flowing through these cables, with heavy penalties for non-compliance. We think we can help get more distributed acoustic sensing into our fibres in two ways: by demonstrating it can live side-by-side in modern optical communications systems with data, and by leveraging optical microcomb technologies to make the technology smaller, better, and perhaps cheaper. Our research is showing that the existing fibres that connect Australia to the rest of the world could carry significantly more data than they are currently. They could also reveal new insights about the world around us. By making this technology affordable and deployable, we will make Australia’s future communications networks not only faster, but safer and more resilient. article.content: Home News Technology Telco/ISP AFP assessing report in connection with Perth cable faults By Andrew Colley Aug 11 2026 6:42AM Singapore-Perth link goes dark after shunt faults detected. The Australian Federal Police is assessing a report of a potential crime after the owner of two undersea cables laid in protection zones near Perth revealed faults commonly attributed to ship activity. Bevan Slattery, co-chief and founder of SUBCO, which owns the two Indigo cable systems, confirmed to iTnews that the company reported the incidents to the AFP which, he said, occurred near each other and at a similar time. Slattery first raised the alarm about the incidents in a post on LinkedIn on the weekend, shortly after SUBCO detected “shunt faults” on its Indigo West and Indigo Central cable systems, which together connect Singapore and Sydney with a landing at Perth in-between. Shunt faults in undersea cables refer to a condition where the outer insulating layers of the line become damaged exposing the interior components to sea water and are commonly attributed to ships' anchors and fishing activity. A spokesperson for the AFP told iTnews that the agency was looking into the incident but stopped short of saying it is actively investigating it as a crime. “The AFP has received a report of crime in relation to this matter. This report is currently being assessed based on the information provided. Further comment will be made at an appropriate time,” the spokesperson said. In the LinkedIn post, Slattery pointed to a ship tracking chart showing what he described as “suspicious/coincidental” vessel activity in the area. However, he stopped short of declaring that the cables had been deliberately damaged. “This could be a coincidence or an external aggression event,” Slattery wrote, explaining that the cause of the fault would have been known instantly had the cables been monitored using FibreSense, an advanced detection system used on some of SUBCO’s other undersea cables. “Indigo West and Central do not have FiberSense installed and, unfortunately, the consortium will not know the root cause until the cable is recovered during repair,” he wrote. Nevertheless, Slattery said that it was still important that authorities investigate as it may be the second time such an incident has occurred in a cable protection zone. “This maybe a coincidence, but it’s important for the Australian Federal Police to investigate the issue urgently,” Slattery wrote. Regional internet provider AusInternet, which uses the Indigo West cable, has been advising of an outage on the link on its website since Saturday evening, saying that it has been routing traffic around the apparent break. Early yesterday it was advising customers that the earliest fix to the cable was expected August 26. “The Indigo team has engaged their marine maintenance operator for vessel allocation and planning of the repairs. ETA is on August 26 2026. All timelines remain subject to clearance, logistics arrangement and weather conditions,” it advised. Slattery said that SUBCO would be following up its report to the AFP with more information soon. Add iTnews as your trusted source Got a news tip for our journalists? original_text: Indigo West and Indigo Central, the two systems affected, serve different routes: Indigo West connects Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, while Indigo Central links Perth to Sydney, Victoria and Tasmania. Both developed shunt faults, where a breach in a cable’s outer insulation allows seawater to reach the internal power conductor, shorting the circuit that powers the optical repeaters along its length.
original_text_zh: 受影响的Indigo West和Indigo Central系统服务于不同的路线：Indigo West连接珀斯与印度尼西亚和新加坡，而Indigo Central连接珀斯与悉尼、维多利亚和塔斯马尼亚。两者都出现了分流故障，即电缆外部绝缘层破损导致海水渗入内部电源导体，短路为沿电缆长度提供电力的光中继器供电的电路。

article.content: This prompted an Australian Federal Police assessment and arriving days before a government-funded paper argued Australia should position itself as the region’s safest place to land a cable. What happened Indigo West and Indigo Central, the two systems affected, serve different routes: Indigo West connects Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, while Indigo Central links Perth to Sydney, Victoria and Tasmania. Both developed shunt faults, where a breach in a cable’s outer insulation allows seawater to reach the internal power conductor, shorting the circuit that powers the optical repeaters along its length. The faults occurred inside the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone, a corridor extending roughly 100-112km offshore where anchoring and seabed-contact activities are restricted. SUBCO founder and co-chief executive Bevan Slattery raised the issue publicly, describing the faults as occurring “straight after each other and in close proximity to each other.” He flagged what he called suspicious or coincidental vessel activity near the location and timing of the faults, but was careful not to assign cause: “This could be a coincidence or an external aggression event,” he said, adding that root cause won’t be confirmed until the cable is physically recovered, since neither Indigo system has FibreSense monitoring installed. The Australian Federal Police confirmed on 11 August that it had received a report of crime and was assessing the information provided. It has not characterised the incident as sabotage, named a vessel, or confirmed a cause. Repairs are being planned through Indigo’s marine maintenance operator, with an estimated completion date of 26 August, subject to clearance, logistics and weather. Why attribution remains genuinely uncertain The instinct to read deliberate action into two near-simultaneous faults inside a protected zone is understandable, but the base rate cuts against it. The International Cable Protection Committee estimates that roughly 70-80% of global cable faults are caused by fishing gear and ship anchors, ordinary accidents rather than sabotage. This same Perth protection zone has direct precedent for exactly that outcome: in 2021, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau found a vessel had damaged cables here after dragging its anchor, and the AFP later charged that ship’s master. Independent vessel-tracking analysis has added a layer of scrutiny without resolving the question. Maritime intelligence firm Windward ran a multi-sensor review combining AIS behavioural history, electro-optical imagery and synthetic aperture radar, and found a vessel whose movements aligned with the timing and location of the damage. No vessel has been named publicly, and alignment in time and space does not establish cause. Why the timing matters more than the incident itself The faults landed just days before the ANU National Security College published a government-funded paper making the case that Australia should market itself as the Indo-Pacific’s preferred, safest cable-landing hub. The paper, produced under a Department of Defence strategic policy grant, argues that Australia’s political stability, legal protections and distance from contested maritime chokepoints position it to capture landing stations, repair infrastructure and route diversity that hyperscalers are increasingly seeking as they route around less stable waters. That argument aligns with the 2024 New York Joint Statement, a commitment endorsed by the US, Australia, the EU and the UK to favour low-risk cable providers and coordinate repair and maintenance practices. The Perth incident functions, whether by coincidence or not, as an unplanned early test of whether that framework holds up in practice: a live investigation, a firm repair timeline, and a protection zone whose enforcement is now under fresh scrutiny, all playing out just as the policy case for Australia’s hub ambitions was published. article.content: This prompted an Australian Federal Police assessment and arriving days before a government-funded paper argued Australia should position itself as the region’s safest place to land a cable. What happened Indigo West and Indigo Central, the two systems affected, serve different routes: Indigo West connects Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, while Indigo Central links Perth to Sydney, Victoria and Tasmania. Both developed shunt faults, where a breach in a cable’s outer insulation allows seawater to reach the internal power conductor, shorting the circuit that powers the optical repeaters along its length. The faults occurred inside the Perth Submarine Cable Protection Zone, a corridor extending roughly 100-112km offshore where anchoring and seabed-contact activities are restricted. SUBCO founder and co-chief executive Bevan Slattery raised the issue publicly, describing the faults as occurring “straight after each other and in close proximity to each other.” He flagged what he called suspicious or coincidental vessel activity near the location and timing of the faults, but was careful not to assign cause: “This could be a coincidence or an external aggression event,” he said, adding that root cause won’t be confirmed until the cable is physically recovered, since neither Indigo system has FibreSense monitoring installed. The Australian Federal Police confirmed on 11 August that it had received a report of crime and was assessing the information provided. It has not characterised the incident as sabotage, named a vessel, or confirmed a cause. Repairs are being planned through Indigo’s marine maintenance operator, with an estimated completion date of 26 August, subject to clearance, logistics and weather. Why attribution remains genuinely uncertain The instinct to read deliberate action into two near-simultaneous faults inside a protected zone is understandable, but the base rate cuts against it. The International Cable Protection Committee estimates that roughly 70-80% of global cable faults are caused by fishing gear and ship anchors, ordinary accidents rather than sabotage. This same Perth protection zone has direct precedent for exactly that outcome: in 2021, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau found a vessel had damaged cables here after dragging its anchor, and the AFP later charged that ship’s master. Independent vessel-tracking analysis has added a layer of scrutiny without resolving the question. Maritime intelligence firm Windward ran a multi-sensor review combining AIS behavioural history, electro-optical imagery and synthetic aperture radar, and found a vessel whose movements aligned with the timing and location of the damage. No vessel has been named publicly, and alignment in time and space does not establish cause. Why the timing matters more than the incident itself The faults landed just days before the ANU National Security College published a government-funded paper making the case that Australia should market itself as the Indo-Pacific’s preferred, safest cable-landing hub. The paper, produced under a Department of Defence strategic policy grant, argues that Australia’s political stability, legal protections and distance from contested maritime chokepoints position it to capture landing stations, repair infrastructure and route diversity that hyperscalers are increasingly seeking as they route around less stable waters. That argument aligns with the 2024 New York Joint Statement, a commitment endorsed by the US, Australia, the EU and the UK to favour low-risk cable providers and coordinate repair and maintenance practices. The Perth incident functions, whether by coincidence or not, as an unplanned early test of whether that framework holds up in practice: a live investigation, a firm repair timeline, and a protection zone whose enforcement is now under fresh scrutiny, all playing out just as the policy case for Australia’s hub ambitions was published. Google, Meta and other hyperscalers are already redrawing Indo-Pacific cable routes to avoid geopolitical chokepoints, part of the broader shift toward hyperscaler-led cable investment reshaping the region’s connectivity logic . original_text: Pakistan’s telecom authority reiterated on Wednesday that faults in two international undersea Internet cables are to blame for slow Internet across the country, saying that one of them is likely to be repaired by early October. “The ongoing Internet slowdown across the country is mainly due to fault in two (SMW4, AAE-1) of the seven international submarine cables connecting Pakistan internationally,” the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) said in a message. “It is updated that fault in SMW-4 submarine cable is likely to be repaired by early October 2024,” the authority added.

accident_location: Off the coast of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
original_text: On 12 May 2024, two fiber optic submarine cables—SEACOM and EASSy—were damaged off the coast of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, significantly reducing Internet connectivity in multiple East African countries. The cause of the damage is a suspected dragging ship anchor, a common source of submarine cable cuts. All cables were repaired as of 3 June 2024—approximately three weeks after the initial damage.
original_text_zh: 2024年5月12日，南非夸祖鲁-纳塔尔省海岸附近的两条海底光缆——SEACOM与EASSy——遭到破坏，导致多个东非国家的互联网连接大幅中断。破坏原因疑似为船只拖锚所致（这是海底电缆中断的常见诱因）。截至2024年6月3日，即受损约三周后，所有光缆均已修复完成。
title: 2024 East Africa Submarine Cable Outage Report.txt
url: 2024 East Africa Submarine Cable Outage Report.txt

affected_area: Connections between Asia and Europe, and Yemen’s waters
original_text: Repairs have finally commenced on three subsea telecommunications cables that were damaged in the Red Sea in February, even as Houthi militants escalate their attacks on ships in the area. The AAE-1 cable, a 25 000km fibre-optic link between Asia and Europe, was repaired by a ship owned by E-Marine, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi-based Emirates Telecommunications Group. The cable came online this week, a Yemeni government official said. The same ship, Niwa, remains in Yemeni waters to repair the remaining two cables, Seacom and EIG. Repairs to the cables have depended on gaining access to infrastructure in Yemen’s waters, a task complicated by the country’s split government and the fact the Red Sea is a conflict zone.

article.content: Nigeria’s digital economy is becoming too important to depend on infrastructure that can fail at a single point. The question is no longer simply whether the country has enough fibre, submarine cables, data centres, mobile networks and international capacity. It is whether those systems are sufficiently independent to keep essential services operating when one component fails, or when an extraordinary regulatory intervention restricts access to communications infrastructure. That is the real meaning of network resilience: multiple routes, geographically diverse infrastructure, spare capacity, tested failover and safeguards that prevent one disruption from becoming a national digital crisis. The distinction matters because Nigeria has already seen how apparent redundancy can conceal common vulnerabilities. Advertisement In March 2024, a suspected underwater rock slide off Cote d’ivoire damaged four major submarine cables, ACE, SAT-3, WACS and MainOne, disrupted connectivity across several West African countries. The Internet Society found that the cables converged around the same physical area off Côte d’Ivoire, creating a common point of failure. Nigeria was among the affected countries. The lesson is straightforward: five cables are not necessarily five independent routes. If multiple networks converge at the same landing zone, share the same terrestrial corridor or depend on the same metropolitan infrastructure, an apparently diversified system can still fail together. Nigeria therefore needs diversity in the physical sense: different submarine routes and landing points, separate terrestrial backhaul corridors, resilient Internet exchanges, alternative international transit paths and enough spare capacity to absorb traffic when one route is lost. Advertisement The terrestrial network presents an equally serious vulnerability. The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) reported more than 5,000 fibre-cut incidents in the first six months of 2026, attributed largely to road construction, excavation and related civil works. The Commission has consequently worked with the Federal Ministry of Works on measures to protect fibre during road projects. This is more than an operational inconvenience. Fibre now carries the infrastructure of banking, digital payments, commerce, healthcare, education, government and communications. The NCC’s designation of telecommunications networks, fibre-optic cables, data centres, towers and Internet exchange points as Critical National Information Infrastructure recognises precisely that wider dependence. But another source of systemic disruption deserves attention: emergency government intervention. Under Section 148 of the Nigerian Communications Act 2003 , the NCC has emergency powers that can, in specified circumstances involving a public emergency or public safety, include suspending a licence, taking temporary control of network facilities, withdrawing the use of services or facilities from a licensee, person or the general public, and issuing orders affecting communications. These are statutory emergency powers intended for exceptional circumstances. National security and public safety can legitimately require extraordinary action. But in a digital economy, the exercise of such powers can itself become a source of systemic disruption. That does not make the powers illegitimate. It makes the safeguards surrounding them part of digital resilience. A network can have multiple cables and fibre routes yet still become unavailable to large numbers of users if an intervention affects several providers or a significant geographic area. The resilience question therefore has to extend beyond: Advertisement What happens if the cable is cut? It must also ask: What happens when access to the network is deliberately restricted, and what protections exist for essential services and legitimate users? That question is particularly important because the same legal framework that provides emergency intervention powers also recognises the need for telecommunications networks to survive crises. Section 149 of the NCA provides for disaster plans relating to the survivability and recovery of services and network facilities during disasters, crises or civil emergencies. The policy objective should consequently be continuity, not simply restoration. Hospitals, emergency responders, banks, payment systems, utilities and government services cannot always wait for a network to be restored after disruption. Critical users need layered continuity arrangements: alternative connectivity, independent routes, emergency communications and tested procedures for operating through disruption. That principle should apply whether the disruption comes from a submarine cable fault, a road construction accident, equipment failure, vandalism, a cyber incident or a lawful emergency intervention. There is also an important regulatory distinction between protecting the state from communications-related risks and protecting society from unnecessary communications disruption. Both are legitimate public interests. The challenge is to ensure that measures taken in pursuit of security or public safety are appropriately targeted and accompanied, where practicable, by safeguards for essential services, clear authorisation, defined duration, communication to affected stakeholders and post-event review. Nigeria’s digital economy cannot afford to treat this as an abstract question. A communications interruption can mean failed payments, interrupted business operations, inaccessible government platforms, disrupted healthcare communications and lost working hours. The economic consequences can extend far beyond the telecommunications companies whose networks are directly affected. This is why the country’s next phase of infrastructure development should measure resilience, not simply capacity. Project BRIDGE, which is intended to substantially expand Nigeria’s national fibre backbone, presents an opportunity improve route diversity, presents an opportunity to embed that principle into the network now being built. The important metric should not simply be kilometres of fibre laid, but the number of genuinely independent paths connecting critical locations and the amount of traffic that can survive the loss of any one route. The same principle applies internationally. More submarine cables are valuable, but their resilience depends on where they land, how they are connected inland and whether alternative routes can actually carry traffic when one system fails. Nigeria should therefore begin to think of digital infrastructure in layers: physical diversity — different cables, ducts and corridors; technical diversity — alternative networks, power supplies, data centres and failover systems; geographic diversity — infrastructure that does not converge unnecessarily on the same locations; service continuity, arrangements protecting critical economic and public services; and regulatory safeguards, ensuring that emergency powers are exercised within a framework that recognises the consequences of communications disruption. The NCC’s major-outage reporting requirements provide a useful foundation for identifying recurring physical and operational weaknesses. The next step is to use that information to identify systemic dependencies, the places where several apparently independent networks remain exposed to the same failure. The principle is ultimately simple. Nigeria cannot eliminate every threat to its digital infrastructure. Cables will fail. Fibre will be cut. Equipment will malfunction. Power will fail. Security emergencies will occur. Government may sometimes need to intervene. Resilience means ensuring that none of these events automatically becomes a national digital failure. That requires more than building more infrastructure. It requires building infrastructure with independent routes, spare capacity, tested alternatives and appropriate legal and institutional safeguards. Nigeria’s digital transformation has reached the point where connectivity is no longer merely a telecommunications service. It is economic infrastructure. And an economy built on digital infrastructure cannot afford a single point of failure, whether that point is a cable, a road corridor, a data centre, a network operator or an emergency intervention that could have wider consequences for service continuity.
article.title: Why Nigeria’s Digital Economy Cannot Afford a Single Point of Failure

article.content: In Islamabad, two fiber-optic cables linking Pakistan globally have been severed from separate locations. This incident is expected to cause significant disruptions for internet users across the country. According to sources within the Telecommunications Authority, the damage to these major fiber optic cables will impact both mobile and landline internet users, leading to difficulties in accessing the internet. Both the SMW-4 and SMW-Fa cables have been cut along routes from Dubai and Oman, and repairs have not yet been completed. Mobile phone companies have notified users via SMS about anticipated slow internet speeds.
article.title: Internet again down in Pakistan: Here’s why

The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan which includes the Kinmen and Penghu islands, all of which lie in the Taiwan Strait. The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by 2 submarine cables, Taima No. 2 and Taima No. 3, and soon Taima No. 4. The Taiwan Strait is a relatively shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this sea floor are vulnerable to mishaps with ship-based activity, such as being snagged by fishing equipment or ship anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky in that respect. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been 4 more major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025. But that’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered a large number of faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables as well as undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, that’s a very unlucky track record. These days there is a large volume of subsea communications cables, estimated at a total of some 1.5 million kilometres, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1). They are not just important, but they are absolutely critical to the world’s telecommunication service. If they are put out of service for any reason, then our inventory of satellite systems simply could not step in and carry the massive traffic loads that are carried by this cable system. In such a catastrophic scenario there are likely to be affected communities that would be totally isolated, and this would have severe logistic and economic ramifications. Figure 1: Submarine Cables, October 2026, https://www.submarinecablemap.com/ , Telegeography These days we regard this collection of submarine cable systems as part of our portfolio of critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take some care to make these systems as resilient as we can make them. At the same time, modern warfare has its elements of deliberate disruption of communications systems, so the foes that are working against the continued working of these cable systems are not only the whims of geology and the vagaries of accidental mishaps with ships, but also deliberate actions intended to sabotage these cables. In 1914, on the night of the 4 th of August, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German trans-Atlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram . This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York. Protecting the Cable These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable to various mishaps, whether it’s geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips, or being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor, or the result of deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment. How can cables defend against such risks? An obvious action is to take the inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath and wrap it in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour cladding. This is intended to reduce its vulnerability to various hazards but mostly shipping mishaps (as shown in Figure 2). Figure 2: Cross-section of a submarine cable (from Telegeography ) This image of a cross-section of a submarine cable is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of a submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components of optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath, used to power the cable repeaters, and wrapped in polyethylene. It has no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose. The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically somewhat drab secured facilities that have reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point that does not have a large volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and preferably at a location that rises steeply from the deep-sea floor. As cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better. Figure 3: Cable Landing Station (from https://www.vertiv.com/en-anz/solutions/cable-landing-stations/ ) Many countries also declare “Cable Protection Zones” as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas. Cable Routing Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are a number of objectives in a cable route, and it’s typical that not all of these objectives can be optimised at the same time. The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length costs in terms of capital cost, light budgets and repeater placement, and increases end-to-end signal delay. Geology also plays a role, and cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair. Sometimes there are geographic “choke points” through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which some 16 cables also pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection. Figure 4: Cable Routes in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, https://www.submarinecablemap.com/ , Telegeography There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for some 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait which also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping. Figure 5: Cable Routes in the Singapore Strait, https://www.submarinecablemap.com/ , Telegeography Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all of the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back to an operational state. Figure 6: Cable Routes in the Luzon Strait, https://www.submarinecablemap.com/ , Telegeography The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented from the Ukraine war. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict in Ukraine make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance. Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to a number of FCC constraints, including banning the use of equipment or services from companies the FCC has deemed as posing a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable lands in a country that the US deems to be a foreign adversary. Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Cable Faults Around 200 submarine cable faults are reported worldwide each year, a figure that the International Cable Protection Committee notes has stayed broadly steady in recent years even as the total cable inventory increases. The cables themselves are remarkably reliable. It is the maritime traffic above them that is the cause of most of the problems. Some 86% of cable faults are likely due to fishing activity or anchoring, and fishing activity is around twice as prevalent as anchoring incidents. Geological events, such as submarine landslides and seabed movement, account for about 7% of cable faults, cable abrasion for 4 percent, and component failure (in repeaters) for only 4 percent. With the high correlation of faults to maritime activity, it is unsurprising that just under one-half of cable faults occur in territorial waters and most of the remainder occur in exclusive economic zones, with just 2 percent on the high seas. Cables are most vulnerable close to shore, in shallow water, where fishing is concentrated, where ships anchor, and where the cable has to come ashore at a landing station alongside every other cable serving that coast. The deep ocean, where there is little in the way of seabed fishing activity or ships anchoring, is the safest location for a cable. National jurisdictions do not stop at the low tide mark of a territory, but extend out into the sea and the seafloor. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea defined sovereign territorial waters as a 12-mile zone extending out from a country’s coast. Every coastal country has exclusive economic rights to the oil, gas, and other resources in the seabed up to 200 nautical miles from shore or to the outer edge of the continental margin, whichever is the further, subject to an overall limit of 350 nautical miles (650 km) from the coast or 100 nautical miles (185 km) beyond the 2,500-metre isobath (a line connecting equal points of water depth). What does this mean for submarine cables? At the point where the cable enters territorial waters, any physical activity related to the cable requires the permission of the country. It also implies that all cable construction and repair operations carried out in these sovereign areas also require the permission of the country that has exclusive rights to the sea and seafloor. Location and Repair Locating a cable break is straightforward. An optical pulse will be reflected at the point of a cable break, which can provide the distance to the fault from the start of the cable with considerable precision. At that point it becomes a marine operation. A specialist cable repair ship has to be engaged, which, in turn, must obtain the relevant country’s permission to work at the location of the cable fault (don’t forget that only 2% of outages occur in international waters). Once at the break location, the repair vessel drags a grapnel along the seabed to hook the cable, cuts it, recovers one end, buoys it off, then recovers the other end. A new section is spliced into the cable aboard the ship in a jointing cabin, the fibre is fusion-spliced and tested, the joint rebuilt and sealed against pressure, and the repaired cable laid back down with enough slack to reach the seabed. The cost of a repair can vary greatly, depending on the location and depth of the fault, the nature of the contracted arrangements for cable repair, the amount of time the cable operator is willing to wait for a repair vessel and crew, and the weather. The cost of a cable repair would normally run in the vicinity of one half to one million dollars per repair. While the number of cables has grown, the time taken to obtain permission to operate repairs in territorial waters has generally increased. Industry data indicates repair response times have more than doubled over the past decade, and the longest single repair recorded in 2023 took 947 days, with the delay caused by waiting for permission to undertake the repair. Lurking behind the permission delay is this issue of repair vessels. The industry has roughly 60 ships capable of repairing a submarine cable, operated under maintenance agreements that pool the cost of running this fleet across cable owners for each geographic region. These collective Submarine Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreements are used in the Atlantic Ocean, the North American Western Coastal region, the Mediterranean, South East Asia and the Indian Ocean and Yokohama in the North Pacific. (Figure 7). Figure 7: Areas covered by the five “zone” agreements for pooled submarine cable maintenance and repair (from International Cable Protection Committee - https://www.iscpc.org/documents/?id=203) Analysis by TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics has found that around two-thirds of cable maintenance vessels will reach the end of their service lives by 2040, while total cable kilometres are projected to grow by about 48 percent over the same period. Closing that gap would take some $3 billion, entailing fifteen replacement ships plus five additional vessels simply to hold current service levels as the submarine cable network expands. The immediate problem is that nobody obviously owns this bill. Cable maintenance is funded through shared agreements that have been optimised for decades to be as cheap as possible, which worked when the fleet was young and is precisely the wrong structure for financing a fleet renewal. This is the core of the cable resilience problem. Adding cable routes is comparatively easy, because today’s hyperscale cloud companies fund much of the new construction themselves and have strong commercial reasons to do so. However, no individual cable is so critical that it can sustain a business case to operate a dedicated repair fleet, so the industry uses pooled resources, and such pooled resources typically suffer from under-investment. Sabotage or Accident? A rundown of recent cable outages includes: Subsea cables were damaged in October 2023 by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged NewNew Polar Bear operating in the Baltic Sea. Three cables in the Red Sea were cut in February 2024 by the drifting Rubymar vessel after it was struck by a missile. The C-Lion1 and the BCS East-West Interlink cables were cut in the Baltic in November 2024 with the Chinese bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 nearby. Four cables were damaged in December 2024, with anchor drag marks on the Baltic seabed and the Cook Islands-registered tanker Eagle S detained. Taiwan recorded incidents in January and February 2025 on the Matsu cables. Three major cables including SEA-ME-WE 4 and IMEWE were cut in the Red Sea in September 2025. Finland and Estonia lost connections again in December 2025, with anchor drag confirmed by March 2026 on Baltic cables. In August 2026, the Indigo West and Indigo Central cables off Perth were damaged with a UAE-managed tanker under investigation by Australian Federal Police. The outcomes are much less uniform than this list suggests. Swedish authorities found no conclusive evidence of wrongdoing in the Yi Peng 3 case and ruled the January 2025 Latvia to Gotland damage accidental. A Finnish court dismissed the case against the Eagle S captain in October 2025. United States and European officials concluded that several of the Baltic incidents were accidental rather than sabotage. The captain of the Hong Tai 58 was convicted in Taiwan and sentenced to three years over the Taiwan to Penghu No. 3 cable, and the NewNew Polar Bear captain faced criminal damage charges in Hong Kong. The April 2026 Matsu fault turned out to have been caused by the wreck of a stranded fishing boat shifting onto the cable. Anchor dragging is a common occurrence, particularly among poorly maintained merchant vessels in bad weather, which is why it accounts for a large share of ordinary faults every year and probably why investigators keep reaching inconclusive findings in good faith. However, the cluster of incidents in the Baltic and offshore from Taiwan is anomalous, and while individual cases have mostly not been proven to be deliberate, the cluster of outages is in itself a pointer to more deliberate acts of sabotage. Who is Responsible for Cable Resilience? Cable systems have changed in recent decades. The old telephone system regarded each cable system as a self-contained system and the cable owner was responsible for its own resilience, independent of any other cables that may exist on similar routes. The telephone’s data carriage system typically used a ring architecture, where any outage in the ring caused the traffic to flow along the other half of the ring. As long as the ring used diverse paths then any individual outage in the ring could be repaired immediately. However, the implication of this design was that the actual capacity of the system was double the usable capacity. The cost of using such a cable included a component that reflected this 50% carriage efficiency. In their search for cheaper services, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) wanted to purchase non-backed-up cable capacity, at a price that reflected this greater efficiency of cable use. They purchased this cheaper form of cable capacity on multiple cable systems. This implied that individual outages on non-backed-up cable systems caused a break in that cable’s service, but the ISP could re-route their traffic to use capacity that had been purchased on other cable systems which were not affected by the outage. For Internet traffic this failover function is readily achieved in the routing system. The overall outcome was that the responsibility for resilience shifted from the individual cable operator to the network operator. Cable outages would still cause a drop in available capacity, but as most Internet traffic is elastic, the drop in capacity would cause a drop in performance but not cause a complete shutdown. Resilience and National Critical Infrastructure Considerations Submarine cable systems are built by private consortia, repaired by private contracts that collectively fund the operation of a commercial repair fleet, regulated by coastal states individually, and governed internationally by international conventions drafted long before the internet existed. It would be good if permissions to repair submarine cables were granted in a streamlined manner so that the repair work was not stalled for months awaiting a nation’s approval to operate in their waters. It would be even better if emergency procedures were agreed in advance rather than negotiated during an outage. Collectively the industry needs to invest in repair capacity to upgrade an ageing repair fleet. Who undertakes this investment and how the repair capability is managed as a common asset are proving to be difficult issues. In the worst case it will be back to every cable for itself, and the inevitable outcome of higher costs and potentially slower repairs. Geographic choke points will persist, geology will not stop, extreme weather and changing sediment conditions will continue to pose a threat to these cables. Route diversity is an effective response to these challenges, but economic clustering plays a role in working against cable route diversity. Each cable would like to run through the shortest and cheapest route, and no cable is specifically motivated to spend additional sums to take a diverse route to the other existing cables. None of this is technologically difficult. But it can be institutionally and economically difficult, which is harder. Looking Forward The telephone company consortium model that funded and operated almost all of the world’s subsea cables some 30 years ago has not only come to an end, but the service life of the entire inventory of cables and service vessels that they operated is also coming to an end. Approximately a quarter of the world’s current subsea cable kilometres are projected to be decommissioned and retired by 2030. This massive retirement of capacity, amounting to 845,000 kilometres of subsea fibre-optic cables, is due to the end-of-life cycle for submarine infrastructure laid during the massive Internet boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Specifically, TAT-8 and TAT-14 in the Atlantic Ocean are being decommissioned, SEA-ME-WE-3, linking Europe to Asia, has been retired, and Japan-US and China-US have ended operations. In addition, more than one half of the current repair vessel fleet will have reached their retirement point by 2040. In their place are cable projects that are either fully funded or partially funded by the current US digital behemoths. This raises sovereign risk eyebrows in many countries, where the only communications conduits for a country are owned and operated by a foreign entity. It also raises the question of the sovereign control over the submarine repair vessel fleet and the existing maintenance pooling arrangements through submarine cable maintenance zones. By 2028 Google will own the largest set of cables, measured by kilometres, in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and based on current plans it will have more than 50% of the entire cable inventory under its control in the Indo-Pacific region. Similar centralization scenarios are playing out in the Atlantic Ocean as well. At this point the sovereign risk eyebrows should be hitting the ceiling, as such a dominant position gives this single company unilateral control over the maintenance arrangements and associated repair vessel operations for the entire world’s communications network. This is a serious issue for us, both as individuals and as a collection of national communities, as we try and preserve the integrity and utility of our common communications infrastructure. The stability and productivity of our societies rely on our ability to communicate with each other seamlessly, efficiently and privately. Passing the investment and operational costs of the public telecommunications services from private to public hands in the latter part of the 20th century was seen as an adroit move to obtain private finance to fund the re-invigoration of national telecommunications infrastructure as it shifted from time-based voice switching to a far larger packet switching architecture to support computer-mediated communications and service provision. However, we are seeing some more uncomfortable outcomes looming in the near future. It was thought that the discipline of competition would rein in the potential abuses by private operators in terms of abuse of users and the privileged position of the operator of a public communications service. But this was a vain hope, particularly in the global realm. Not only is the function of public telecommunications systems largely in private hands these days, we are seeing the core of the global telecommunications system being passed over to no more than a couple of private enterprises in its entirety, and likely no more than a single such entity in the near future. There is no competition. Their accountability is certainly not to any public entity, nor even to the population of users of the service. Their accountability is to their institutional investors to continually improve their value and profitability. Nothing else. So where does this leave the submarine cable system and the efforts to maintain its critical function with the appropriate levels of resilience that reflect their critical role in global communications? Outside the US, few individual countries, if any, have the wherewithal to respond in meaningful ways to this challenge. The EU has taken some action to contribute to funding a fleet of repair vessels and taken measures to improve surveillance on submarine cables as a matter of regional security, but no other countries appear to be following this lead. It would certainly be ironic if this EU money were to end up simply funding the maintenance of Google’s submarine cable assets! Back to the topic of cable resilience, viewed at a global level, communications resilience is largely an ocean infrastructure question. Answers to this question rely on detailed and current seabed surveys, shipping controls to prevent anchoring and seabed fishing in declared subsea cable protection zones, a distributed repair fleet and crews trained to perform repair tasks, with rapid clearance to operate in territorial waters. Some coordination of actions is necessary to open up diverse cable routes and avoid single points of vulnerability and potential failure. The global cloud, for all its connotations of weightless air, firmly rests on the solidity of the seabed, and it can be no more reliable than the conventions that we collectively adopt to look after it. By Geoff Huston , Author & Chief Scientist at APNIC — (The above views do not necessarily represent the views of the Asia Pacific Network Information Centre.) original_text: A physical fault occurred within the SMW5 submarine cable. Because of this fault, Transworld Associates (TWA) lost a significant portion of its international IP transit capacity. Therefore, users across the country experienced internet connectivity issues.
