article.content: The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has officially confirmed the full restoration of the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5) international submarine cable system. Consequently, internet traffic across Pakistan has returned to normal this morning, July 3, 2026. This development resolves the widespread internet disruption that affected users starting last night. Following the restoration, all services are now operating as usual. The connectivity issues began on Thursday night. A physical fault occurred within the SMW5 submarine cable. Because of this fault, Transworld Associates (TWA) lost a significant portion of its international IP transit capacity. Therefore, users across the country experienced internet connectivity issues. Fortunately, authorities took immediate steps to mitigate the impact. During the outage, providers rerouted internet traffic through alternate international links. This temporary measure successfully minimized service degradation while the main line remained down. Meanwhile, Transworld Associates (TWA) coordinated directly with the SMW5 Consortium to restore connectivity. Throughout the incident, the PTA monitored the situation closely. Furthermore, the regulatory body worked alongside TWA and other stakeholders to support the earliest possible restoration of services. Now, the SMW5 cable is fully operational again. PTA officials verify that internet services have stabilized, and routine traffic has resumed across Pakistan.

article.content: By Sibahle Malinga , ITWeb senior news journalist. Johannesburg, 19 Oct 2026 The undersea cable systems associated with Openserve’s South African infrastructure and international connectivity include the Equiano. Openserve is introducing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into its Network Operations Centre (NOC), to help detect potential fibre faults before they disrupt connectivity. This, as the telecommunications infrastructure provider works towards more autonomous network management. During Digital Council Africa’s Conext 2026 annual event, Dr Sunil Piyarlall, executive for network architecture and modelling at Openserve, delivered a keynote presentation titled: “The future of fibre: Building resilient, intelligent and scalable networks”. He noted the company is using fibre sensing technology to distinguish between normal activity around its fibre routes and vibrations that could indicate potential damage. Openserve’s NOC monitors connectivity across the company’s terrestrial fibre network, submarine cable infrastructure and satellite services, including its existing geostationary satellite connectivity. The undersea cable systems associated with Openserve’s South African infrastructure and international connectivity include: the Equiano, SAT-3/WASC, South Africa Far East cable, West Africa Cable System (WACS), and the EASSy submarine cable. See also SA fibre operators hit by dual submarine cable break Openserve diverts traffic after dual submarine cable break According to Piyarlall, the centre monitors national fibre routes, optical transport equipment, IP networks, internet breakout points and major customer networks to track performance, detect faults, maintain alternative routes and coordinate repairs, helping preserve domestic and international connectivity. He added that the emerging technologies being integrated into the centre can flag suspected interference so Openserve can investigate and take preventative action. “We're using fibre sensing. The technology allows the network to learn from vibration patterns over time, helping it identify unusual activity and alert teams to investigate before a fibre cable is damaged. “So, we know that if a car is going over the bridge and a fibre vibrates in a certain way it's normal traffic. The system learns that over time if someone's digging with a spade, it sends a very different type of sonar wave to alert us. “And that's AI starting to work, and then it would alert you and say we suspect something is happening at that point, please go have a look, and that is how we do preventative maintenance.” In March 2024, multiple undersea cable breaks off the coast of Côte d’Ivoire disrupted South Africa’s international internet connectivity, affecting mobile and fixed-line services, cloud platforms and online applications. The affected systems included the WACS, Africa Coast to Europe and SAT-3/WASC, alongside MainOne, which does not extend to South Africa. The damage was attributed to a suspected underwater landslide, and the loss of capacity forced network operators to reroute traffic through remaining connections. Dr Sunil Piyarlall, executive for network architecture and modelling at Openserve. (Image supplied) Widescale monitoring Piyarlall says the centre's highly-secure operating environment reflects the national importance of the infrastructure it oversees. The centre monitors millions of network elements, ranging from fibre-to-the-home optical terminals, to Ethernet access devices. Its monitoring responsibilities also extend to network equipment and environmental conditions at exchanges, including temperature levels that could affect operations. The facility uses a large video wall to display different parts of the network, enabling teams to monitor faults, network performance and major customer connections, he noted. The company employs more than 3 000 technicians on the ground to carry out installations, network assurance and repairs. Piyarlall said Openserve has sufficient technical resources, supplemented by subcontractors when additional support is required. “Openserve categorises faults according to severity, allowing teams to prioritise incidents that pose the greatest risk to connectivity. The operations centre is supported by a self-healing network designed to reroute traffic automatically when a fibre route fails. “So, as soon as a fibre breaks, that traffic is automatically routed onto another five and that incident gets flashed on our video wall and we got teams that start fixing the fibre that's broken.” However, the resilience of this arrangement depends on alternative routes remaining available and having sufficient capacity to carry diverted traffic. Piyarlall points to an incident in 2025 in which a fibre break in the Western Cape was followed by another break affecting a route in the Free State. The second incident occurred while teams were responding to the first fault, which was in a dangerous area requiring security support. “With two routes unavailable, traffic was diverted to the third route, which could not accommodate the full load. The disruption demonstrated the consequences of multiple failures affecting the same network and the importance of redundancy and sufficient capacity. “Openserve subsequently addressed the issue and has since upgraded its national transport network following a major outage.” Modern speed Openserve is introducing AI across several functions, particularly as it works towards autonomous network operations. However, Piyarlall says the technology’s effective deployment depends on modernising legacy infrastructure and ensuring network equipment can communicate with one another. The company is decommissioning much of its legacy infrastructure, including copper networks and exchanges, while refreshing equipment to support newer technologies. “We have started introducing it across processes: we run the process of our technicians and our specialists through machine learning. Telecommunications infrastructure requires substantial capital investment, and Openserve is continually refreshing equipment to maintain network efficiency and accommodate changing technology requirements.” The company expects fibre cables installed underground to last between 20 and 30 years, but the equipment operating alongside them changes much more frequently, he commented. Critical services Openserve is Telkom’s wholesale fibre and connectivity business, supplying network infrastructure through channels to the market, rather than dealing directly with every end customer. According to Telkom’s latest results for the quarter ended 30 June 2026, Openserve performed strongly, with revenue rising 5.6% to R3.32 billion, EBITDA increasing 6.7% to R1.10 billion and external revenue growing 18.2% year-on-year. During his presentation, Piyarlall explained the company’s fibre network spans more than 90 000km and could potentially reach eight million locations across SA, highlighting the scale of the wholesale network operator’s existing infrastructure. The eight-million-location estimate is based on mapping a 5km radius around the company’s fibre-ready nodes, according to Piyarlall. He said the calculation takes into account the network’s fibre infrastructure and its potential reach. “Openserve has fibre infrastructure in every municipality in the country, although some smaller municipalities do not have their own points-of-presence and receive connectivity from neighbouring municipalities. “Infrastructure plays an important role in supporting connectivity across multiple sectors of the economy, including financial services, fuel distribution and other services that depend on communications networks.” The network also has 34 internet breakout points across the country, access to three submarine cables and four international routes, with one route through Brazil under development. Piyarlall added the NOC's continuous monitoring and fault-management processes are central to maintaining network availability and limiting the impact of disruptions. Openserve continues to upgrade its infrastructure to support higher bandwidth requirements. Piyarlall stated the company has deployed 10Gbps passive optical network technology and has tested speeds of 50Gbps on its network in the Kruger National Park area. Wider deployment of higher-speed services to homes will depend partly on whether consumer devices and the market can make practical use of the additional capacity. “Openserve has also introduced fibre-to-the-room as an extension of fibre-to-the-home, targeting households where WiFi performance deteriorates in rooms far from the main router. The service uses fibre-connected access points to create a mesh network throughout a property.” Piyarlall says Openserve expects demand for such services to grow as consumers become more familiar with the benefits of consistent connectivity across larger homes. “For our network operations, the immediate focus remains on modernising infrastructure, using machine learning to identify potential faults and improving the ability to maintain connectivity before incidents affect customers,” he concluded. article.content: Memorandums Cable repairs: The case for a British sovereign capability The Memorandum | No. 53.2026 Liberty Hunter Oct 19, 2026 2 2 1 Share Image generated using Artificial Intelligence The Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy (JCNSS) has recommended that His Majesty’s (HM) Government acquire a sovereign capability for cable repair by 2030. With the United Kingdom (UK) already committed to resource sharing with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), how important is a sovereign capability for the security of British Critical Underwater Infrastructure (CUI), and what options does HM Government have? The necessity of cable repair capability In the early 20th century, British telecommunications companies championed the undersea cable industry, with giants such as Cable and Wireless operating 14 cable ships out of British ports by 1929. These ships, while private, could be requisitioned by the state in times of need – as would happen ten years later in 1939. The UK’s success in maintaining its CUI during both world wars owed much to the rapid response made possible by these privately owned, British-based assets. Today, the UK relies more heavily on CUI than ever before. Upwards of 97% of communications data transits the undersea cables that also carry the data underpinning the economy. Indeed, £1.4 trillion in daily British transactions – 23% of the world’s total – relies on subsea cables. In peace time, damage is rare and manageable. As Al Carns, then Minister for the Armed Forces, told the JCNSS in May 2025, the UK averages five cable breaks a year, 80% accidentally caused by routine shipping (primarily anchor drag). These breaks are generally repaired within eight days – a rate three times faster than the global average. However, a wartime precedent for the strategic importance of cable repair means that Britain cannot take peacetime performance for granted. Severing communications cables has historically been an efficient way to disarm and disorient an adversary early in a conflict before other forms of engagement occur. As an island nation with security commitments across the Irish Sea, the High North, and to European allies, the UK’s posture needs to be agile and proactive; ready to respond quickly to several simultaneous incidents at once, and across a substantial geographic range. What is available today? Multilateral cooperation towards defence of CUI has increased significantly over the past ten years, providing different routes for Britain to contribute both to its own and to allied CUI protection. The UK currently has access to just three cable repair ships through the Atlantic Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreement (ACMA). Four cable ships owned by Keppel Corporation, a Singaporean company, are registered to Britain, although these ships have competing national contracts. More broadly, the UK is involved in CUI defence initiatives through NATO, such as BALTIC SENTRY and hosting NATO’s Maritime Centre for the Security of Critical Undersea Infrastructure within the alliance’s Maritime Command; through the JEF via Operation NORDIC WARDEN; and with AUKUS investment in Uncrewed Undersea Vehicles (UUVs) to protect undersea cables. Britain does, of course, also benefit from support from its allies. France has access to around nine French-flagged repair vessels, and Norway and Italy have three each. However, in the event of war and a period of sustained attack on communications, allies will have their own priorities to contend with, and it is uncertain whether these capabilities would be enough. It is unlikely that the UK will be operating alone in a period of sustained attack. However, considering the burden of being an island nation, relying on 64 communication cables and ten subsea electricity interconnectors – alongside the reliance on transatlantic cables that is not felt so acutely by its European allies – a sovereign capability would be beneficial for national security. The sovereign fleet solution? British industry leaders have raised concerns about reliance on foreign-flagged repair ships, as well as the security implications of cable repair passing through foreign-owned companies. Many ships are foreign-flagged and foreign-crewed, which leads to complications in wartime repairs. Current insurance for commercial vessels does not cover war risk, and crews are not necessarily prepared to sail into contested waters once standard cover lapses. Furthermore, governmental war risk insurance, as envisioned in the War Risks Act of 1952, is untested in the modern environment where ‘grey zone’ threats are more likely than a declared, conventional war. This is the sort of political reality technically required for the roll-out of governmental war risk insurance schemes. In both peacetime and wartime, the UK has the responsibility to help lead a NATO and JEF cable repair effort, potentially built around the Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA), with sovereign capabilities – a unique position given Britain’s geography spanning the High North, the continental shelf shared with Ireland, and its role supporting Euro-Atlantic allies. The JCNSS’ 2030 target is not arbitrary. ACMA’s UK-based CS Sovereign was built in 1991 at a cost of £32 million, and cable repair ships typically have a service life of 35-40 years, meaning its retirement is on the horizon. Without taking action, Britain risks losing even its existing, modest access to domestic repair capacity just as the geopolitical threat picture worsens. A sovereign fleet solves many of these problems, but comes at a huge price. CS Sovereign cost £32 million while RFA Proteus cost £70 million to purchase in 2023. A dedicated repair vessel would cost a similar amount to the latter. However, a full sovereign fleet is not necessarily required, nor affordable or politically palatable. A middle path, closer to the United States’ (US) retainer model and Cable Security Fleet – whereby Washington has paid privately owned, US-flagged vessels an annual retainer of US$5 million (£3.8 million) for guaranteed availability for laying, maintaining, and repairing critical cables – is more realistic. This option would comprise one or two UK-owned, UK-flagged vessels using the benchmark of £70-£100 million set by RFA Proteus as a financial guide. It would be backstopped by retainer agreements with multinational operators covering the remainder of Britain’s current access to roughly seven vessels (through the ACMA and Keppel-registered vessels), alongside government-backed wartime insurance. In peacetime, these could be leased to industry when necessary. The personnel factor A further, and often underappreciated, area of undersea cable repairs, both today and throughout history, is the skill and training necessary to fix the cables and operate the vessels required. During both world wars, cable ships were sitting ducks while the specialist crews worked tirelessly to repair the UK’s telecommunication cables. Notably, the CS Alert was sunk in 1945 while carrying out this exact mission. An additional bottleneck arises around the importance of a trained British crew. John Wrottesley, Executive Director of the European Subsea Cables Association, told the JCNSS directly that ‘skills and workforce is probably one of the most pressing challenges’ facing the sector, not just training naval reservists. Alasdair Wilkie, Chairman of the ACMA, also told the Committee that a repair ship takes around three years to build, while the staff needed to crew and operate a vessel takes closer to ten years to train. Wrottesley similarly expressed a need for better support from HM Government on cable repairs in a ‘conflict-type situation’. A trained, sovereign crew solves a critical challenge in the UK’s repair capabilities by providing British personnel for commercial vessels attending to cable damage in wartime that would not be covered by standard insurance. However, given the ten-year training horizon, a workforce programme started today would only reach maturity around 2036 – six years after the JCNSS’ own capability deadline. Conclusion Over the next 10-15 years, the UK’s dependence on undersea cables is expected to increase. As the British economy digitises, data traffic will increase in line with increased investments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), 5G and 6G, and the Internet of Things (IoT). These important technologies require protected and capable undersea cables. In peacetime, a middle-path, hybrid, sovereign capability would reinforce the UK’s position as a leading maritime security provider – an island economy dependent on cables, with responsibilities towards the Republic of Ireland, the High North, and NATO and JEF allies. In wartime, it would offer a capability better matched to the task of CUI repair in a contested and targeted contingency, as was guaranteed during both world wars. HM Government should therefore look towards internal training issues while acquiring the base of a sovereign repair fleet, new retainer contracts between itself and private repair vessels, and the means to protect these crucial capabilities. Liberty Hunter is the Sir Julian Corbett Adjunct Fellow in Maritime Security at the Council on Geostrategy. She works as a Project Manager and Researcher at the Ax:son Johnson Institute for Statecraft and Diplomacy, and is also a Research Associate at the Hertford College Diplomacy Centre. article.content: Iran's IRGC identified Hormuz undersea cables as potential targets. Saudi Arabia's Red Sea routes offer some protection — but GCC neighbours have no alternative. October 20, 2026 RIYADH — Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC’s spokesman, stood in Tehran’s Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October and told Iran’s state television that seven major internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz — and that they “could become Iran’s new targets.” Saudi Arabia has spent months defending its airports against Houthi attack — intercepting ballistic missiles over Riyadh, deploying coalition forces under the Makkah pact, drawing in Pakistani, Turkish and French air defences according to the coalition — but Mohebbi’s statement identified a category of infrastructure that none of that apparatus can reach. The International Cable Protection Committee counts five active cable segments in the strait, not seven, but the discrepancy is not the point: Iran has moved from threatening ships, airports and oil infrastructure to threatening the digital connective tissue on which Saudi Arabia has staked its entire economic future, and Riyadh has never publicly addressed whether Vision 2030 can survive it. Mohebbi’s language was conditional, not declarative — a threat broadcast on IRIB and disseminated by Fars news agency, not an operational order. But it arrived at the end of a progression that began in May 2026, when Iran’s military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari said Tehran would “impose fees on internet cables” transiting its claimed offshore territory in the Strait of Hormuz. Five months later the IRGC dropped the pretence of a commercial claim and framed the cables as military targets. Prediction market Polymarket prices the probability of Iran or its proxies physically damaging undersea cable infrastructure at 4% by end-October and 12% by end of year, according to Benzinga. The editorial question is not whether Iran will cut them tomorrow but whether Riyadh has ever priced the possibility into a modernisation programme that runs on the assumption of uninterrupted connectivity. Table of Contents What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) The Cables Iran Is Threatening Why Does the Repair Problem Matter More Than the Attack? What Does This Mean for Vision 2030’s Digital Layer? Who Has Actually Done This Before? Can International Law Protect Undersea Cables? What Are Riyadh’s Options? Frequently Asked Questions What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) Two Iranian officials, at two levels of authority, framed undersea cables as potential targets within the same month — and neither committed to actually striking them. Mohebbi, speaking at the Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October, told Fars news agency that “all of the world’s internet and commercial data” depend on the cables beneath Hormuz, and that “new targets will be unveiled, new weapons will be unveiled.” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, had gone further earlier in October, warning that undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities linked to US interests could be targeted if the conflict widened — but then added a qualifier that inverted the threat: “We have not yet included these assets among our targets.” 📚 Related Guides Riyadh Travel Guide 2026 → Things to do, where to stay, metro and Diriyah Riyadh Season Calendar → Month-by-month events guide Jeddah Travel Guide 2026 → Al-Balad, diving, F1 and gateway to Mecca Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, called Rezaei’s warning “fundamentally about deterrence” aimed at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha “as much as at Washington.” The threat, Krieg said, “reflects a new category of strategic infrastructure tying Gulf economic diversification to US technology.” That reading reframes the cables not as a military target in the conventional sense but as a pressure point in the broader contest over who controls the economic future of the Gulf — and who can threaten it at low cost. The precedent for reading Iran’s conditional language as something more than rhetoric was set in May 2026, when Zolfaghari’s announcement about cable fees appeared at first to be a revenue play, an attempt to monetise Iranian territorial claims in the strait. Within five months, the IRGC had moved from charging for access to the kind of two-track posture it has applied to every other dimension of the Hormuz crisis — offering mediation while expanding the target set. IRGC speedboats conduct aggressive manoeuvres near US Navy vessels in the Persian Gulf — the same force whose spokesman in October 2026 identified undersea cables as a new category of military targets, framing them as pressure points in the contest over the Gulf’s economic future. Photo: US Navy / Public Domain The Cables Iran Is Threatening TeleGeography, the industry authority on subsea infrastructure, identifies three active cable systems crossing the Strait of Hormuz: AAE-1 (Asia-Africa-Europe 1), which connects Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt with landing points in the UAE, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia; FALCON, linking India and Sri Lanka to Gulf countries; and the Gulf Bridge International Cable System, known as GBICS or MENA, which connects all Gulf states including Iran itself. TATA TGN-Gulf also appears on TeleGeography’s submarine cable map of the region. The ICPC’s count of five active cable segments exceeds the three named systems because some run multiple segments through the strait, but falls short of Mohebbi’s claimed seven — a discrepancy that suggests the IRGC is either counting planned systems that have not been laid, or inflating the number for rhetorical effect. The HOS Daily Brief The Middle East briefing 3,000+ readers start their day with. One email. Every weekday morning. Free. Get the Daily Brief → ✓ You're in. First brief tomorrow morning. Active submarine cable systems transiting the Strait of Hormuz Cable system Route Key Gulf landing points AAE-1 Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt UAE, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia FALCON India and Sri Lanka to the Gulf Multiple Gulf states Gulf Bridge International (GBICS/MENA) Intra-Gulf connectivity All Gulf states including Iran TATA TGN-Gulf India to the Gulf Gulf states The critical nuance that most coverage of Mohebbi’s threat has missed is that Saudi Arabia is not the Gulf state most exposed to a Hormuz cable cut. The kingdom draws most of its international bandwidth from cables on its Red Sea coast — the PEACE cable lands at Jeddah — and AAE-1 reaches Saudi Arabia via the Gulf of Oman and the UAE side, not directly through Hormuz. John Wrottesley, ICPC’s operations manager, has noted that cable traffic through the Strait of Hormuz represents “under 1% of global international bandwidth,” and that “cable networks are built around resilience and redundancy.” That fraction sounds reassuring until you consider who it serves. Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq are the states most acutely exposed to Hormuz-route disruption because they have fewer alternative cable routes, and for those states a severed Hormuz cable would be the primary disruption, not a secondary one. An attack on Bahrain’s bandwidth is an attack on GCC financial clearing systems that Saudi banks depend on — and Riyadh has no mechanism to defend fibre that sits on the seabed in waters Iran now treats as its own. Why Does the Repair Problem Matter More Than the Attack? The immediate damage from a cable cut is measurable: degraded bandwidth, rerouted traffic, latency spikes that financial systems can tolerate for hours but not for weeks. The lasting damage comes from what happens after — or, more precisely, what does not happen, because the infrastructure that makes cable repair possible has already withdrawn from the region. France-based Alcatel Submarine Networks, one of the world’s largest cable repair operators, paused all regional repair operations as of May 2026, according to The National News. Maritime data provider Windward warned that, with Red Sea cables already degraded by 2024 damage, the Alcatel pause “threatens the primary remaining data link between Europe and Asia.” Alan Mauldin, research director at TeleGeography, has identified the deeper structural problem: even when a repair vessel is available, permitting to enter territorial waters is “possibly the biggest source” of delays. Repair ships operate under flags that require transit permissions from every coastal state whose waters they must cross — and in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has declared that passage requires coordination with Iranian forces , those permits could take months rather than weeks, assuming Tehran grants them at all. On the satellite question, Mauldin’s assessment was categorical. “It’s not as though you could just switch to satellite. That’s not an alternative.” Alan Mauldin, research director, TeleGeography Masha Kotkin, a geopolitical and energy analyst, reinforced that assessment, calling Starlink “a boutique solution, which is not scalable to millions of users, at this time.” Kotkin warned that “damaged cables mean the internet slowing down or outages, e-commerce disruptions, delayed financial transactions” — and added the dimension that makes the repair problem worse than the attack itself: “The longer this conflict lasts, the higher the likelihood of unintentional damage.” A mine drifting into a cable route, an anchor dragging across fibre during evasive manoeuvres, a repair crew blocked from getting permits — these are not hypotheticals but the actual conditions in a mined strait where Alcatel has stopped working and Iran has declared the seabed part of the battlefield. The ICPC records approximately 150 to 200 cable faults per year globally, attributing 70 to 80 per cent to accidental causes — fishing gear and ship anchors. Hormuz vessel transits ran at roughly 120 per day under normal conditions, according to Gulf News citing Kpler data, and had fallen to approximately 105 commodity-carrying vessels in the first 18 days of the conflict — even reduced traffic in a mined, contested strait poses more risk to seabed infrastructure than normal traffic in a peaceful one. The Global Sentinel, a Tyco Submarine Systems cable ship, lays a submarine cable at sea — the type of specialised vessel required for any Hormuz cable repair. France-based Alcatel Submarine Networks paused all regional repair operations in May 2026; even if a vessel were available, permitting to enter Iranian-controlled waters could take months. Photo: Nc tech3 / CC BY-SA 4.0 What Does This Mean for Vision 2030’s Digital Layer? Saudi Arabia designated 2026 as the Year of AI. The kingdom’s data centre capacity grew from approximately 68 megawatts in 2021 to 467 megawatts in early 2026, according to IMARC Group — a nearly sevenfold expansion in five years, all of it predicated on the assumption that the bandwidth connecting those facilities to the global internet would remain available. SDAIA’s Hexagon Data Center in Riyadh, with a planned capacity of 480 megawatts, had its foundation stone laid in January 2026. Microsoft confirmed in March that its Saudi Arabia cloud region would be available from Q4 2026, intended to “power Vision 2030 cloud and AI ambitions,” as reported by Intelligent CIO. When Saudi Arabia built the East-West pipeline — designed to carry approximately 7 million barrels per day from the Eastern Province to Yanbu on the Red Sea, according to Saudi Gazette — it created a terrestrial bypass for oil that could circumvent Hormuz disruption. The pipeline was a physical answer to a physical chokepoint , and despite operational interruptions during the current conflict it remains the structural insurance policy that keeps Saudi crude flowing when the strait does not. No equivalent exists for data. There is no East-West fibre trunk carrying Saudi Arabia’s internet traffic from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea in a hardened terrestrial corridor, and no public plan to build one. The AWS drone attacks of early March 2026, which struck data centres in the UAE and Bahrain, already demonstrated that Gulf digital infrastructure is a live target — the first confirmed attacks on cloud facilities in the current conflict, causing physical damage, power disruptions and outages, according to Benzinga. Those attacks hit the physical plants that store data; an attack on the cables would hit the connections that move it, and the combination of both — degraded physical infrastructure and severed connectivity — is the scenario that Vision 2030’s risk model has never publicly addressed. The kingdom’s revised 2026 deficit estimate of 245 billion riyals, up from a budgeted 165 billion according to Reuters via Zawya, already reflects the cost of a conflict that has hammered oil revenues and delayed investment timelines. FII, the flagship investment summit, has been postponed to 2027 . Riyadh Season was due to open on 21 October; the EU-GCC summit was set for Riyadh on 24 October. In February 2024, three submarine cables in the Red Sea — AAE-1, the Europe India Gateway and Seacom — were damaged, not by a deliberate military strike but by anchor drag from the Rubymar, a cargo vessel hit by a Houthi missile that drifted for days before sinking. The strait is narrower, the territorial claims are more aggressively enforced, the repair infrastructure has already withdrawn, and the coastal state whose permits would be required for any repair operation is the same state whose military spokesman just identified the cables as potential targets. If an accident in the Red Sea — a drifting anchor, not a military operation — took five months to repair on one system and disrupted a quarter of intercontinental traffic, a deliberate cut in Hormuz, or even accidental damage in an environment where supertankers have hit mines , could leave Gulf states with degraded connectivity for far longer. The Baltic Sea offers the other recent case study. Between December 2025 and January 2026, a Congressional Research Service report documented at least six instances of suspected sabotage or disruption to undersea cables in the Baltic. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius stated that “no one believes that these cables were cut accidentally,” but attribution proved elusive — Swedish prosecutors ruled that damage to a Sweden-Latvia cable by the vessel Vezhen was accidental, and Finland’s intelligence service Supo cautioned against over-reliance on the “hybrid warfare” label. Scholars at the Observer Research Foundation and elsewhere have argued that Article 113 is structurally too narrow for deliberate state-directed sabotage — it was written for an era of accidental damage by fishing trawlers, not for an IRGC that announces on state television which cables it might cut. A state that cuts a cable in its claimed territorial waters can argue sovereign prerogative; a state that cuts a cable in international waters can deny attribution; and a state that simply creates the conditions in which cables are damaged by mines, anchors or conflict — without ever issuing the order to cut — occupies the grey zone that Article 113 was never designed to address. More than 95% of all international data traffic travels on subsea cables, according to researchers cited in The Conversation. What Are Riyadh’s Options? Saudi Arabia is, by an accident of geography, less exposed to Hormuz cable disruption than any other major Gulf state — its primary bandwidth routes west through the Suez corridor, not east through the strait. That advantage is real but incomplete, because the digital economies of the GCC do not operate in isolation, and the Gulf states with the most acute Hormuz cable exposure are the same states whose financial, logistics and cloud systems Saudi Arabia’s economy depends on daily. Kuwait said after the 10 October airport strikes that Saudi security is “an inseparable part of the security” of Kuwait and the GCC, according to Fortune and the Associated Press. The same principle applies to digital infrastructure: a cable cut that degrades Kuwaiti government connectivity or takes Bahraini clearing systems offline is a Saudi problem, regardless of whether Riyadh’s own internet stays up. Riyadh has spent years building a regional economic architecture that assumes integrated digital connectivity across the Gulf, and that architecture is only as resilient as its weakest cable route. The options are limited and none of them are fast. Cable rerouting — building new submarine systems that bypass Hormuz — is a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar undertaking, and multiple new systems planned for the region are already on hold or delayed, according to TeleGeography. Satellite backup sounds intuitive but, as both Kotkin and Mauldin have established, it cannot carry enterprise cloud traffic, financial settlement systems or AI workloads at the scale Vision 2030 requires — and permitting a repair vessel into Hormuz would take months under present conditions even if one were available. A hardened terrestrial fibre route across the Arabian Peninsula, connecting Gulf-coast data centres to Red Sea cable landing points, would be the digital equivalent of the East-West pipeline — but no Gulf state has announced such a project, and the engineering lead time would be measured in years. Krieg framed the deeper problem by describing the cable threat as directed “as much as at Washington” as at the Gulf capitals, which means it serves Iran’s purpose whether or not a cable is ever cut — it forces Gulf planners to factor digital infrastructure risk into every investment decision, every cloud contract, every AI deployment. The physical risk in Hormuz has already been priced by markets: vessel transit rates and war risk premiums have repriced dramatically. The digital risk has not been priced at all, and the question Vision 2030’s planners have not answered is whether they have a contingency for the day it is. Saudi Arabia expanded its data centre capacity from 68 megawatts in 2021 to 467 megawatts by early 2026 — a sevenfold build-out predicated on uninterrupted connectivity that no terrestrial fibre bypass yet exists to protect. Photo: CC BY-SA 4.0 Frequently Asked Questions Would a Hormuz cable cut affect Saudi Arabia’s internet immediately? Not as severely as it would affect Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain or Iraq, which have fewer Red Sea routing alternatives. The more consequential impact would be indirect: Bahrain hosts GCC clearing and settlement systems, Kuwait’s sovereign wealth infrastructure runs cross-border financial flows, and the shared enterprise platforms and cloud architectures that Vision 2030’s regional supply chains depend on span all five GCC states. A cable cut that degrades Bahraini or Kuwaiti connectivity degrades Saudi Arabia’s financial infrastructure, regardless of whether Riyadh’s own internet stays up. How long would it take to repair a severed cable in the Strait of Hormuz? In peacetime, cable repairs typically take two to four weeks from fault identification to restoration. In the Strait of Hormuz right now, that baseline is irrelevant: there is no available repair operator in the region, and even if one agreed to deploy, its vessel would require transit permits from the state whose military spokesman just named the cables as targets. The closest real-world comparison — 2024 Red Sea damage, in far less restricted waters — took five months on the AAE-1 system alone, a timeline that becomes a floor, not a ceiling, in Hormuz. Has any state deliberately cut an undersea cable as an act of war? No confirmed case of deliberate state-on-state cable cutting exists in modern international law, which is precisely what makes the threat attractive as a tool of coercion. The Baltic Sea incidents of 2025-2026 involved at least six cable disruptions that Western intelligence services attributed to hostile action, but Swedish prosecutors ruled at least one case accidental. Cable sabotage occupies a grey zone — it causes measurable economic damage, is extremely difficult to attribute with legal certainty, and the primary international legal instrument, UNCLOS Article 113, applies only to the saboteur’s own flag state or nationals. article.content: Iran's IRGC identified Hormuz undersea cables as potential targets. Saudi Arabia's Red Sea routes offer some protection — but GCC neighbours have no alternative. October 20, 2026 RIYADH — Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC’s spokesman, stood in Tehran’s Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October and told Iran’s state television that seven major internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz — and that they “could become Iran’s new targets.” Saudi Arabia has spent months defending its airports against Houthi attack — intercepting ballistic missiles over Riyadh, deploying coalition forces under the Makkah pact, drawing in Pakistani, Turkish and French air defences according to the coalition — but Mohebbi’s statement identified a category of infrastructure that none of that apparatus can reach. The International Cable Protection Committee counts five active cable segments in the strait, not seven, but the discrepancy is not the point: Iran has moved from threatening ships, airports and oil infrastructure to threatening the digital connective tissue on which Saudi Arabia has staked its entire economic future, and Riyadh has never publicly addressed whether Vision 2030 can survive it. Mohebbi’s language was conditional, not declarative — a threat broadcast on IRIB and disseminated by Fars news agency, not an operational order. But it arrived at the end of a progression that began in May 2026, when Iran’s military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari said Tehran would “impose fees on internet cables” transiting its claimed offshore territory in the Strait of Hormuz. Five months later the IRGC dropped the pretence of a commercial claim and framed the cables as military targets. Prediction market Polymarket prices the probability of Iran or its proxies physically damaging undersea cable infrastructure at 4% by end-October and 12% by end of year, according to Benzinga. The editorial question is not whether Iran will cut them tomorrow but whether Riyadh has ever priced the possibility into a modernisation programme that runs on the assumption of uninterrupted connectivity. Table of Contents What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) The Cables Iran Is Threatening Why Does the Repair Problem Matter More Than the Attack? What Does This Mean for Vision 2030’s Digital Layer? Who Has Actually Done This Before? Can International Law Protect Undersea Cables? What Are Riyadh’s Options? Frequently Asked Questions What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) Two Iranian officials, at two levels of authority, framed undersea cables as potential targets within the same month — and neither committed to actually striking them. Mohebbi, speaking at the Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October, told Fars news agency that “all of the world’s internet and commercial data” depend on the cables beneath Hormuz, and that “new targets will be unveiled, new weapons will be unveiled.” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, had gone further earlier in October, warning that undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities linked to US interests could be targeted if the conflict widened — but then added a qualifier that inverted the threat: “We have not yet included these assets among our targets.” 📚 Related Guides Riyadh Travel Guide 2026 → Things to do, where to stay, metro and Diriyah Riyadh Season Calendar → Month-by-month events guide Jeddah Travel Guide 2026 → Al-Balad, diving, F1 and gateway to Mecca Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, called Rezaei’s warning “fundamentally about deterrence” aimed at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha “as much as at Washington.” The threat, Krieg said, “reflects a new category of strategic infrastructure tying Gulf economic diversification to US technology.” That reading reframes the cables not as a military target in the conventional sense but as a pressure point in the broader contest over who controls the economic future of the Gulf — and who can threaten it at low cost. The precedent for reading Iran’s conditional language as something more than rhetoric was set in May 2026, when Zolfaghari’s announcement about cable fees appeared at first to be a revenue play, an attempt to monetise Iranian territorial claims in the strait. Within five months, the IRGC had moved from charging for access to the kind of two-track posture it has applied to every other dimension of the Hormuz crisis — offering mediation while expanding the target set. IRGC speedboats conduct aggressive manoeuvres near US Navy vessels in the Persian Gulf — the same force whose spokesman in October 2026 identified undersea cables as a new category of military targets, framing them as pressure points in the contest over the Gulf’s economic future. Photo: US Navy / Public Domain The Cables Iran Is Threatening TeleGeography, the industry authority on subsea infrastructure, identifies three active cable systems crossing the Strait of Hormuz: AAE-1 (Asia-Africa-Europe 1), which connects Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt with landing points in the UAE, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia; FALCON, linking India and Sri Lanka to Gulf countries; and the Gulf Bridge International Cable System, known as GBICS or MENA, which connects all Gulf states including Iran itself. TATA TGN-Gulf also appears on TeleGeography’s submarine cable map of the region. The ICPC’s count of five active cable segments exceeds the three named systems because some run multiple segments through the strait, but falls short of Mohebbi’s claimed seven — a discrepancy that suggests the IRGC is either counting planned systems that have not been laid, or inflating the number for rhetorical effect. The kingdom draws most of its international bandwidth from cables on its Red Sea coast — the PEACE cable lands at Jeddah — and AAE-1 reaches Saudi Arabia via the Gulf of Oman and the UAE side, not directly through Hormuz. Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq are the states most acutely exposed to Hormuz-route disruption because they have fewer alternative cable routes, and for those states a severed Hormuz cable would be the primary disruption, not a secondary one. An attack on Bahrain’s bandwidth is an attack on GCC financial clearing systems that Saudi banks depend on — and Riyadh has no mechanism to defend fibre that sits on the seabed in waters Iran now treats as its own. article.content: Iran's IRGC identified Hormuz undersea cables as potential targets. Saudi Arabia's Red Sea routes offer some protection — but GCC neighbours have no alternative. October 20, 2026 RIYADH — Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC’s spokesman, stood in Tehran’s Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October and told Iran’s state television that seven major internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz — and that they “could become Iran’s new targets.” Saudi Arabia has spent months defending its airports against Houthi attack — intercepting ballistic missiles over Riyadh, deploying coalition forces under the Makkah pact, drawing in Pakistani, Turkish and French air defences according to the coalition — but Mohebbi’s statement identified a category of infrastructure that none of that apparatus can reach. The International Cable Protection Committee counts five active cable segments in the strait, not seven, but the discrepancy is not the point: Iran has moved from threatening ships, airports and oil infrastructure to threatening the digital connective tissue on which Saudi Arabia has staked its entire economic future, and Riyadh has never publicly addressed whether Vision 2030 can survive it. Mohebbi’s language was conditional, not declarative — a threat broadcast on IRIB and disseminated by Fars news agency, not an operational order. But it arrived at the end of a progression that began in May 2026, when Iran’s military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari said Tehran would “impose fees on internet cables” transiting its claimed offshore territory in the Strait of Hormuz. Five months later the IRGC dropped the pretence of a commercial claim and framed the cables as military targets. Prediction market Polymarket prices the probability of Iran or its proxies physically damaging undersea cable infrastructure at 4% by end-October and 12% by end of year, according to Benzinga. The editorial question is not whether Iran will cut them tomorrow but whether Riyadh has ever priced the possibility into a modernisation programme that runs on the assumption of uninterrupted connectivity. Table of Contents What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) The Cables Iran Is Threatening Why Does the Repair Problem Matter More Than the Attack? What Does This Mean for Vision 2030’s Digital Layer? Who Has Actually Done This Before? Can International Law Protect Undersea Cables? What Are Riyadh’s Options? Frequently Asked Questions What Iran Actually Said (and What It Didn’t) Two Iranian officials, at two levels of authority, framed undersea cables as potential targets within the same month — and neither committed to actually striking them. Mohebbi, speaking at the Sacred Defence Museum on 19 October, told Fars news agency that “all of the world’s internet and commercial data” depend on the cables beneath Hormuz, and that “new targets will be unveiled, new weapons will be unveiled.” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, had gone further earlier in October, warning that undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities linked to US interests could be targeted if the conflict widened — but then added a qualifier that inverted the threat: “We have not yet included these assets among our targets.” 📚 Related Guides Riyadh Travel Guide 2026 → Things to do, where to stay, metro and Diriyah Riyadh Season Calendar → Month-by-month events guide Jeddah Travel Guide 2026 → Al-Balad, diving, F1 and gateway to Mecca Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, called Rezaei’s warning “fundamentally about deterrence” aimed at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha “as much as at Washington.” The threat, Krieg said, “reflects a new category of strategic infrastructure tying Gulf economic diversification to US technology.” That reading reframes the cables not as a military target in the conventional sense but as a pressure point in the broader contest over who controls the economic future of the Gulf — and who can threaten it at low cost. The precedent for reading Iran’s conditional language as something more than rhetoric was set in May 2026, when Zolfaghari’s announcement about cable fees appeared at first to be a revenue play, an attempt to monetise Iranian territorial claims in the strait. Within five months, the IRGC had moved from charging for access to the kind of two-track posture it has applied to every other dimension of the Hormuz crisis — offering mediation while expanding the target set. IRGC speedboats conduct aggressive manoeuvres near US Navy vessels in the Persian Gulf — the same force whose spokesman in October 2026 identified undersea cables as a new category of military targets, framing them as pressure points in the contest over the Gulf’s economic future. Photo: US Navy / Public Domain The Cables Iran Is Threatening TeleGeography, the industry authority on subsea infrastructure, identifies three active cable systems crossing the Strait of Hormuz: AAE-1 (Asia-Africa-Europe 1), which connects Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt with landing points in the UAE, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia; FALCON, linking India and Sri Lanka to Gulf countries; and the Gulf Bridge International Cable System, known as GBICS or MENA, which connects all Gulf states including Iran itself. TATA TGN-Gulf also appears on TeleGeography’s submarine cable map of the region. The ICPC’s count of five active cable segments exceeds the three named systems because some run multiple segments through the strait, but falls short of Mohebbi’s claimed seven — a discrepancy that suggests the IRGC is either counting planned systems that have not been laid, or inflating the number for rhetorical effect. Active submarine cable systems transiting the Strait of Hormuz Cable system Route Key Gulf landing points AAE-1 Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt UAE, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia FALCON India and Sri Lanka to the Gulf Multiple Gulf states Gulf Bridge International (GBICS/MENA) Intra-Gulf connectivity All Gulf states including Iran TATA TGN-Gulf India to the Gulf Gulf states The critical nuance that most coverage of Mohebbi’s threat has missed is that Saudi Arabia is not the Gulf state most exposed to a Hormuz cable cut. The kingdom draws most of its international bandwidth from cables on its Red Sea coast — the PEACE cable lands at Jeddah — and AAE-1 reaches Saudi Arabia via the Gulf of Oman and the UAE side, not directly through Hormuz. John Wrottesley, ICPC’s operations manager, has noted that cable traffic through the Strait of Hormuz represents “under 1% of global international bandwidth,” and that “cable networks are built around resilience and redundancy.” That fraction sounds reassuring until you consider who it serves. Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq are the states most acutely exposed to Hormuz-route disruption because they have fewer alternative cable routes, and for those states a severed Hormuz cable would be the primary disruption, not a secondary one. An attack on Bahrain’s bandwidth is an attack on GCC financial clearing systems that Saudi banks depend on — and Riyadh has no mechanism to defend fibre that sits on the seabed in waters Iran now treats as its own. Why Does the Repair Problem Matter More Than the Attack? The immediate damage from a cable cut is measurable: degraded bandwidth, rerouted traffic, latency spikes that financial systems can tolerate for hours but not for weeks. The lasting damage comes from what happens after — or, more precisely, what does not happen, because the infrastructure that makes cable repair possible has already withdrawn from the region. France-based Alcatel Submarine Networks, one of the world’s largest cable repair operators, paused all regional repair operations as of May 2026, according to The National News. Maritime data provider Windward warned that, with Red Sea cables already degraded by 2024 damage, the Alcatel pause “threatens the primary remaining data link between Europe and Asia.” Alan Mauldin, research director at TeleGeography, has identified the deeper structural problem: even when a repair vessel is available, permitting to enter territorial waters is “possibly the biggest source” of delays. Repair ships operate under flags that require transit permissions from every coastal state whose waters they must cross — and in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has declared that passage requires coordination with Iranian forces , those permits could take months rather than weeks, assuming Tehran grants them at all. On the satellite question, Mauldin’s assessment was categorical. “It’s not as though you could just switch to satellite. That’s not an alternative.” Alan Mauldin, research director, TeleGeography Masha Kotkin, a geopolitical and energy analyst, reinforced that assessment, calling Starlink “a boutique solution, which is not scalable to millions of users, at this time.” Kotkin warned that “damaged cables mean the internet slowing down or outages, e-commerce disruptions, delayed financial transactions” — and added the dimension that makes the repair problem worse than the attack itself: “The longer this conflict lasts, the higher the likelihood of unintentional damage.” A mine drifting into a cable route, an anchor dragging across fibre during evasive manoeuvres, a repair crew blocked from getting permits — these are not hypotheticals but the actual conditions in a mined strait where Alcatel has stopped working and Iran has declared the seabed part of the battlefield. The ICPC records approximately 150 to 200 cable faults per year globally, attributing 70 to 80 per cent to accidental causes — fishing gear and ship anchors. Hormuz vessel transits ran at roughly 120 per day under normal conditions, according to Gulf News citing Kpler data, and had fallen to approximately 105 commodity-carrying vessels in the first 18 days of the conflict — even reduced traffic in a mined, contested strait poses more risk to seabed infrastructure than normal traffic in a peaceful one. The Global Sentinel, a Tyco Submarine Systems cable ship, lays a submarine cable at sea — the type of specialised vessel required for any Hormuz cable repair. France-based Alcatel Submarine Networks paused all regional repair operations in May 2026; even if a vessel were available, permitting to enter Iranian-controlled waters could take months. Photo: Nc tech3 / CC BY-SA 4.0 What Does This Mean for Vision 2030’s Digital Layer? Saudi Arabia designated 2026 as the Year of AI. The kingdom’s data centre capacity grew from approximately 68 megawatts in 2021 to 467 megawatts in early 2026, according to IMARC Group — a nearly sevenfold expansion in five years, all of it predicated on the assumption that the bandwidth connecting those facilities to the global internet would remain available. SDAIA’s Hexagon Data Center in Riyadh, with a planned capacity of 480 megawatts, had its foundation stone laid in January 2026. Microsoft confirmed in March that its Saudi Arabia cloud region would be available from Q4 2026, intended to “power Vision 2030 cloud and AI ambitions,” as reported by Intelligent CIO. When Saudi Arabia built the East-West pipeline — designed to carry approximately 7 million barrels per day from the Eastern Province to Yanbu on the Red Sea, according to Saudi Gazette — it created a terrestrial bypass for oil that could circumvent Hormuz disruption. The pipeline was a physical answer to a physical chokepoint , and despite operational interruptions during the current conflict it remains the structural insurance policy that keeps Saudi crude flowing when the strait does not. No equivalent exists for data. There is no East-West fibre trunk carrying Saudi Arabia’s internet traffic from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea in a hardened terrestrial corridor, and no public plan to build one. The AWS drone attacks of early March 2026, which struck data centres in the UAE and Bahrain, already demonstrated that Gulf digital infrastructure is a live target — the first confirmed attacks on cloud facilities in the current conflict, causing physical damage, power disruptions and outages, according to Benzinga. Those attacks hit the physical plants that store data; an attack on the cables would hit the connections that move it, and the combination of both — degraded physical infrastructure and severed connectivity — is the scenario that Vision 2030’s risk model has never publicly addressed. The kingdom’s revised 2026 deficit estimate of 245 billion riyals, up from a budgeted 165 billion according to Reuters via Zawya, already reflects the cost of a conflict that has hammered oil revenues and delayed investment timelines. FII, the flagship investment summit, has been postponed to 2027 . Riyadh Season was due to open on 21 October; the EU-GCC summit was set for Riyadh on 24 October. Every one of these events depends on the kind of connectivity that Mohebbi’s threat puts at risk — not just for Saudi Arabia, but for the Gulf states whose delegates, investors and broadcasters would rely on Hormuz-routed bandwidth to participate. Who Has Actually Done This Before? In February 2024, three submarine cables in the Red Sea — AAE-1, the Europe India Gateway and Seacom — were damaged, not by a deliberate military strike but by anchor drag from the Rubymar, a cargo vessel hit by a Houthi missile that drifted for days before sinking. HGC Global Communications reported that the damage disrupted approximately 25% of internet traffic flow between Asia, Europe and the Middle East. Repairs on AAE-1 were completed by July 2024 — five months for a single cable, in waters that were dangerous but not under active naval blockade — while EIG and Seacom were repaired by E-Marine, an Etisalat subsidiary. The Strait of Hormuz in October 2026, where mines are in the water, Alcatel has withdrawn its repair operations, and vessel traffic has fallen to its lowest sustained level since the conflict began, is the hardest of those chokepoints by every measure that matters for cable survivability. Three cables crossing these waters — AAE-1, the Europe India Gateway and Seacom — were damaged in February 2024 when the Houthi-struck vessel Rubymar drifted and dragged its anchor, disrupting approximately 25% of internet traffic between Asia, Europe and the Middle East. UNCLOS Article 113 requires signatory states to criminalise wilful or culpably negligent damage to submarine cables beyond the territorial sea. article.content: × Select your language English (UK) 简体中文(中国) Search Insights Exclusive: Re-Evaluating Vietnam’s Internet Resilience —— A Deep Analysis of Subsea Outages, Terrestrial Corridors, and IP-Layer Strategic Solutions Details By Winston Qiu Winston Qiu Category: Insights 31 August 2026 Executive Summary The recurring, simultaneous outages across Vietnam’s primary international submarine cable systems —including recent concurrent disruptions on SJC2, AAE-1, AAG, and TGN-IA —have once again exposed the fragile nature of the nation’s international connectivity. According to Vietnam news, with approximately 30% of Vietnam’s aggregate international bandwidth capacity impaired during major multi-cable incidents, establishing a reliable, high-capacity failover strategy is a critical national priority. The actual international bandwidth loss might be much more than 30% At the policy level, Vietnam's Digital Infrastructure Master Plan to 2030 establishes a decisive national strategy to resolve this vulnerability by expanding the subsea network. The master plan targets adding at least 10 new subsea cables to bring the country's total to 15 or more systems with a minimum capacity of 334–350 Tbps by 2030. However, complex subsea cable engineering—encompassing desktop route studies, environmental permitting, consortium alignment, and specialized marine installation—means that bringing these new marine highways online will realistically take another 3 to 5 years, if not longer . During this interim period and beyond, viable terrestrial solutions must not be abandoned ; rather, overland fiber networks must be actively developed and optimized as an essential, immediate resilience buffer. While expanding terrestrial fiber optic networks appears to be the most obvious immediate alternative, physical and operational realities complicate this approach. The Indochina terrestrial corridor (e.g., VNPT’s VSTN system running through Laos, Thailand, and Malaysia to Singapore) is plagued by chronic instability, particularly along the Thai transit segment. Conversely, the overland corridor through Mainland China to Hong Kong offers superior stability and path density, yet remains severely underutilized due to commercial misalignments and security hesitations surrounding physical transmission-layer (L1/L2) circuit sales. Furthermore, significant regulatory restrictions prevent Chinese operators from leasing or provisioning terrestrial cross-border lines on a dark-fiber or fiber-pair basis. This report presents a comprehensive analysis of Vietnam’s current subsea and terrestrial infrastructure, evaluates operational bottlenecks, and proposes a strategic paradigm shift: transitioning from Layer 1/Layer 2 transport leases to Layer 3 (IP-Layer) dynamic burstable IP Transit cooperation with Chinese Tier-1 carriers. Combined with an empirical BGP routing topology analysis of Vietnam's four dominant operators, in-country content localization, and subsea route diversification, this approach provides a scalable roadmap for Vietnam’s digital resilience. 1. Subsea Infrastructure Assessment & Outage Dynamics Vietnam relies on a small cluster of high-capacity submarine cable systems to carry the vast majority of its international data traffic. The loss of multiple systems simultaneously creates severe bottlenecks. 1.1 Fault Breakdown of the 4 Disrupted Cables SJC2 Aug 25, 2026 Date of Break: August 25, 2026 Location: S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok (Hong Kong) Status & Impact: Critical loss of high-density intra-Asia capacity. No restoration schedule announced. AAE-1 Aug 25, 2026 Date of Break: August 25, 2026 (6:22 PM) Location: S1.H2 segment Status & Impact: Severed direct western/European routing. Repairs projected for late September 2026. AAG Pre-existing Date of Break: Pre-existing (Prior to Aug 25, 2026) Location: Transpacific main trunk Status & Impact: Unresolved pre-existing fault reduced transpacific capacity via Guam. Pending repair ship availability. TGN-IA Late Aug 2026 Date of Break: Late August 2026 Location: Regional Asia-Pacific route Status & Impact: Restricted direct intra-Asia failover bandwidth. Repairs scheduled for early September 2026. 1.2 Active Subsea Inventory (Post-Retirement of SMW-3) Following the official retirement of legacy systems SMW-3, Vietnam’s active subsea network is concentrated across six primary cables: Cable System Key Regional Destinations Current Status Impact on Egress SJC2 Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan Impaired Severe loss of high-density intra-Asia capacity AAE-1 Hong Kong, Singapore, Middle East, Europe Impaired Loss of direct western/European routing AAG US West Coast via Guam/Hawaii Impaired Loss of direct transpacific capacity TGN-IA Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, Philippines Impaired Loss of regional redundancy APG Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, Singapore Operational Carrying primary failover traffic ADC Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, Philippines Operational Carrying primary failover traffic 1.3 Clarifying the "30% Loss" Phenomenon Capacity, Not Total Disconnection: The "30% loss" (or might be more) figure represents an estimated 30% reduction in Vietnam’s total aggregate available international bandwidth capacity, not the loss of connectivity for 30% of users. Domestic Traffic Unaffected: In-country services (local banking, news, domestic cloud apps, government portals) run at 100% normal speed. Peak-Hour Congestion: The capacity deficit creates latency spikes, packet loss, and localized buffering primarily during evening peak hours when users access foreign-hosted content (e.g., overseas cloud services, global streaming, foreign gaming servers). 2. Emergency Operator Countermeasures & The Core Pain Point To mitigate international egress bottlenecks, Vietnamese internet service providers (ISPs)—including VNPT, Viettel, FPT, and CMC Telecom —have implemented four primary emergency protocols: 1. Subsea Failover Re-routing Automatically load-balancing outbound traffic onto remaining operational subsea routes (APG and ADC). 2. Terrestrial Capacity Scaling Increasing bandwidth throughput over cross-border optical routes crossing China, Laos, and Cambodia. 3. Reserve Capacity Drawdown Activating pre-purchased emergency reserve pools across international partner networks. 4. CDN & Edge Caching Utilizing local Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) to serve cached overseas media directly from Vietnamese data centers. The Persistent Industry Pain Point: International egress congestion during subsea cuts remains an unresolved headache for all Vietnamese carriers. Emergency terrestrial leases are costly to scale on short notice, and backup subsea paths quickly become saturated during peak hours. A long-term, scalable failover mechanism is urgently needed. 3. Comparative Dilemma of Terrestrial Failover Corridors While terrestrial fiber optic networks offer vital redundancy during subsea cuts, operational reality demonstrates that not all terrestrial routes offer equal reliability. Southern Corridor (Vietnam – Laos – Thailand – Malaysia – Singapore / VSTN) High Physical Instability The Thailand Transit Bottleneck: The industry faces ongoing challenges with overland fiber traversing Thailand, most of which are overhead cables . The Thai transit segment experiences frequent cuts caused by highway expansion, civil construction, power instability, severe monsoon flooding, and frequent physical damage to aerial fiber cables resulting from human activities and wildlife (particularly monkeys ). Stacked Transit Tariffs: Routing traffic across four foreign nations (Laos, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore) incurs stacked right-of-way (RoW) fees and transit tariffs, driving up the cumulative cost per Gbps. High Failover Risk: Attempting to failover onto an overland path that is itself prone to frequent cuts risks compounding a subsea crisis with a terrestrial disruption. Northern Corridor (Vietnam – Mainland China – Hong Kong) Superior Physical Stability High Physical Security & Diversity: Built on China’s heavily protected and buried national optical backbone via multiple border crossings (Pingxiang, Dongxing, Lao Cai), offering low fault rates and dense route diversity. Low Latency to Global IXPs: Provides direct, high-speed terrestrial links into Hong Kong's major international exchange points. The L1/L2 Roadblock: The corridor remains underutilized due to commercial friction and cost barriers. The prohibitive pricing of physical transport circuits stems from joint tariff expectations on both sides—driven by both Vietnamese and Chinese operators, rather than Chinese carriers unilaterally. As a result, maintaining large-scale, idle L1/L2 bandwidth leases purely as standby redundancy remains cost-prohibitive for Vietnamese ISPs, while Chinese regulatory restrictions prevent Chinese operators from leasing or provisioning terrestrial cross-border lines on a dark-fiber or fiber-pair basis. Furthermore, deep physical-layer access presents mutual cybersecurity and regulatory concerns for both nations.. 4. The Solution: Shifting to Layer 3 (IP-Level) Burstable Cooperation To bypass the commercial and security friction inherent in Layer 1/Layer 2 transport circuit sales, cooperation should shift to the IP Layer (Layer 3). Rather than treating the Northern Corridor as a static pipe lease, Chinese Tier-1 operators (China Telecom, China Unicom, China Mobile) and Vietnamese ISPs (Viettel, VNPT, FPT, CMC) can establish high-capacity, burstable IP Transit interconnects at border nodes. 4.1 How the Burstable L3 IP Transit Model Works 1. Low Baseline Commitment Vietnamese ISPs maintain active, high-capacity BGP interconnects with Chinese carriers at border points (Pingxiang and Dongxing), paying a modest baseline commit fee to keep BGP sessions online without heavy idle costs. The BGP routers of Chinese carriers might be located at gateways in Nanning, Kunming or Guangzhou. 2. Automated BGP Bursting When subsea cables break, policy-based BGP routing automatically bursts traffic across border interconnects. Chinese Tier-1 networks immediately route Vietnamese traffic across terrestrial backbones to Hong Kong IXPs. 3. Usage-Based Settlement Vietnamese operators pay for expanded transit bandwidth based on actual burst duration and throughput, providing a highly cost-effective emergency backup model. 4.2 Advantages of L3 Burstable IP Transit vs. L1/L2 Circuits Feature Dimension Traditional L1/L2 Circuits Proposed L3 Burstable IP Transit Financial Model High fixed monthly CapEx/OpEx for idle capacity Low baseline fee + pay-as-you-burst during cuts Security Friction Concerns over physical fiber/wavelength access Standardized BGP routing with defined IP boundaries Operational Agility Slow manual provisioning during emergencies Automated BGP failover within seconds/minutes 4.3 Empirical BGP Routing Topology Analysis of Dominant Vietnamese Carriers An empirical analysis of IPv4 BGP route propagation maps for Vietnam's four dominant operators— VNPT (AS7643 / AS45899) , Viettel (AS24086 / AS7552) , FPT Telecom (AS18403) , and CMC Telecom (AS45903) —was conducted using routing topology data from bgp.he.net . 1. VNPT (AS7643 / AS45899) Direct Chinese Carrier Integration: VNPT exhibits the most direct IPv4 BGP transit connectivity with Chinese state-owned Tier-1 operators. Its primary Autonomous System (AS45899) actively receives IP Transit directly from CTGNet (China Telecom Global - AS23764) and CMI (China Mobile International - AS58453) . Other Upstreams: Connects to Zenlayer (AS4229) , Hurricane Electric (AS6939), Tata Communications (AS6453), and Telstra (AS4637). 2. Viettel Group (AS24086 / AS7552) Global Tier-1 Reliance: Viettel Group (AS7552) relies primarily on global Tier-1 backbones including NTT (AS2914), PCCW Global (AS3491), Cogent (AS174), Tata (AS6453), and Telia (AS1299). Indirect Exposure via Zenlayer: Direct BGP sessions from CTGNet or CMI are absent in its IPv4 route propagation graphs, but Viettel actively utilizes Zenlayer (AS4229) as an upstream transit/edge provider. 3. FPT Telecom (AS18403) Western/Global Transit Focus: FPT Telecom routes IPv4 traffic through Lumen/Level 3 (AS3356), Telia (AS1299), Telstra (AS4637), Orange (AS5511), and Zayo (AS6461). Zenlayer Bridge: Connects directly to Zenlayer (AS4229) for regional Asia-Pacific connectivity, but lacks direct BGP peering with CTGNet or CMI in its primary IPv4 paths. 4. CMC Telecom (AS45903) Direct CMI & Zenlayer Transit: CMC Telecom maintains direct BGP transit connections with CMI (China Mobile International - AS58453) and multiple Zenlayer Autonomous Systems ( AS4229 and AS21859 ). Other Upstreams: Leverages Hutchison/HGC (AS9304 -> AS15412), Telia (AS1299), Cogent (AS174), and PCCW (AS3491). Key BGP Analytical Findings: Zenlayer as a Universal Asia-Pacific Bridge: All four dominant Vietnamese operators maintain active BGP transit or peering connections with Zenlayer (AS4229 / AS21859) . As an edge cloud and Tier-2 carrier with strong Chinese operational origins, Zenlayer acts as an active, neutral IP transit bridge linking Vietnamese eyeball networks to Chinese and global digital ecosystems. Selective Adoption of Chinese Tier-1s: Currently, only VNPT and CMC Telecom maintain direct BGP routing sessions with Chinese state-owned Tier-1 operators (CTGNet for VNPT; CMI for both VNPT and CMC). Viettel and FPT route overland traffic through intermediate bridges like Zenlayer or global Tier-1 transit providers (NTT, PCCW, Tata). The China Unicom (CU) Gap: Across all four leading Vietnamese operators, China Unicom (CUG / AS4837 / AS10099) is notably absent as an IP Transit provider in these IPv4 BGP route propagation profiles. Strategic Failover Opportunity: The presence of CTGNet, CMI, and Zenlayer in Vietnamese BGP routing tables proves that L3 IP Transit collaboration is operationally mature. Establishing direct CTGNet and CMI BGP sessions with Viettel and FPT, while bringing China Unicom into the transit mix for all four operators, represents an immediate, low-cost opportunity to build robust L3 emergency failover capacity. 5. Comprehensive Action Plan for Vietnam’s Internet Resilience To achieve long-term digital sovereignty and network stability, Vietnam should execute a multi-layered resilience framework combining international cooperation, domestic caching, and subsea expansion: Pillar 1 L3 Burstable IP Transit Formalize burstable BGP transit agreements between all the leading ISPs and Chinese Tier-1s. Bridge the China Unicom gap and extend direct CTGNet/CMI sessions to Viettel and FPT. Pillar 2 Content Localization Incentivize global CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai, Google, Meta, AWS) to expand edge nodes inside Vietnamese data centers, keeping 60–70% of daily traffic local. Pillar 3 Domestic IXP Peering Expand the capacity of the Vietnam Internet Exchange (VNIX) and enforce mandatory local peering between domestic ISPs to prevent foreign traffic tromboning. Pillar 4 Subsea Master Plan Execute the Digital Infrastructure Master Plan to 2030 to deploy 10+ new subsea cables, dispersing landing stations across Quy Nhon, Da Nang, and Vung Tau. 6. Conclusion The recurring disruptions on Vietnam’s subsea cable network highlight the limitations of relying solely on subsea cable paths for international bandwidth . While Vietnam's Digital Infrastructure Master Plan to 2030 provides a clear long-term roadmap to expand subsea cable systems, the 3-to-5-year operational lead time mandates that viable terrestrial solutions remain a core component of national internet resilience. Empirical BGP route propagation analysis reveals that Vietnamese operators already maintain active L3 connections with Chinese carriers (CTGNet, CMI) and Chinese-oriented bridge providers (Zenlayer), but these relationships remain fragmented and unoptimized for emergency bursting. By filling key gaps—such as engaging China Unicom and extending direct Tier-1 BGP sessions to Viettel and FPT Telecom—Vietnam can transform its terrestrial connection with Mainland China into an automated, highly stable, burstable Layer 3 failover backbone. Combined with aggressive content localization and long-term subsea expansion, this strategy provides a practical, immediate path toward a resilient national digital infrastructure.
