article.content: From 1 January 2027, payment transaction data generated in Nigeria has to be stored in Nigeria. The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) set that deadline in a circular dated 15 June 2026, addressed to banks, microfinance banks, mobile money operators, switches and other licensed payment firms, as tech.africa reported in July . That turns local cloud in Lagos, Nigeria, from a sales pitch into a compliance requirement, and carriers are positioning accordingly. TelCables Nigeria is the West African subsidiary of Angola Cables, which owns the SACS cable between Angola and Brazil and capacity on WACS and MONET. Its parent upgraded its Atlantic systems with Ciena last month. Fernando Fernandes, chief executive of TelCables Nigeria and West Africa since 2023, answered tech.africa’s written questions on what Nigerian banks and fintechs now ask for, where route diversity still falls short, and where the company is investing next. Buy Cloud Servers to target North, West, and Southern Africa. This Q&A has been edited for house style and length. The answers are Fernandes’s own words. Fernando Fernandes, chief executive of TelCables Nigeria and West Africa. Image: TelCables Nigeria For readers meeting TelCables Nigeria for the first time: what do you run today, and who buys from you? TelCables Nigeria is the Nigerian subsidiary of Angola Cables, a multinational telecommunications and digital services provider. Its other subsidiaries include TelCables Southern and East Africa, TelCables Middle East, TelCables Europe and TelCables Brazil. We sell international capacity and IP transit over our own subsea cables, SACS, WACS and MONET, and over partner systems including EllaLink, Equiano and 2Africa. The company owns and operates a 33,000 km subsea network and extends its reach to more than 50,000 km through those partnerships. That gives us direct, low-latency routes from West Africa to the US, South America and London. On top of the network we offer: Global connectivity: IP transit to Tier 1 carriers including Tata, Telxius, GTT and Cogent, dedicated internet access without the customer needing its own autonomous system number, and remote peering to more than 27 internet exchange points (IXPs) worldwide. Clouds2Africa: local infrastructure and platform services, virtual machines, backup, disaster recovery, business continuity and content delivery network (CDN) services. Go4AI: local GPU infrastructure to host AI workloads. Security and integration: Shields2Africa distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) protection with 15 Tbps of mitigation capacity and 12 scrubbing centres, SD-WAN, and direct on-ramps to AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Our customers range from banks, fintechs and payment service providers to Tier 1 content providers such as Netflix, Facebook, Apple, Cloudflare and Akamai, as well as ISPs, OTT services, CDNs, research institutions, and small businesses and startups that need virtual machines on demand. Nigeria has no shortage of carriers and data-centre operators chasing the same enterprise and banking customers. What does TelCables Nigeria offer that they do not? Very simple, and those who know us know it very well. I will point out three things. First, we have route diversity that others don’t have. Our SACS cable is the only direct South Atlantic route from Africa to Latin America. Combined with MONET, WACS and EllaLink, we offer low-latency southern routes to the US, Brazil and Europe that bypass the congested West African coast. That has become a critical factor after the recent WACS cuts and disruptions. Second, our local cloud is truly local, technically and commercially. Clouds2Africa runs two live cloud nodes in Nigeria today, in the Tier III data centres of Rack Centre on the mainland and Digital Realty in Victoria Island. Because the data stays in Nigeria, there are no egress fees for most use cases and no migration fees. Bandwidth and IP are included, and billing is in naira via Paystack. The large international cloud providers charge in US dollars and bill for capacity or traffic. Third, it is compliant. Clouds2Africa holds Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) certification, plus ISO, SOC 1 and SOC 2, uses an AWS-compatible architecture, and is backed by a team of more than 30 engineers who can move workloads securely without downtime. What are banks and fintechs asking you for now that they were not asking for two years ago? Two years ago it was uptime with affordable international transit. Now it’s: CBN compliance: mandatory localisation of transaction data by 1 January 2027. Naira-priced cloud, to remove FX volatility. In-country backup and disaster recovery: two nodes, not one. Zero egress costs and predictable pricing, with a calculator. Local AI: Go4AI and a new multi-model AI API that gives one integration to Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Kimi, with DDoS protection embedded. The conversation has shifted from “connect me” to “keep my data sovereign, compliant, AI-ready and secure”. Your op-ed makes the case for local cloud and resilient infrastructure. Which parts of that does TelCables provide itself, and where do you rely on partners? Angola Cables and TelCables provide the international backbone (SACS, WACS and MONET, with partner connections to anywhere), an extensive global network of more than 500 cloud nodes and the Clouds2Africa platform, Go4AI, Shields2Africa, IP transit and Global Data Centre Interconnect. With partners, we provide route diversity and physical resilience. We colocate in Rack Centre, Medallion and other Tier III facilities, and use metro networks such as Djoliba for West African reach. We also partner for hybrid cloud on-ramps, and for payments, with Paystack handling naira wallets. Which gap in Nigerian infrastructure costs your customers most today, and what is TelCables doing about it? There are essentially two hidden costs: FX and egress fees, and the fragility of depending on a single route, WACS, along the West African coast. What we are doing about it: terabit-scale dark-fibre rings interconnecting the major Lagos data centres, dual in-country nodes for backup and disaster recovery, southbound subsea diversity to reduce cable-cut risk, zero egress fees and naira billing. That localises traffic, cuts latency and removes transfer costs. Power and the last mile remain challenges. We address them through our multiple Tier III sites and our partnerships across Africa and the rest of the world. Where is TelCables Nigeria investing over the next two years, and why there? Deepening our footprint in Lagos: more capacity on the dark-fibre rings, and hardening the second mainland node. Expanding points of presence beyond Lagos: Abuja and Port Harcourt are the next logical step, following demand and the NFW multi-city expansion [Nigeria Fintech Week, which in 2026 ran programmes in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt]. More local GPU capacity for sovereign AI. More data-centre integrations. Besides our connections to around 27 IXPs, we have access to more than 1,000 data centres globally, which is a particular advantage for hybrid cloud operators. Through partners such as Megaport, whose virtual fabric stretches across the globe, we can provide several “as a service” offerings depending on client requirements. Nigeria Fintech Week has just closed. Did anything you heard there change your plans? Three points stood out: Fintechs must move beyond payments to become economic infrastructure for credit, insurance and savings. Resilience is not about preventing failure, but about detecting, containing and recovering from disruptions. Scale is now massive. NIBSS Instant Payment processed about 11 billion transactions in 2024, against 5 billion in 2022, so dependence on infrastructure is that much higher. We have not changed our plans or our direction. We have accelerated them, with more focus on resilient dual-node cloud, naira economics, and payment infrastructure that can go cross-border from local bank accounts, a point Remita also made at the event.

article.content: An illustration of undersea cables. Image: Getty Images via Unsplash UK proposes 14-year prison terms for undersea cable sabotage The British government proposed on Thursday introducing prison sentences of up to 14 years and unlimited fines for damaging undersea cables and pipelines. It comes amid growing concerns over the vulnerability of subsea cables to so-called “hybrid warfare” by hostile states, including physical and cyberattacks targeting the cables themselves or the installations and digital systems on land. According to the consultation’s white paper , the new criminal offenses would cover telecommunications cables, electricity interconnectors and pipelines carrying 99% of the U.K.’s international data traffic and supplying 74% of its gas. The proposals would replace the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, a Victorian-era law that carries a maximum fine of £1,000 — a fraction of the repair costs — and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage. Repairs to the Estlink 2 electricity cable between Finland and Estonia — damaged by the anchor of the Eagle S oil tanker on Christmas Day 2024 — were estimated by grid operator Elering at €50 million to €60 million ($56 million to $67 million). Attempts to prosecute senior officers of that ship are ongoing . Under the new proposed law, alongside the 14 years for those found guilty of deliberate damage, perpetrators of reckless damage would face up to 10 years in prison and those of gross negligence up to two years. The government said it plans to introduce statutory security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications operators, with powers to direct cable and repair providers on national security grounds. Separate rules would govern fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but could expose sensitive information. Telecoms minister Ian Murray and energy minister Michael Shanks said in a joint foreword that the risks to critical subsea infrastructure was involving, citing a warning earlier this year that a Royal Navy attack submarine had surfaced near a Russian spy ship mapping this infrastructure in British waters. Matt Western, the chair of Parliament’s Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, welcomed the proposals, stating “the legislation covering attacks on undersea cables was written in a different age and it is right that a White Paper has been brought forward to bring it up to date.” Questions over jurisdiction in incidents of cable damage have complicated prosecutions elsewhere, alongside questions over whether they were truly reckless accidents or intentional attempts by Russia to undermine Europe. Finnish investigators initially suspected deliberate damage, but officials from several North Sea and Baltic countries later told Recorded Future News they increasingly believed that incident and other Baltic Sea cable breaks were accidental, citing investigations, intelligence and shipping data. The British government says the country’s cable network remains highly resilient and that most faults result from anchors, fishing nets, environmental hazards or technical failures while also warning of growing suspicious activity. In April, the Ministry of Defence said British and allied forces had tracked a Russian attack submarine and vessels linked to Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, or GUGI, near cables and pipelines north of Britain, allegedly mapping such infrastructure for potential wartime sabotage. The 12-week public consultation closes January 14, 2027. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. article.content: Spread the love Sri Vijaya Puram, Feb. 27:The submarine optical fibre cable project connecting the Andaman and Nicobar Islands with mainland India has significantly strengthened digital connectivity across the archipelago and is playing a vital role in the region’s development. This was stated by Dr. S. Murty, Principal General Manager, BSNL, Chennai , while explaining the importance and functioning of the Chennai–Andaman and Nicobar Islands (CANI) submarine optical fibre cable project. Talking to a media delegation, led by PIB, Port Blair, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dr. Murty said the project was funded by the Government of India through the Department of Telecommunications under the Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF), which is now known as the Digital Bharat Nidhi (DBN). The total capital cost of the project was about ₹980 crore, and Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) was entrusted with the responsibility of implementing and maintaining the project. He informed that the submarine cable project was commissioned in July 2020 and has been functioning successfully for nearly five and a half years. According to him, the system has been running smoothly with only one major fault reported so far near Car Nicobar during September–October 2025. The fault was restored within one month through coordinated efforts, which he described as a significant achievement since submarine cable repairs normally take between three and six months. Dr. Murty explained that the project involved laying about 1,500 kilometres of submarine optical fibre cable under the sea from Chennai to Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair). From Sri Vijaya Puram, the network has been extended to several other islands through additional cable links, ensuring high-speed connectivity across the region. A total of eight cable landing stations have been established under the project. Each cable coming from the sea terminates at a Beach Manhole (BMH) before being connected to the cable landing station through land-based optical fibre. To ensure reliability, the land cables have been laid through two separate routes—Path A and Path B—so that communication services remain uninterrupted even if one line is damaged. From Sri Vijaya Puram, three northern islands—Long Island, Swaraj Dweep (Havelock) and Rangat—have been connected through the network. On the southern side, connectivity has been extended to Hut Bay in Little Andaman, Car Nicobar, Kamorta and Campbell Bay in Great Nicobar. These connections have enabled the islands to receive high-speed bandwidth that supports modern communication and digital services. Dr. Murty said that optical fibre technology offers extremely high data capacity. At present, the CANI project provides a bandwidth capacity of around 400 gigabits per second. However, he explained that the fibre itself has virtually unlimited capacity and that the bandwidth can be increased further simply by upgrading the terminal equipment at both ends without replacing the existing cable. Under the project, four optical fibre pairs have been laid. Two fibres are used for the main and standby communication links, one fibre has been allocated for defence communication purposes, while the fourth fibre has been kept as a spare to ensure redundancy and reliability. He further said that in case the submarine cable is damaged, communication services in the islands would temporarily shift to satellite bandwidth, which was the earlier mode of connectivity before the submarine cable project was implemented. However, satellite bandwidth is limited compared to optical fibre connectivity, and internet speeds would be significantly reduced during such situations. Dr. Murty also mentioned that the Government of India is considering plans for additional submarine cable connectivity to the islands from another route to strengthen redundancy and expand connectivity to more remote islands. However, he clarified that the final decision and detailed plans would be announced by the Department of Telecommunications. Highlighting the importance of the project, he said the submarine optical fibre cable has transformed digital infrastructure in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands by providing reliable high-speed internet connectivity for residents, government services, tourism, education and defence operations. He added that continuous monitoring and maintenance systems have been put in place to ensure uninterrupted services and safeguard the cable infrastructure.
article.title: BSNL’s Submarine Optical Fibre Cable Project Strengthening Digital Connectivity in Andaman & Nicobar Islands

article.content: New laws could see those who damage subsea cables around Shetland jailed By Andrew Hirst - a.hirst@shetlandtimes.co.uk Published: 05:30, 24 October 2026 Repair works were are carried out on the Shefa-2 cable off Orkney after damage caused by Storm Amy. New laws which could see those who damage subsea cables jailed are hoped to prevent the sort of disruption that has caused communication blackouts in Shetland. The UK government’s new criminal penalties regime has been proposed to protect critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) and improve the nation’s security. A white paper published this week outlines the UK’s growing dependence on CUI for modern digital services, as well as subsea pipelines and interconnectors. It also warns of growing risks posed by Russian submarines surveying cables in British waters, including near Shetland. Over recent years, Shetland has suffered several periods of disruption caused by damage to the Shefa-2 communications cable. Emergency services declared a major incident in 2022 when a complete communications blackout was caused when the cable was damaged in two places, leaving it without any backup. Further cable breaks caused prolonged disruption twice last year; first due to a mainland registered scallop dredger and then by Storm Amy. The white paper seeks to update the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, which remains the UK’s principal piece of legislation designed specifically to protect subsea cables from harm. While it says the STA’s core rationale remains sound – that CUI warrants specific protection in criminal law, it also states the legislation is “very outdated” and does not reflect the growing importance of undersea infrastructure, or the evolving threat environment. New offences would be based on a three-tier culpability structure depending on whether the conduct is intentional, reckless or grossly negligent. Intentional conduct could result in up to 14 years’ imprisonment; whereas for gross negligence the jail term would be up to two years. Orkney and Shetland MP Alistair Carmichael has today welcomed the proposals - and would like to hear local views. He said: “Having been banging this drum for some time I am glad that the government is taking the security of subsea infrastructure more seriously. This is only the start of the process but there is a lot here that is to be welcomed, if it is enacted properly. “Telecommunications resilience is an especially acute issue here in the isles but it really ought to be a concern for the entire United Kingdom – so it is vital that we get this right and that islanders get their say. “We know that what looks like a “resilient” system from a Whitehall perspective is not necessarily resilient when viewed from the Northern Isles. “That is why I am calling on anyone with an interest in these matters to send me their views on these proposals and the wider issue of resilience, so that I can make the strongest possible submission on behalf of our islands.” Visit the UK government website to read the white paper. Crime Politics Shetland Islands Council Andrew Hirst

Authored On Oct 25, 2026 17:46 Modified Oct 27, 2026 02:59 Europe mostly protects gas and data revenue it already earns Frigates get billions; cable repair gets tens of millions Accidents, not sabotage, cause most seabed damage so far According to figures from the European Commission, Norway accounted for 31% of natural gas imports to the EU in 2025. This number has been steadily increasing from 24% in 2021 and positions Norway as the biggest natural gas exporter to the EU from outside the union. The majority of this gas is transported via pipeline. In 2025, 86 billion cubic metres were sent to EU customers via Norwegian pipelines. That represents 54% of all natural gas sent by pipeline to the EU. Gassco, the state-owned pipeline operator for the 8,800 kilometres of pipeline running across the North Sea, sent a combined total of 114.9 billion cubic metres to Germany, the UK, Belgium, France and Denmark. There is a clear distinction between the debate over North Atlantic security and that of the Bering Strait . The commercial benefit of the Bering Strait comes from increased trade in the Arctic. Right now, that is just speculation. Whereas the benefit to the North Atlantic between Norway and the UK is already built and in use on the ocean floor. There is an implication that if money is spent on defence in these areas, most of that money is going towards assets that would earn money regardless. The question becomes: is it lowering the expected costs of not making that money by more than what is spent on defence? When talking about defence spending in these areas, there are many numbers being mixed together. First are actual amounts that are being spent. For example, Norway recently placed a £10 billion order with the UK for Type 26 Frigates. Next are plans that have no attached cost. The EU recently released its Arctic Strategy on the 20th of October 2026. Much of that plan fits this description. The last number is how much would be lost if a certain event occurred. With these three numbers in mind, Europe is spending more money on ships and less money on the ability to fix things when they break. Norwegian Gas Is Something Europe Cannot Replace Not only is Europe dependent on Norway for gas. Norway is also dependent on Europe. Crude oil, natural gas, natural gas liquids and condensate made up 1,000 billion NOK of Norwegian exports in 2025, according to information released by the Ministry of Energy and the Norwegian Offshore Directorate. This represented 57% of the total amount of goods exported from Norway. Gas brought in more than oil. Almost all of this gas travels through a few key points. The refining facilities in Kollsnes, Kårstø and Nyhamna. Various pipes travel through the North Sea. And the ports in the UK and Germany. The addition of the Arctic has allowed for gas to be shipped to ports by tanker from Hammerfest. Around 6.5 billion cubic meters are shipped from here each year. This is efficient when everything is working but can be devastating if one of these points fails. No matter what causes the issue (which is likely to be a mechanical failure). Europe has already seen the impact that one of these failures can have. At the beginning of June 2024, Gassco announced that a pipe had cracked on the Sleipner riser platform. This caused Nyhamna and Easington to shut down production. This removed 56 million cubic metres of gas from production that day. According to Argus Media, the Dutch TTF future price for gas to be delivered in July jumped from 34.43 euros per megawatt hour to 38.60 euros at one point that day. That is an increase of 12% because of a cracked pipe. No bad actor was involved. This can be extrapolated to what Europe would lose if a large gas supplier stopped sending gas to Europe. A good comparable would be the loss of Russia from the equation. After Russia stopped sending gas to Europe, governments across Europe allocated approximately 651 billion euros to protect their citizens from rising prices , according to Bruegel's fiscal response tracker. Norway has many more fail-safes in its pipeline network. So this is a high estimate of what Europe would lose if Norway stopped sending gas. Figure 1: Planned September shutdowns cut flows by nearly a quarter, a preview of what an unplanned outage would do. Data Cables Carry Risks Insurers Will No Longer Cover There is less information available on the costs of failing data cables. They are just as vulnerable as the pipelines. The European Commission released its Action Plan on Cable Security in February 2025. It states that 99% of all trans-oceanic internet traffic travels through undersea cables. Many of these travel to and from Ireland, the UK, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Norway. Information on undersea cables in the Arctic is limited. On the 7th of January 2022, one of the two cables that ran from mainland Norway to Svalbard lost power. This cable also serves the SvalSat ground station. It houses over 100 antennas to receive satellite information. Norwegian police stated that they found evidence that humans may have been involved but later dropped the case. The other cable continued to send traffic during this time. About nine months later, the SHEFA-2 cable that goes around Shetland lost power on both ends. Leaving many on the island without phone and internet. It took until the 23rd of October to repair. The cable company Faroese Telecom believes that a fishing boat caused the damage. Figure 2: Europe’s gas and data lifelines converge on a few Norwegian and British points, and the documented incidents so far trace back to accidents. While both of these could have been the work of a state, it is unlikely that every time a cable breaks, it's because of the Russians. By labeling these attacks, governments funnel money towards deterrence. The last two incidents in the Arctic could have easily been caused by fishing boats. Attribution no longer matters to one group of people. On the 6th of July 2026, the High Court in London ruled that Nord Stream AG would not be able to collect the 580 million euros it claimed from Lloyd's Insurance Company and Arch Insurance. They determined that the explosion that occurred in 2022 was covered under the policy's war exclusion. The court did not have to determine who was responsible for the attack. Companies that provide insurance for fixed structures that are on the ocean floor may not offer coverage for sabotage in the future. Gallagher Re warned of this in 2025. If a structure breaks in the Norwegian Sea, the owner may not be able to prove who did it or get reimbursed for the damage. This leaves companies and the public to pay for these losses. Repair Ships Are the Weak Point in North Atlantic Security If a cable breaks, a ship is needed to fix it. There will not be enough ships in 10-15 years, according to a study commissioned by the SubOptic Association in 2025. TeleGeography calculated that two-thirds of the ships that repair cables will reach the end of their lifespan by 2040. Maintaining current repair times would cost around $3 billion to build 15 new ships. And have another 5 as backups. Europe is spending very little on the ability to repair its cables. In the spring of 2026, the EU opened a 20 million euro project to develop modules to repair cables in the Baltic Sea. Then in June opened another call for proposals worth 40 million euros. To develop modules that can be used to repair cables in the Atlantic, Mediterranean and other seas. They also committed 5.8 million euros to two cable hubs. One in the Baltic and one in the Mediterranean. According to The Brussels Times. No cable hub yet covers the Norwegian Sea. Or off the coast of Shetland. The new Arctic Strategy mentions the development of an Arctic Cable Hub that can be used to monitor, defend, and help repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. But the document did not mention how much they would spend on any of these. The EU has committed 66 million euros so far to help repair cables. Norway is spending £10 billion on frigates. The EU has committed 533 million euros to help with submarine cables for 2024-2027. They have awarded 186 million to 25 projects so far. It would only pay for a fraction of one frigate. Defence planners argue that the ships will be there to deter attacks on infrastructure. That is true. But the evidence shows that most damage will likely come from fishing boats or old pipes. Deterrence will not help. The Centre for Eastern Studies said that Norway will receive its first Type 26 in 2030. That leaves a few years where, if something breaks off the coast of Scotland, it will be in line with the rest of the world's aging repair ships. The Defense Market Rewards Platforms Over Repair With the signing of the Lunna House Agreement on the 4th of December 2025. The UK and Norway will share a fleet of 8 British Type 26 Frigates and at least 5 Norwegian Type 26s. These ships will be able to work together. The UK Ministry of Defence stated that the Norwegian order will create over 4000 jobs in the UK. Norway will also receive a promise that Norwegian companies will receive industry benefits equal to the amount spent on frigates. This agreement also allows for the UK to work with Norway on building ships that can house autonomous mine-hunting and underwater warfare vehicles. These two nations will also lead NATO in the development of autonomous systems . This will open up a market for these types of technology. Companies from Norway and the UK are sure to benefit from this. Kongsberg ended 2025 with a record order backlog of 157 billion NOK. They made 58.6 billion NOK in revenue. They stated that the increase is due to their missile and air defense technology. They are also seeing an increase in sales of their subsea and sensor products. They plan to separate their non-military division, Kongsberg Maritime, in 2026. Norway recently voted to spend 1,635 billion NOK on defense from 2025-2036. In March of 2026, the Norwegian Government added another 115 billion. Reuters stated that Norway will not be purchasing long-range maritime surveillance drones due to the high cost and rate of advancement in this area. This shows that money will continue to be spent on larger defense platforms. And that there will be a lack of sensors and the ability to monitor the seabed. Figure 3: More than half of Kongsberg’s defence backlog is not delivered until 2028 or later, so the new spending reaches the water slowly. The new NATO spending guidelines from the Hague Summit in June 2025. Could allow for more money to be spent on monitoring infrastructure. Countries will have to spend 5% of their GDP on defense. Up to 1.5% can be spent on critical infrastructure, networks, civil defense, and the defense industrial base. Countries can choose to spend this money on ships and sensors that can help fix cables and pipelines. Or they can just rename money they are already spending and claim they are meeting the goal. Prevention Costs Are Known, Disruption Costs Are Not Europe is spending money on prevention but does not know how much money it will lose if its infrastructure is damaged. Of course, some amount of spending will make sense. Norway is only spending the equivalent of two years of petroleum exports on its defense budget. Including the extra 115 billion they added in 2026. So it is possible to protect Norway's oil and gas. The question is how much of that money is going towards the things that will save the most money. It doesn't look like much is being spent on things that will help if a cable or pipeline breaks. Insurance does not cover these incidents and the EU is doing little to help repair the cables. There are steps that can be taken by those who control the money . Energy departments and Gassco could look into spending money to make sure that if one pipe breaks, gas can still reach customers. Those who own cables can look into getting insurance. Or ask the government to create a program similar to Pool Re in the UK. That provides insurance for buildings that may be attacked. Those looking to spend money towards the new 1.5% category can spend it on ships that can fix cables and sensors that can monitor the seabed. Norway could also use its industry benefits to build ships that can help repair the infrastructure. All of these would cost less than building a new frigate. Europe is spending money to protect things it already has. The 31% of natural gas Europe receives from Norway was flowing before this debate began. As is the data that travels through undersea cables. By building more ships, Europe is helping protect the money it is already making. There is a new market for ships and sensors. But it will take time to grow and will mainly benefit a few companies. It is unclear whether Europe is spending too much or too little on defense. It is unclear what would be lost if the infrastructure failed. But it is clear that Europe is not spending as much on fixing its cables as it is on building ships. article.content: Submarine fibre-optic cables (subsea telecommunications cables) handle up to 99% of our global internet traffic and communications, underlining the operations of numerous businesses and institutions across the world. Their continued proliferation will bring higher network speeds and connect more people and regions to digital communications. Yet, whilst the world is on a roll in laying down more of this critical infrastructure, it is severely underequipped in properly maintaining them. Sub-Saharan Africa is no exception. As the region with the fastest-growing population and a large gap to fill in terms of internet connectivity, Sub-Saharan Africa is occupying an increasingly important position in the world’s network of submarine fibre-optic cables. Sub-Saharan Africa in the growing demand for Subsea telecommunications cables repairs Once a subsea telecommunications cable is laid, many potential costs are incurred: the future need for repairs due to factors such as human activity, natural disasters, and mechanical failure. Filling this role is the registered fleet of 63 ships that has subsea telecommunications cable repair capabilities, 60% of which are not solely dedicated to repairs but are also cable-laying ships. For Sub-Saharan Africa, it is serviced by the 44-year-old Léon Thévenin , the sole permanent subsea telecommunications cable repair vessel stationed at Cape Town to care for the cables connected to this massive region. Figure 1. Photo of the Léon Thévenin by Vessel Finder It is true that many cables are soon to be retired, with forecasts predicting the decommissioning of roughly 450,000 kilometers of cable over the course of 2026–2035. This means there will be legacy cables that no longer require constant maintenance or fault servicing. Yet, the laying of new cables far outpaces this retirement trend, with an expected 1,010,000 kilometers of new cable laid during that same time period. New cables carry higher technical resilience, but they remain just as vulnerable to external physical force, which accounts for the vast majority of subsea telecommunications cable faults. Consequently, overall demand for repairs will likely increase rather than shrink. Following the global trend, a net increase of subsea telecommunications cables and subsequent faults is expected for Sub-Saharan Africa. Major new subsea telecommunications cables are planned for Sub-Saharan Africa – such as Via Africa and the ReuNION Cable, with multiple landing sites in the region. It is imperative that regional repair capacity increases to match growing infrastructural needs. Existing deficiencies in repair capacity According to industry reports, Sub-Saharan Africa’s current situation seems to be fine on paper. In fact, it was forecasted that only around one vessel is needed to cover not just the region but the whole continent’s repair demands. It makes sense if we are only looking at the amount of expected subsea telecommunications cable faults, but this is not the case as we take distance into consideration. To illustrate how this relying on a single permanently stationed repair vessel is insufficient in answering potential demands in Sub-Saharan Africa, a report by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) in July 2026 highlighted how vulnerable this one-ship baseline really is through a hypothetical scenario where subsea telecommunications cable faults occur simultaneously near Mombasa and Dakar. One vessel clearly couldn’t cover both faults at the same time, not to mention the long transit time needed for the vessel to travel from one side of the continent to the other. North Africa is comparatively more well covered, such as by the Mediterranean Cable Maintenance Agreement (MECMA) , which provides two repair vessels based in nearby European ports to answer maintenance demands. And it should be noted that even so, the Mediterranean region itself is currently suffering from a repair vessel shortage. Even though Sub-Saharan Africa is technically supplemented by several vessels that are based in other regions, the overall repair readiness has proven to be insufficient. Recalling the high profile case of the 2024 underwater landslide in the Trou Sans Fond Canyon off the coast of Cote d’Ivoire , damaging four cables – MainOne, West Africa Cable System (WACS), Africa Coast to Europe (ACE), South Atlantic-3 (SAT-3). Under the ACMA (Atlantic Cable Maintenance Agreement), the C.S Sovereign arrived from London to repair the MainOne, WACS and ACE. The remaining cable (SAT-3) was repaired by the Léon Thévenin , which was directly responsible for the cable’s maintenance. It took the vessel 16 days to reach the fault area, and the repair operation by C.S Sovereign was even slower as it had to travel from London, taking more than a month since incident to fully repair the first cable (ACE). Distance matters as in another major incident the same year offshore of the Mtunzini Cable Landing Station, it only took the Léon Thévenin 4 days in transit to reach the site, repairing both the SEACOM and Eastern Africa Submarine Cable System (EASSy) cables in 3 weeks and restoring full internet capacity to East Africa. Fulfilling demands whilst balancing the books It is clear that Sub-Saharan Africa requires new ships and new local bases of operations to fulfil subsea telecommunications cable repair demands. However, the situation is more complex than simply buying more vessels. The maintenance cost of subsea telecommunications cables is highly fragmented between various entities within regional maintenance agreements. Simply calling for adding more repair vessels and supporting port infrastructure is not nuanced enough to solve the repair shortage on its own. To start, we must first understand more about these maintenance consortia and their subsea telecommunications cable repair vessels. Existing maintenance consortia (such as 2OCMA) are usually composed of private sector companies (e.g Orange) and state owned enterprises (e.g China Telecom). This includes telecom companies, technology corporations (e.g Meta). These consortia are also run on a non-profit basis (e.g ACMA ), with members pooling up resources to fund things such as repair vessel and remotely operated vehicle contracts. The mode of commission of repair vessels under these consortia varies. For instance, the 2OCMA has a long-term contract with Orange Marine (which is a subsidiary under Orange), to provide a permanent stationed vessel – the Léon Thévenin . The ship is based in Cape Town, and the depot is owned by Telkom SA . Other consortia hire external, third-party marine companies such as the Global Marine Group to fulfil their repair vessel needs. Figure 2. Consortium agreement distribution map by Orange Marine Hence, we must look toward expanding the contracted fleets of existing consortium agreements like 2OCMA and ACMA. For example, upscaling the 2OCMA from its one-ship configuration by contracting multiple vessels – which allows for simultaneous response to faults on different sides of the continent. If possible, to establish another contracted repair vessel base in either East or West Africa to provide quick, localised responses. ACMA may also set up a contracted forward base in West Africa, adding to the four existing bases in Europe, Bermuda and the Caribbean. Beyond consortia, private regional agreements such as APMA and E-marine technically cover parts of Sub-Saharan Africa, and should be considered and coordinated during these expansion efforts. Notwithstanding the higher costs of maintaining an expanded repair fleet, expanding repair capacity still deserves serious consideration given the astronomical costs of unaddressed faults. The high-profile Cote d’Ivoire underwater landslides in 2024 demonstrated this reality, with Nigeria alone suffering an estimated 593.6 million USD in economic losses from cable disruptions in the first four days. Even though it is unlikely that having more repair vessels can reduce this upfront loss, it can reduce the cascading systemic risks that are incurred as the cable remains unrepaired for weeks. On the other hand, the expected cost of maintaining a repair vessel goes up to 100,000 USD per day, with individual missions costing up to 3 million USD. These costs are undoubtedly heavy, yet this is to avoid the unquantifiable ripple effects from cascading systemic risks. And in the unlikely event that even the rerouted cables also suffered from damage, a delayed repair response could result in a prolonged internet blackout with insurmountable losses. It is understandable that not all telecom companies operate on the scale of hyperscalers or can afford the high maintenance costs of an expanded fleet and infrastructure. Since cost is usually shared, governments and hyperscalers active in the region should actively close possible funding gaps – aligning financial contributions directly with their systemic exposure. Just as the ITU recommended the establishment of Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) for underserviced regions , establishing PPPs for this purpose will likely help streamline the process by providing platforms for easier coordination. Alternatives for consideration It is also possible to consider improving the operational capacity of existing vessels. Similarly challenged by a deficit in repair capacity despite a growing network of subsea telecommunications cables, the European Commission announced on June 23, 2026, its efforts to fund adaptable modules that can be “rapidly installed and deployed by existing repair vessels” . Tentatively costing 40 million Euros, this initiative aims to bolster Europe’s local cable repair capabilities. As peers facing a similar challenge, organisations such as the African Union can consider establishing similar, localized mechanisms to strengthen regional repair readiness. The positioning of such modules in Cape Town could allow the Léon Thévenin to respond to crises even faster. South Africa at the present already stands out globally as the country with the shortest “commencement time” , only needing 1.95 days on average before the repair vessel disembarks. With the world’s median at 8 days , South Africa’s system provides a powerful blueprint for future regional bases in Africa and the rest of the World. This would likely bolster the operational capacity of repair vessels in the region, yet, it does not fully remedy the dangers caused by the insufficient amount of repair vessels in Sub-Saharan Africa. Governments in the region should also ensure the relative ease and convenience in acquiring repair permits in Exclusive Economic Zones, avoiding bureaucratic delays to minimize service disruption. This could be achieved through explicitly exempting cable repairs from cabotage laws, implementing fast track, single-window approval for repair vessels that have been previously registered. This would allow them to carry out repair work much faster than before, with minimal delays once arriving on site. It is important to note that interventions surrounding repair vessels are not the sole answer to this problem. Increasing cable resilience through the use of tougher materials, optimized positioning of cables, and real-time monitoring can serve as vital, simultaneous interventions to alleviate strain on the repair network and protect the region’s network stability. Yet, it does not distract us from the centrality of repair needs. Expanding repair readiness is not merely about staying online — it is about ensuring that Sub-Saharan Africa remains a resilient and fast-growing region.

article.content: 1.8 min read PTCL Warns of AAE-1 Repair-Related Slowdown Mian Nadeem, Pakistan Point News October 28, 2026 Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited has warned that internet users in Pakistan may experience slower speeds during peak hours while emergency repairs are carried out on the AAE-1 international submarine cable. In its October 28, 2026, announcement, PTCL said work had begun on the section between Italy and France and described the potential service decline as minor, particularly during busy periods. The company’s advisory extends through November 2, 2026, and asks users for patience and cooperation while the repair work is underway. AAE-1, or Asia-Africa-Europe 1, is a 25,000-kilometer consortium cable connecting Southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt. Its route includes Pakistan, Italy, and France, with the Pakistani landing at Karachi. The system also connects major carrier-neutral points of presence, including Marseille. The official AAE-1 system page lists an original minimum design capacity of 40 Tbps. That figure describes the system’s original design specification, not the capacity currently available during the repair window or the amount of traffic affected by the work. The announcement is significant for Pakistan because AAE-1 is one of the country’s most important routes for international internet traffic. Its European connections include landing points in Greece, Italy, and France, placing the repair location on the European portion of a system serving Pakistan. According to the source report, customers could notice effects most clearly during the evening traffic peak, especially for European-hosted websites and services. The advisory therefore connects a repair on the cable’s European section with a potential change in the experience of users in Pakistan, without quantifying that change. The confirmed operational status is that repair work has begun, with PTCL warning of possible peak-hour slowdowns through the stated window. November 2 is the expected end of that repair window, not a confirmed completion date. The announcement does not establish that repairs will be finished or normal service conditions restored on that day. For now, PTCL’s guidance remains a notice of possible temporary service degradation during the work, rather than a report that the cable repair has been completed. article.content: The Iran war has become a nursery for asymmetric warfare and newer ways of warfighting. Iran, a regional military power dwarfed by the economic, military and diplomatic might of the US, has defied the pre-eminent superpower for nearly eight months. The war is now in an ‘election intermission’. President Trump’s “no fresh strikes before the 3 November midterms” is holding. There is, however, no sign of a conflict closure. Even Trump’s “mother of all bombs” threat has failed to scare the IRGC. Instead, the underdog keeps coming up with innovative counter-threats and randomly prodding the soft underbelly of America’s allies in the region. Iran is also making sure the world feels the pain through energy shortages and economic damage and has successfully spread its ‘war pain’ across the globe. The timing could hardly be worse for the oil-rich Gulf economies. They were accelerating efforts to diversify beyond hydrocarbons by pouring billions into technology, wooing global tech firms and aspiring to become major technology and AI hubs. Data centres and subsea cables sit at the core of this push. Microsoft’s recent announcement of a $10 billion investment in the Gulf by 2030 is part of this initiative. The plan includes $400 million for subsea and terrestrial connectivity. Iran war has exposed how vulnerable and how unprepared the region is to geopolitical shocks. Their plan to diversify beyond oil has handed Iran levers to pressure Washington to back off. In early March, Iranian drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the UAE and a third in Bahrain. Iran also claimed hitting an Oracle data Centre in Dubai. Iran’s Parliament Speaker has warned that if the US attacked Iran’s power plants and other infrastructure, vital infrastructure across the Gulf would become legitimate targets for Iran. The state media issued a statement that American companies will be targeted. Yadollah Javani, the IRGC’s deputy head of political affairs, expanded the threat further by recently announcing that the internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz are also on Iran’s target list. Subsea cables converge near maritime chokepoints as they traverse the globe. In terms of numbers, the English Channel leads the list with 44 cables passing through it, followed by the US East Coast shelf and the Strait of Sicily with 32 each, and the Strait of Malacca with 29. The Red Sea and the waters around Taiwan have 17 apiece, and Suez 13. Cutting just 15 cables in the English Channel or off the US East Coast has the potential to disrupt 20 to 25 per cent of global data flows. Hormuz is a vital artery for the Gulf countries, but is not a passage for the Europe–Asia systems. Damage from cuts in Hormuz cables may thus remain largely regional. But in the case of the Red Sea, major Europe–Asia systems run through it. This presents the Iran-backed Houthis, who retain the ability to operate around Bab-el-Mandeb, a set of attractive targets to strike. A warning came in September 2025 when the SMW4 ( South East Asia-Middle East-Western Europe 4) and IMEWE ( India-Middle East - Western Europe) cables were cut near Jeddah. This caused performance degradation in internet services to South Asia, West Asia and parts of Europe. The cause of the cable severance remained suspicious. This signalled the capability of the players involved and the distinct possibility of a serious cable disruption in the Red Sea, if Iran is pushed against the wall. Satellites hog the limelight when we think of instant data and global high-speed internet. In reality, the unsung hero of the piece is the fibre-optic cables on the seabed. Cables carry upwards of 95 per cent of global data traffic, and by some assessments 99 per cent of intercontinental traffic; satellites account for well under 1 per cent. These cables are the backbone of the internet, telecommunications, virtual meetings, bank transactions and well over ten billion emails every hour. The gap in data transmission speed is even more striking. NASA, some time back, claimed achieving 200 gbps, the fastest satellite data transfer achieved. Compared to this, the transatlantic MAREA cable, between Virginia Beach and Bilbao, can transmit data at about 200 terabits per second across eight fibre pairs (1 terabit = 1,000 gigabits). Trans-ocean telecom cables have a long history. The earliest attempts to lay subsea cables were made in the 1840’s. The first successful transmission using subsea cable was an 1858 trans Atlantic transmission. The mission, however, lasted only a few hundred messages over a few weeks, due to cable damage. By 1866, a functional cable was successfully installed across the Atlantic Ocean. Cables improved over the years, and the first fibre-optic undersea cable was laid between the US, the UK and France in 1988. Today, over 600 systems are in service, stretching some 1.5 million kilometres. Another 100 are planned. Major new cable systems are the Juno system (Japan–California, about 10,000 km, 350 Tbps), Amazon’s Fastnet (US–Ireland, over 320 Tbps) due in 2028, and Meta’s Petal (US–France, about 7,000 km), billed as the first petabit-class cable, capable of one million Gbps, due in 2029. India is in the middle of its own cable rush. Reliance Jio’s twin systems, IAX and IEX (India-Asia Xpress and India-Europe Xpress), together span over 16,000 km with more than 200 Tbps capacity, and are expected to be commissioned soon. MIST (Myanmar/Malaysia-India-Singapore Transit), about 8,100 km, Mumbai-Chennai to Singapore, is nearing launch. Bharti Airtel, invested in 34 international cables, holds about 20% of the 19,200-km SEA-ME-WE 6 (Southeast Asia–Middle East–Western Europe), which runs from Singapore to France via Egypt and is due in service in 2026. Google’s America-India Connect, with a new gateway at Visakhapatnam, is in the pipeline, while Microsoft, Tata Communications, Singtel and Lightstorm are building I-2SEA (India–South East Asia), targeted for the end of 2029. Subsea cable deployment involves high capital investment. The complex marine environment calls for special customised cable laying vessels and equipment as well as specialised technology & skills. These vessels need unique onboard systems like the Dynamic Positioning systems that hold the cable-laying ship on precise navigation coordinates, the Linear cable engines that continuously monitor cable tension and feed the delicate fibre optic cable and the Subsea ploughs which operate remotely. Redundancy is a standard design feature of subsea network architecture. The underwater environment is harsh. Apart from normal wear & tear, earthquakes, landslides, fishing and anchor drags pose maintenance challenges. Deliberate acts of war have also entered this list now. Submarine fibre-optic cables are generally designed for a 25-year life. Globally, there are about 150 to 200 subsea telecom cable faults a year. About 70 to 80 per cent of them come from fishing gear and ship anchors in shallow waters, and are repaired quickly. Natural hazards account for less than 10 per cent, but can be devastating. In 2020, Congo River floods triggered a sediment-laden underwater avalanche in a deep-sea canyon off West Africa and severed two major cables. The repair fleet is a real bottleneck. There are only about 60 subsea cable laying / maintenance ships worldwide. About half of this fleet will reach the end of its service life by 2040. An ageing fleet, surge in demand, limited number of specialist carrier manufacturers and preference for building high-margin LNG carriers are some of the challenges faced by the subsea cable industry. Politics adds its own friction. Laying a subsea cable needs regulatory approval from every coastal state whose territorial waters or Exclusive Economic Zone it crosses, each with its own clearance authorities and timelines. UNCLOS guarantees the freedom to lay cables on the high seas and in EEZs, yet cable companies regularly face fee demands on assorted counts, delays in approvals and security-driven restrictions in disputed waters like the South China Sea. The world is getting irrevocably integrated, digitally. Statista expects global data generation to triple between 2025 and 2029 – roughly 30 per cent growth a year. Amid this data tsunami, a quieter and equally significant change is under way in who owns the cables. Until the 1990s, subsea cables were typically built by consortia of national telecom carriers such as AT&T, British Telecom, Telstra etc. Lately, the content and cloud giants–Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon–have become the leading investors, often building private cables on their own or with a few partners. TeleGeography data show them as stakeholders in over two-thirds of the systems now being planned. A 2026 National Bureau of Economic Research paper estimates that 70 per cent of global data flows today traverse at least one US-owned cable somewhere along the route, up from under 20 per cent in the early 1990s. Deliberate disruption of subsea cable systems by adversaries or even non-state actors is a real threat. This, combined with concentrated corporate control, vulnerable chokepoints and the relative ease of severing these cables, makes our digital future slippery and inadequately secure. Are the subsea telecom cables becoming the world’s new Achilles’ heel? Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results A fourth undersea fiber-optic cable serving Vietnam has developed a fault, further disrupting international Internet connectivity with three other cables remaining out of service. The SJC2 cable, which connects Vietnam with other parts of Asia, developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, on Tuesday, according to an international undersea cable operator. The simultaneous problem with four undersea cables has badly affected Vietnam's international Internet traffic, the operator said. The AAE-1 cable has been experiencing problems in its S1.H2 segment since February and has yet to be repaired. The Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the U.S., and the Intra Asia (IA) cable are also experiencing problems, with repairs expected to begin in early September. Undersea fiber-optic cables carry the bulk of Vietnam's international Internet traffic, and so its international bandwidth has been substantially reduced. Internet service providers have been balancing loads, rerouting traffic and adding capacity through other connections to minimize the impact on users. Ethernet cables connected to the LAN ports of a Wi-Fi modem/router. Photo by VnExpress/Luu Quy Network provider VNPT said it rerouted traffic through available connections immediately after the problems emerged to make the best use of its remaining capacity. But Internet access would "be affected to some extent" during peak hours, it said. Users might experience slower connections when browsing websites, streaming videos, or playing games hosted on overseas servers, though Internet services generally remain stable because of backup infrastructure, it said. The company described the incident as a force majeure event that affects all Internet service providers in Vietnam. A Viettel spokesperson told VnExpress that the company has been affected by the problems with the IA and AAE-1 cables. Its AAE-1 connection has been completely disrupted, sharply reducing the company's international capacity though its backup systems have not recorded any overload. To compensate for the lost capacity, Viettel added 800 Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable Wednesday. It is also adding 300 Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway, with the additional capacity expected to be available by Aug. 31. It has also rerouted some international traffic through a terrestrial cable running via Laos to Singapore and plans to add another 1.5 Tbps of capacity on that route by the end of the month. It said it could increase capacity on its Asia Direct Cable (ADC) to 50 Tbps if needed to "handle all international Internet traffic." The ADC, which was installed in 2025, links Vietnam with three major Asian connectivity hubs Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan. Vietnam is linked by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems, AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC and SJC2, the last two being the newest. The systems have suffered some 10 incidents a year since 2022. Repairs to undersea cables typically take several months to half a year and can sometimes take as long as a year. To reduce its dependence on undersea cables, Vietnam launched its first VSTN terrestrial fiber-optic cable in 2025 and has also approved trials of satellite Internet services. Earlier this month, Elon Musk's Starlink became the first company to be licensed to provide such services. Get VnExpress first in Google Search See more of the news you trust. article.content: Vietnam has once again been plagued by multiple subsea cable outages. As reported by VN Express , four of the six subsea cables that connect the country have suffered disruptions due to multiple simultaneous faults within these cables, though the specifics of these faults have not been revealed. 26 Aug 2021 What is a submarine cable? Subsea fiber explained Our wireless world depends on a few hundred fiber cables laid on the ocean floor Vietnam is connected by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2, with the last two being the newest cables. The cables impacted include parts of the SJC2 cable, which connects the country to other parts of Asia; the AAE-1 cable, which has seen issues since February; the Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the US; and the Intra Asia (IA) cable have also seen issues. Repairs on the AAG and IA cables are expected to start this month. The SJC2 cable is the latest to suffer disruption, notes VN Express, which reports that the cable developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, last week. These faults have led to mobile network operators in the country reporting network disruption, including VNPT and Viettel, while around 30 percent of Vietnam's international Internet traffic. In order to navigate these challenges, Viettel has added 800Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable on Wednesday, and is also adding 300Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway. It's not the first time the country's subsea cables have suffered severe disruption. In 2024, three cables connecting Vietnam (IA, APG, and AAE-1) were all hit by outages, while a year earlier, all five cables that connected the nation at the time were down simultaneously. article.content: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The subsea cable links Orkney, pictured, to mainland Scotland Published 26 July 2025 Updated 27 July 2025 Hundreds of people in Orkney and Shetland have experienced disruption to their internet and phone services because of damage to a subsea cable. Shetland Telecom said the Shefa-2 cable between Orkney and Banff sustained damage at about 03:00. It was initially thought that thousands of customers would be affected. The switchboard at Balfour Hospital in Kirkwall was down throughout Saturday and overnight into Sunday before the service was restored. Internet provider OpenReach said: "We'll continue to assess, but customer broadband impact is more limited than initially thought, with hundreds of customers disrupted." It added: Landline calls were never impacted, and we'll continue to work hard to resolve and repair." The cable, which links Orkney, Shetland and the Faroe Islands to mainland Scotland, was last damaged three years ago in an incident thought to have been because of a fishing vessel. The BBC understands emergency calls have not been impacted. A timescale for repairs will depend on a number of conditions including wind strength and direction. More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds Openreach, which supplies broadband in Orkney, apologised to those who had been affected. A spokesperson said: "Customers can still make landline calls, and whilst we're constantly assessing customer impact, we believe up to 10,000 customers in Faroe, Shetland and Orkney islands could have disruption to their broadband services. "We're working on repairs as soon as we can and will update further once we can confirm our specific work and timeline. Anyone experiencing any issues should report it to their service provider for further investigation as usual." Communications in Shetland were severely disrupted in October 2022 when the south subsea cable between the islands and the mainland was cut. Police declared a major incident with landlines and mobiles unusable. At the time, BBC News heard reports that many shops were unable to take card payments. The scale of the current incident is still being investigated.
