article.content: Strategic Assessment of Undersea Communications Resilience, Maritime Security, Restoration Sovereignty, Industrial Dependencies and Allied Crisis-Response Capabilities Scope: Global assessment of submarine telecommunications infrastructure and wartime restoration capabilities, with particular attention to the United States, NATO, the European Union, Italy, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the Baltic Sea, the Mediterranean, the Arctic and the Indo-Pacific; documentary baseline through 5 November 2026 and strategic outlook to 2031. Executive Summary / Bottom Line Up Front The principal strategic vulnerability of global submarine communications is not simply the possibility of cable damage. It is the risk that multiple geographically dispersed disruptions could exceed the capacity of the international repair system while military conflict restricts vessel access, commercial insurance, specialised components and operational coordination. – Submarine cables carry approximately 99% of intercontinental internet traffic, according to the European Commission. Their continuity is therefore inseparable from international finance, cloud infrastructure, commercial connectivity and government communications. Commission Increases Submarine Cable Security with €347 Million Investment and New Toolbox — European Commission — Feb 2026 . – The United States maintains a statutory two-vessel Cable Security Fleet, supported by privately operated commercial vessels. Its FY2027 Maritime Administration budget request proposes no new programme funding, compared with $10 million enacted for FY2026. This is a budgetary request, not proof that all existing operating obligations have ceased. 46 U.S.C. §53202 — United States Congress — 2019 ; MARAD FY2027 Congressional Budget Request, Cable Security Fleet, pp. 85–87 — U.S. Department of Transportation — 2026 . – The European Union has established a €347 million strategic cable-investment envelope under CEF Digital, while separate repair-capacity calls announced in 2026 total €60 million. The calls should not be interpreted as proof of installed, operationally available repair capacity. European Commission — Feb 2026 ; European Health and Digital Executive Agency — Jun 2026 . – Taiwan provides documented evidence of concentrated physical vulnerability. At the end of February 2026, its network comprised 15 international and 10 domestic submarine cables. Six international systems suffered disruptions following seismic activity in late 2025, demonstrating that multiple simultaneous faults can arise without hostile intervention. MODA Releases 2025 Submarine Cable Damage Analysis Report — Taiwan Ministry of Digital Affairs — Apr 2026 . – The United Kingdom initiated a legislative consultation on 22 October 2026 concerning critical undersea infrastructure, including security obligations and government intervention powers. These remain legislative proposals rather than enacted powers under the consultation. Proposals for New Legislation to Strengthen the Security and Resilience of Critical Undersea Infrastructure — UK Government — Oct 2026 . – NATO’s Baltic Sentry initiative demonstrates a documented increase in maritime surveillance and deterrence, but detection and military presence do not themselves establish the ability to repair multiple damaged cable systems under hostile conditions. NATO Launches Baltic Sentry to Increase Critical Infrastructure Security — NATO — Jan 2025 . Principal judgment: Submarine cable resilience must be evaluated as an integrated restoration system involving available ships, qualified personnel, compatible equipment, maritime access, legal authority, commercial risk allocation and geographically distributed redundancy. Without these elements, nominal network redundancy may provide only temporary protection during a sustained, multi-theatre crisis. Red Sea Submarine Cable Disruptions and Microsoft’s Surveillance Collaboration: Geopolitical Impacts on Global Connectivity and Privacy in 2025 The War Beneath the Sea: Why Western Defence Still Depends on an Unsecured Digital and Energy Lifeline The United States and Europe are investing in submarine cable security, but neither has demonstrated that it can restore essential military, telecommunications and electricity infrastructure during simultaneous maritime crises. The contradiction is becoming a matter of national expenditure, industrial sovereignty and military readiness. In 2026, the European Union allocated €347 million to strategic submarine cable projects, while Washington requested no new funding for its two-vessel Cable Security Fleet in fiscal year 2027. NATO strengthened maritime surveillance, France expanded its publicly controlled cable industry, and Italy entered a new phase of submarine telecommunications integration through Prysmian and Fincantieri. Yet surveillance, manufacturing and emergency legislation do not automatically create a functioning restoration capability. The unresolved question is who can mobilise compatible equipment, specialist vessels and qualified personnel when damaged infrastructure must be repaired in waters where commercial operators cannot safely work. The numbers reveal a procurement contradiction, not a shortage of political declarations More than 99% of international data traffic travels through submarine cables, according to the International Telecommunication Union. Its 2025 Global Connectivity Report identifies more than 500 operational systems and approximately 1.4 million kilometres of network infrastructure, while the International Cable Protection Committee applies a different reporting basis and estimates approximately 1.8 million kilometres in 2026. International bandwidth has reportedly grown by approximately 22% annually since 2021. The physical network is expanding, but its capacity to recover from concurrent failures cannot be inferred from either route length or transmission bandwidth. The economic model was designed around manageable accidents. The International Cable Protection Committee estimates approximately 150–200 submarine telecommunications cable faults annually , predominantly associated with fishing and anchoring. The ITU reported more than 170 repairs during 2025, while its technical guidance places typical mean repair time at approximately one to three weeks, depending on operating conditions. These statistics describe a system functioning largely under commercial assumptions. They do not measure its effective capacity when several regions require the same specialist vessels or when armed conflict prevents repairs from proceeding. The financial contrast is revealing. The European Commission’s €347 million CEF-Digital programme for 2026–2027 includes €60 million in submarine repair-capacity calls: €20 million initially directed toward the Baltic and €40 million subsequently covering the Mediterranean, Atlantic and outermost regions. Another €5.8 million was announced in June 2026 for the first Baltic and Mediterranean Regional Cable Hubs. These amounts concern different functions within the wider European framework and must not be added as independent commitments. Across the Atlantic, the United States’ Cable Security Fleet , established under Title 46 of the US Code, provides access to two privately owned vessels. The Maritime Administration recorded $10 million in FY2025 expenditure, $10 million enacted for FY2026 and zero new funding requested for FY2027 . The request does not abolish the statutory programme. It does, however, expose the difference between possessing legal access to a commercial capability and maintaining a financially supported, operationally assured national-security resource. The European procurement model contains a similar qualification. The 2026 CEF-Digital repair programme requires equipment modules capable of installation within three days after a compatible vessel reaches an appropriate port or shipyard. Applicants must identify at least three suitable vessels. That is a mobilisation requirement, not a guarantee of restoring a cable within three days. The vessel must still be available, properly equipped and able to reach the damaged system. The industrial and logistical process begins well before the actual repair. Military infrastructure makes the exposure more serious than an internet outage Commercial telecommunications represent only one part of the undersea infrastructure supporting national security. Military surveillance systems, dedicated communications networks, submarine electricity interconnectors and their supporting shore facilities perform different functions, but can depend on overlapping energy, industrial and communications resources. The US Navy’s Integrated Undersea Surveillance System demonstrates the established military dimension. Its publicly acknowledged mission includes the detection, classification and reporting of submarine activity using fixed, mobile and deployable surveillance capabilities. The system’s origins extend to the Sound Surveillance System, whose first naval facility was commissioned in 1954. Its contemporary configurations are not comprehensively public, preventing a reliable assessment of individual vulnerabilities. The distinction matters because damaging a cable is not necessarily equivalent to disabling the military function it supports. Alternative sensors, communications systems and processing arrangements may preserve essential capabilities. Equally, dedicated defence networks do not eliminate dependence on civilian electricity, telecommunications, ports or defence suppliers. NATO formalised this interdependence in its 15 September 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements , linking continuity of government, energy supplies, civil communications, transport and industrial support to the execution of military plans. The framework identifies seven resilience areas and requires attention to cascading failures and restoration capabilities. The most revealing implication is institutional. A navy may protect maritime infrastructure without controlling the commercial operator responsible for restoring it. A defence ministry may depend on electricity infrastructure managed by civilian transmission operators. A government may possess secure military communications yet remain reliant on civilian networks for logistics, procurement and industrial coordination. National defence continuity therefore depends on more than protected military installations. It depends on whether the civilian economy can continue providing the services required to sustain them. The Baltic proves that one kilometre of damage can mean six months without capacity The EstLink 2 electricity interconnector illustrates why submarine energy infrastructure deserves the same strategic attention as telecommunications. On 25 December 2024 , the 650 MW electricity connection between Finland and Estonia was disconnected following a fault subsequently identified in its submarine cable. Fingrid reported that the incident did not endanger Finland’s electricity system, but it removed an important cross-border transmission capability. The physical intervention involved replacing approximately one kilometre of cable . Offshore work took place during May and June 2025, and commercial service resumed on 20 June 2025 , almost six months after the original interruption. The distinction between physical damage and economic consequence is fundamental. A damaged section accounting for a small fraction of the connection’s approximately 170-kilometre length generated months of lost transmission availability. Yet 650 MW of unavailable transfer capacity cannot simply be converted into an equivalent electricity shortage: the actual consequences depend on generation, alternative interconnectors, reserves and market conditions. The incident occurred within a broader transformation of Baltic energy security. On 9 February 2025 , Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania synchronised their electricity systems with continental Europe through Poland, ending their previous synchronous dependence on Russia and Belarus. The European Commission reported more than €1.2 billion in EU grants supporting the synchronisation programme. These developments illustrate two different meanings of energy sovereignty. One concerns control of the electricity system’s operational architecture. The other concerns its ability to withstand the loss of individual transmission assets. A government can achieve the first while remaining exposed to the second. The same distinction applies to submarine military infrastructure. Possessing an independent surveillance or communications capability does not guarantee that damaged equipment can be repaired promptly, particularly when specialised resources must be mobilised across international jurisdictions. Europe’s industrial assets exist, but national control remains fragmented Europe is not without manufacturing or engineering capabilities. The more difficult issue is converting those capabilities into assured emergency availability. In March 2026, Alcatel Submarine Networks , 80% owned by the French state through the Agence des participations de l’État, announced approximately €100 million of investment over 2026–2028 at Calais and Greenwich. ASN reported three European factories, seven cable-laying vessels and more than 850,000 kilometres of optical systems historically deployed. These figures establish substantial industrial capacity, not a government-controlled emergency repair fleet. Commercial vessel commitments, engineering compatibility and cross-border manufacturing remain relevant even when a government holds a controlling equity interest. Italy’s position changed on 13 October 2026 , when Prysmian completed its acquisition of Xtera Topco through a joint venture owned 80% by Prysmian and 20% by Fincantieri , with an enterprise value of $65 million . The transaction brings together submarine telecommunications cable production, repeater technology and maritime-industrial expertise. The industrial geography extends beyond Italy. Prysmian announced that it was doubling production capacity at Nordenham in Germany and seeking up to 300 additional employees. The company also identified the planned EXA Meridian transatlantic system, with a length of 6,552 kilometres, 24 fibre pairs, more than 500 Tbps of scalable capacity and a target service date of 2029. These are announced production plans and project specifications, not completed emergency restoration assets. They nevertheless demonstrate how the next generation of submarine communications capacity is emerging through industrial groups whose ownership, technology and production are distributed among several allied countries. For Italy, the Prysmian–Fincantieri combination could support a more integrated industrial role in Mediterranean infrastructure. But corporate ownership does not provide automatic national authority over factories abroad, privately contracted ships or production already committed to other projects. For France, majority ownership of ASN provides a stronger direct public-industrial relationship, although manufacturing and vessel operations remain internationally distributed. Germany contributes specialist production capacity. The United Kingdom hosts Greenwich manufacturing and Xtera-related activities while maintaining direct Atlantic maritime interests. The central constraint is not the absence of European industry. It is whether national authorities have enforceable arrangements ensuring that compatible components, qualified engineers and suitable vessels will be available when commercial obligations and national-security requirements collide. Surveillance can detect a threat without providing the means to repair its consequences The military response to undersea security concerns has become more visible. NATO launched Baltic Sentry on 14 January 2025 , increasing maritime presence and surveillance around critical infrastructure. Its October 2026 reporting confirmed the continued participation of mine-countermeasures vessels and underwater systems in regional monitoring. On 9 April 2026 , the United Kingdom disclosed a monitoring operation involving an Akula-class Russian submarine and two specialised submarines associated with Russia’s Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research. British authorities reported an operation lasting more than one month, involving approximately 500 personnel and over 450 aircraft flying hours. These are documented British military observations and assessments. They are not proof that the monitored vessels destroyed a cable. Likewise, the investigation into the December 2024 Eagle S incident in the Gulf of Finland must be distinguished from an established finding of state-directed sabotage. The Finnish proceedings illustrate the legal difficulty. Prosecutors brought charges concerning damage to five cables and cited at least €60 million in direct repair costs . The Helsinki District Court initially declined jurisdiction in October 2025. On 27 August 2026 , the Helsinki Court of Appeal reversed that ruling and returned the matter for examination. The appellate decision established jurisdiction at that procedural stage, not criminal guilt or Russian state responsibility. The strategic problem is that governments may need to protect infrastructure and mobilise repairs before criminal or state attribution has been conclusively established. The United Kingdom’s 22 October 2026 critical undersea infrastructure White Paper addresses part of this difficulty. It proposes stronger resilience obligations, new offences and national-security direction powers extending to relevant infrastructure and repair providers. The consultation closes on 14 January 2027. These remain proposals, not enacted powers. There is also a military-law constraint. A civilian repair vessel does not automatically become a military objective because it operates in contested waters or receives naval assistance. Its status depends on its actual function and the applicable law of armed conflict. Governments considering escorts must reconcile operational protection, lawful military activity and the continued protection of civilians. This produces a difficult allocation problem: naval forces can improve surveillance and deter interference, but specialist restoration remains an industrial operation. A minehunter cannot automatically replace a fibre-optic cable repair vessel, and emergency legislation cannot manufacture missing components. The next 24 months will determine who absorbs the cost of institutional delay The first consequential decisions fall in 2027 . The United States must reconcile Cable Security Fleet requirements with the FY2027 budget process. The United Kingdom must decide what legal powers follow its January 2027 consultation. The European Union must turn its 2026 repair-capacity calls into awarded contracts, delivered equipment and qualified vessels. The implications extend through 2028 , when the credibility of the European approach should be measured through actual mobilisation exercises, compatible spare inventories and the capacity to conduct more than one restoration mission. The three-day equipment-installation requirement will have limited value if no suitable vessel, specialist crew or replacement cable is available at the required location. Industry will face a parallel constraint. ASN’s €100 million programme runs through 2028, while Prysmian’s planned Nordenham expansion and EXA Meridian project extend into the following years. New capacity can strengthen communications networks, but additional infrastructure also creates maintenance obligations. Manufacturing growth does not automatically increase the number of concurrent repairs the system can perform. The costs of inaction will not fall evenly. Governments would bear emergency coordination and security expenditure. Telecommunications and electricity operators would absorb repair liabilities and additional operating costs. Defence organisations could face reduced availability of supporting services. Industrial companies would confront disruptions to cross-border connectivity and energy exchange. Ultimately, businesses and households would pay through service degradation, higher costs or reduced reliability where existing alternatives prove insufficient. The choices made during 2027–2028 will therefore determine whether public expenditure purchases measurable restoration capacity or merely another layer of monitoring and institutional coordination. The central issue is no longer how extensively Western governments recognise the undersea threat. It is whether their budgets, contracts, industries and military authorities can deliver a repair when essential national infrastructure is no longer commercially accessible. Europe’s Cable Repair Gap: Insurance and Sovereignty Master Abstract Submarine Communications as a Strategic Dependency The architecture of international digital connectivity has evolved into a foundational infrastructure for economic exchange, public administration, financial markets, industrial operations and military communications. Although satellite systems, terrestrial fibre networks and alternative transmission technologies provide supplementary connectivity, submarine fibre-optic cables remain the principal physical medium for intercontinental data transmission. The European Commission attributes approximately 99% of intercontinental internet traffic to submarine cables, while the United Kingdom identifies the same proportion for its international data traffic. These figures describe distinct geographic measures and should not be combined into a single global traffic statistic. Commission Increases Submarine Cable Security with €347 Million Investment and New Toolbox — European Commission — Feb 2026 ; Critical Undersea Infrastructure Legislative Consultation — UK Government — Oct 2026 . This infrastructure’s significance extends well beyond conventional telecommunications. International payment processing, cloud-service interconnection, multinational corporate operations, research networks, government data exchanges and selected defence communications depend directly or indirectly on high-capacity international transmission. The strategic consequence is that submarine cable disruption is not confined to the telecommunications sector: depending on the availability of alternative routes, it can propagate into activities whose operating requirements exceed the capacity of surviving links. The severity of disruption, however, cannot be inferred solely from the number of damaged cables. It depends on the traffic carried, surviving route capacity, physical separation, network topology, landing-station arrangements and the ability of operators to reroute services. A cable failure therefore becomes a national-security concern when it diminishes the continuity of functions that governments and economies cannot readily substitute. The Difference Between Cable Protection and Restoration Sovereignty Contemporary submarine cable security policy increasingly recognises the distinction between preventing damage, detecting interference and restoring infrastructure after disruption. NATO’s Baltic Sentry initiative, introduced in January 2025, strengthened maritime presence and monitoring around critical undersea infrastructure, while the February 2026 European Cable Security Toolbox incorporated preventive, detective and recovery measures into a wider resilience framework. In June 2026, the European Commission announced €5.8 million for two Regional Cable Hubs in the Baltic and Mediterranean and a further €40 million call for submarine cable repair capacity. These measures demonstrate an institutional movement toward integrated protection and restoration, but their funding and implementation stages must be separated from demonstrable operational readiness. Restoration sovereignty should be understood as the practical capacity of a government or allied coalition to secure the return of essential communications within an operationally acceptable period, rather than as a requirement for exclusive state ownership of every cable, vessel or component. It requires assured or contractually reliable access to vessels, qualified crews, compatible spares, installation facilities, protected maritime routes and decision-making authority. These resources may be distributed across private operators and national jurisdictions. The resulting strategic question is not merely how many repair vessels exist, but whether a competent authority can mobilise them when commercial obligations, competing national requirements and conflict conditions restrict their availability. The United States and the Governance–Capability Gap The United States illustrates the distinction between commercial repair capability and state-assured mobilisation. Under Title 46, Section 53202 of the United States Code, the Cable Security Fleet comprises two privately owned, United States-documented vessels operating under agreements intended to support national-security requirements. The Maritime Administration’s FY2027 Congressional Budget Request identifies $10 million in FY2025 actual programme funding, $10 million enacted for FY2026 and no new funding requested for FY2027. The same document describes a mechanism through which participating commercial ship operators make vessels available to the Department of Defense upon request. This establishes a defined national-security access arrangement, but not a publicly demonstrated guarantee of simultaneous deployment in different maritime theatres. 46 U.S.C. §53202 — United States Congress — 2019 ; MARAD FY2027 Congressional Budget Request, pp. 85–87 — U.S. Department of Transportation — 2026 . The principal vulnerability is therefore institutional and operational as well as material. An emergency repair operation can require decisions involving telecommunications operators, maritime authorities, defence organisations, port administrations, insurers and foreign governments. Different authorities possess different legal powers, while the entity responsible for financing an intervention may not control the vessel needed to execute it. The United States has strengthened submarine cable licensing and security oversight: FCC rules effective in July 2026 include cybersecurity, physical-security and Covered List certification requirements. These requirements address important dimensions of preventive security, yet they do not independently resolve wartime repair allocation, component availability or naval support. The strategic assessment is that the decisive readiness metric must be the ability to execute a complete restoration operation, not merely the existence of regulatory controls or retained commercial vessels. The Ministry of Digital Affairs reported that, as of the end of February 2026, Taiwan had 15 international and 10 domestic submarine cables, all classified nationally as critical infrastructure. During the four-year period analysed by the ministry, nearshore cable incidents averaged seven to eight annually; anchor dragging accounted for an average of 38.3% of these incidents. For 2025 specifically, three of seven recorded nearshore incidents were attributed to anchor dragging, representing 42.9% of that year’s total. It prevents the automatic attribution of every cable failure to hostile activity, while demonstrating that several cable systems can suffer disruptions within a compressed period through natural events alone. The analytical implication is that deliberate interference could encounter a network already carrying unresolved faults, making restoration priorities and geographic redundancy more important than individual incident counts. A damaged cable may require fault localisation, vessel transit, maritime permissions, safe positioning, recovery of cable sections, compatible components, specialist jointing and technical testing before service restoration. When conflict is present, insurance conditions, crew safety, military activity and competing national repair priorities add further constraints. The relevant operational model is therefore a sequence of interdependent activities, any of which may delay the entire restoration process. Increasing the number of vessels without addressing components, legal access and deployability would improve only one part of that system. The 2027–2031 outlook should accordingly be evaluated through three interconnected variables: the geography and concurrency of cable damage; the effective capacity of restoration resources under conflict conditions; and the extent to which governments can coordinate public and private responsibilities. A favourable trajectory would involve distributed spare inventories, tested mobilisation procedures, accessible vessels and credible alternative communications routes. A deteriorating trajectory would involve rising competition for a small specialist workforce, restricted access to repair areas, slow acquisition of compatible components and political disagreements over emergency priorities. The most consequential unresolved issue is not whether submarine cables can be damaged—they demonstrably can—but whether the international restoration system can maintain essential connectivity when failures accumulate faster than repair resources can be mobilised and deployed. Pillar I — The Physical and Institutional Architecture of Global Submarine Communications Chapter 1 — The Global Submarine Cable System: Strategic Geography, Economic Dependence and Infrastructure Concentration Principal Strategic Judgment The global submarine telecommunications network must be understood as a geographically concentrated, commercially financed and internationally regulated infrastructure system whose operational importance exceeds the territorial jurisdiction of any individual state. Its principal structural vulnerability is not the absence of network redundancy, but the possibility that physically diverse routes, commercial transmission arrangements, landing-station facilities and network-management systems remain dependent on overlapping geographical and institutional resources. This distinction is essential because a country can possess several international cable connections without possessing equivalent independent paths for economic continuity, and a commercial operator can offer multiple network services while relying on a limited number of physical corridors. The decisive measure of resilience is therefore not the number of cables visible on a geographic map, but the ability of those cables, their landing facilities and their associated terrestrial infrastructure to preserve essential communications when individual systems or entire maritime regions become unavailable. The International Telecommunication Union’s Global Connectivity Report 2025 identifies submarine cables as the infrastructure carrying more than 99% of international data flows. The report records more than 500 operational submarine cable systems covering approximately 1.4 million kilometres, while also identifying a substantial transformation in financing, with major cloud and technology companies becoming increasingly important participants in international network investment. The International Cable Protection Committee reports a larger approximate installed network length of 1.7 million kilometres in 2025 and around 1.8 million kilometres in its 2026 public materials. These figures should not be represented as directly comparable observations of annual physical expansion without reconciling their methodologies, coverage and reference dates. They nevertheless establish the scale of a communications system extending across every major ocean and connecting national telecommunications markets to international digital services. The Physical Architecture of International Connectivity A modern submarine telecommunications system comprises several technologically and operationally distinct elements. The submarine cable itself contains optical fibres designed to transmit information using light signals. Submerged repeaters amplify optical signals over long distances, while branching units permit certain network configurations to serve multiple geographic destinations. At the landward end, cable landing stations contain the equipment required to terminate the submarine transmission system and integrate international capacity with terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure. The transmission network then connects through terrestrial fibre systems, exchange facilities and network nodes to data centres, telecommunications providers, enterprise networks and national communications infrastructure. The dependence of the entire system on these interconnected assets means that cable resilience cannot be measured independently from shore-based equipment, energy availability, physical security, terrestrial backhaul and the operational ability to transfer traffic among surviving routes. The distinction between submerged and terrestrial infrastructure has direct strategic consequences. A submarine cable may remain physically intact while services become unavailable because of damage to its landing facilities, a power supply interruption, a failure in associated transmission equipment or a disruption affecting the terrestrial network that carries traffic inland. Conversely, a damaged submarine segment may not cause a substantial interruption to end users when traffic can be transferred to alternative cable systems with sufficient available capacity. This distinction explains why an incident involving a strategically important cable does not automatically translate into measurable national economic losses. It also explains why a small number of facilities near the coast may have significance disproportionate to their physical size: they connect the submerged international network with the terrestrial infrastructure that supports economic and government functions. The ITU’s 2026 International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience explicitly identifies geographic concentration, limited route diversity, regulatory delay and inadequate repair preparedness as structural concerns. Its recommendations include stronger coordination between governments and commercial operators, improvements to permitting, diversification of routes, and arrangements for the timely deployment and repair of infrastructure. The recommendations reflect the physical reality that effective redundancy requires diversity throughout the communications chain rather than duplication of a single component. Global Network Measurements and Their Strategic Meaning The most important quantitative distinction concerns the different measures used to describe submarine telecommunications infrastructure. Cable-system count, total installed length, international bandwidth, usable transmission capacity, occupied capacity and traffic volumes are not interchangeable. A long submarine cable may provide substantial connectivity across an ocean without serving the same number of countries as a branching regional network. A country may host several landing stations but remain dependent on a limited number of international transmission corridors. A capacity upgrade can substantially increase the usable bandwidth of an existing cable without adding another geographically independent physical route. Consequently, strategic analysis that relies exclusively on cable numbers risks confusing nominal infrastructure expansion with actual resilience. A relatively small number of cable corridors may carry an increasing volume of economically critical communications, while the number and geographical distribution of assets capable of restoring those corridors may develop according to different commercial incentives. Ownership, Financing and the Transformation of Infrastructure Governance Historically, submarine telecommunications networks were primarily associated with national telecommunications administrations, international telecommunications carriers and consortia established to finance and operate long-distance communications. The contemporary model increasingly includes major cloud-service providers and technology companies financing infrastructure to support geographically distributed computing, content delivery and international data flows. The ITU identifies hyperscale technology companies as important contributors to the expansion of global submarine infrastructure. This transformation has significant consequences for governance because companies investing in transmission systems may simultaneously operate cloud platforms, digital services and international data-centre networks that depend on those same systems. Infrastructure decisions can therefore reflect a combination of telecommunications economics, cloud-network architecture, operational resilience requirements and strategic commercial competition. The political implications should not be reduced to a simple opposition between public and private ownership. Commercial participation can mobilise substantial capital, support technological innovation and accelerate the construction of high-capacity routes. At the same time, the distribution of ownership, financing, operating authority and security responsibilities may produce institutional fragmentation. The owner of a cable is not necessarily the same entity as the landing-station operator, the telecommunications company providing services over the cable, the ship responsible for maintenance or the government with jurisdiction over a particular maritime segment. These distinctions become especially important when a network disruption has national-security consequences: the public interest in restoring a specific route may differ from the order in which a private company would ordinarily allocate repair resources under its maintenance agreements. A useful national assessment must consequently distinguish five categories of control: legal ownership of cable assets; contractual rights to transmission capacity; operational control of network traffic; physical control of landing facilities; and jurisdiction over the maritime and territorial areas in which infrastructure is located. None of these categories automatically confers all the others. A state may exercise regulatory authority over a domestic landing station without owning the submarine cable connected to it. A multinational company may own or finance transmission infrastructure while relying on independent carriers and maintenance agreements to keep it operational. A cloud provider may be capable of changing digital traffic routes without possessing a dedicated repair vessel. These differences constitute a structural characteristic of contemporary digital infrastructure and must be incorporated into any analysis of sovereignty, resilience and emergency preparedness. The Difference Between Geographic Route Diversity and Effective Network Redundancy Redundancy is frequently presented as the principal reason why the submarine cable system can absorb ordinary accidents. When one cable is damaged, network operators may reroute communications through another system, provided that functioning transmission paths and sufficient capacity remain available. Yet the existence of alternative routes does not establish the level of service that can be preserved during a geographically concentrated disruption. The operational consequences depend on whether surviving systems have spare capacity, whether the affected services can technically use those paths, whether terrestrial interconnection is available, and whether the alternative route depends on infrastructure exposed to the same hazard. These conditions determine whether redundancy is genuine or merely nominal. A distinction must also be made between physical, logical, commercial and jurisdictional diversity. Physical diversity requires transmission paths exposed to different geographic hazards. Logical diversity concerns network configuration and the ability to redirect traffic. Commercial diversity involves independent suppliers or capacity contracts, which may nevertheless rely on common physical infrastructure. Jurisdictional diversity concerns the legal and political environments through which connections pass. A route that avoids one maritime danger may still be vulnerable because its alternative landing facilities are concentrated within the same country, or because the replacement path passes through a region subject to different security or regulatory restrictions. Therefore, two cable services purchased from separate companies cannot automatically be considered two independent physical routes. The Atlantic: High-Capacity Connectivity and Continental Interdependence The Atlantic is one of the principal physical interfaces between the North American and European digital economies. Its strategic importance derives from the combination of international telecommunications traffic, cloud-service connectivity, financial operations and the terrestrial networks associated with major economic centres on both sides of the ocean. The Atlantic cable system should therefore be understood as a distributed infrastructure environment rather than a single transoceanic corridor. Different routes, landing locations and commercial systems contribute to resilience, but their actual independence depends on the relationship between offshore paths and the networks through which traffic is distributed after landing. The United Kingdom occupies an important position in this environment. In its October 2026 consultation on critical undersea infrastructure, the British government stated that submarine telecommunications cables carry approximately 99% of the United Kingdom’s international data traffic. The government also recognised that the infrastructure is highly resilient under ordinary operating conditions, while identifying the possibility of hostile interference and the need to modernise regulatory powers. This simultaneous recognition of routine resilience and strategic vulnerability is analytically significant: it prevents the assumption that ordinary service reliability proves preparedness for deliberate, geographically distributed disruption. Data Centres, Financial Infrastructure and the Economics of Network Continuity Submarine cable systems constitute an important enabling infrastructure for financial, industrial and digital activity, but the economic consequences of disruption must be traced through the actual services affected. International financial transactions depend on communications networks linking institutions and markets, yet individual payment mechanisms may possess different arrangements for routing, processing and recovery. Cloud services depend on connectivity between users, applications and data-centre regions, but their tolerance of transmission interruption varies according to system design, workload location and replication arrangements. Industrial enterprises may depend on international connectivity for supply-chain coordination, engineering, commercial transactions and remote digital services, but the operational consequences of an outage differ across sectors and facilities. The economic mechanism is clear: when international transmission capacity becomes unavailable or insufficient, affected organisations may experience reduced service quality, interruption of digital processes, increased communications costs and delays in activities requiring international data exchange. However, the actual economic outcome depends on the number of services affected, the availability of alternative infrastructure, the duration of disruption and the effectiveness of contingency procedures. The distinction between infrastructure dependence and realised economic loss is fundamental to sound strategic analysis. Chapter 1 — Key Judgments The physical architecture of global submarine telecommunications is best characterised as a distributed international network with concentrated geographic interfaces and divided institutional control. Its scale cannot be measured adequately through cable-system counts alone, and growth in bandwidth, investment or transmission technology does not necessarily produce proportional improvements in physical resilience. The most important distinction for strategic planning is between infrastructure that exists, transmission capacity that is usable, alternative routes that are genuinely independent, and restoration resources that can be mobilised when needed. The Atlantic, Mediterranean, Baltic, Arctic, Red Sea and Indo-Pacific represent different combinations of geographic exposure, commercial dependence and national jurisdiction. Consequently, a uniform global security model would overlook the operational conditions that determine whether essential services remain available during disruption. The chapter’s central conclusion is that network resilience is a property of the complete communications system—including seabed routes, shore facilities, terrestrial networks, commercial rights and restoration arrangements—not an attribute of the submarine cable considered in isolation. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would require revision if independently documented traffic-routing, physical infrastructure and restoration data demonstrated that substantial portions of critical international services possess geographically independent backup capacity sufficient to maintain normal operations during concurrent regional disruptions. Conversely, evidence of shared landing facilities, convergent terrestrial paths, inadequate spare transmission capacity or highly concentrated maintenance resources would strengthen the judgment that nominal cable diversity can overstate effective resilience. Open Official Record The most consequential outstanding records for this chapter are authoritative, comparable inventories of physical cable routes and landing dependencies; national or regulatory assessments of essential-service international bandwidth requirements; independently established spare-capacity figures; and official documentation identifying the degree of physical separation among alternative communications corridors. These records would permit more precise conclusions without relying on commercial network maps as a substitute for operational readiness data. Chapter 2 — Maritime Threats, Cable Disruption Mechanisms and the Operational Geography of Undersea Competition Principal Strategic Judgment The security of submarine telecommunications infrastructure is increasingly shaped by the difficulty of distinguishing ordinary maritime accidents, environmental damage, negligent navigation and deliberate hostile interference before sufficient technical, forensic and legal evidence becomes available. This ambiguity has important strategic consequences because governments must often protect essential infrastructure and restore communications before an incident can be conclusively attributed. The challenge is therefore not limited to preventing hostile action. It includes the ability to recognise abnormal conditions, reconstruct the physical cause of damage, coordinate maritime authorities, preserve evidence and implement proportionate protective measures without treating every operational fault as an act of sabotage. The strongest evidence for this distinction comes from the contrast between global fault statistics and documented national investigations. The International Cable Protection Committee reports approximately 150–200 submarine telecommunications cable faults annually, with roughly 70–80% attributable to accidental human activity, principally fishing and ship anchoring. These figures establish that routine cable damage is a persistent industrial phenomenon rather than an exceptional occurrence. The security environment nevertheless changes when vessels operate near sensitive infrastructure under unusual circumstances, when multiple cable systems suffer damage within a restricted period, or when official investigations identify conduct potentially extending beyond navigational negligence. In such cases, the central analytical problem is determining whether the available observations support an accidental explanation, a deliberate criminal act or an operation directed or supported by a hostile state. Those explanations require different evidentiary thresholds and produce different legal and security consequences. The Physical Mechanisms of Submarine Cable Damage The principal physical hazards affecting submarine telecommunications systems arise from contact with maritime equipment, natural seabed movement and technical failure. Fishing activity can bring equipment into contact with exposed cable sections, while anchors and associated equipment can damage cables through direct contact or movement along the seabed. Seismic activity and submarine landslides can produce geographically concentrated disruption affecting several systems. Technical failures represent a separate category in which service interruption may arise without external mechanical interference. These mechanisms are operationally different, yet their immediate consequences can resemble one another: a cable may lose transmission capability, operators may register a fault, and physical inspection may be needed to determine the precise location and cause. The relationship between water depth and damage mechanism is important, although depth alone cannot determine vulnerability. Nearshore cable segments often interact with coastal maritime activity, including commercial shipping, fishing operations and seabed uses. Deeper offshore segments may face fewer routine human interactions but can be exposed to geological hazards and may require more demanding repair operations. The relevant physical variables include cable protection, local seabed conditions, maritime activity and environmental processes, rather than a universal classification in which shallow water is automatically dangerous and deep water automatically secure. Taiwan’s official 2025 damage analysis provides unusually specific evidence. The Ministry of Digital Affairs reported that, during the four-year observation period, incidents within 24 nautical miles averaged seven to eight annually, with anchor dragging responsible for an average of 38.3%. Of seven nearshore incidents recorded in 2025, three were attributed to anchor dragging, or 42.9%. Two of those incidents involved illegal anchoring by foreign-flagged vessels. The ministry separately identified submarine landslides caused by earthquakes as the principal offshore damage mechanism in its analysis. The 24-nautical-mile threshold is a national statistical classification used in the report and should not be confused with the legal limit of Taiwan’s territorial sea or with a general international definition of nearshore waters. The Evidentiary Problem of State Attribution Attributing an undersea incident to a state requires more than identifying a vessel associated with a particular country’s commercial networks, ownership structures or maritime trade. A vessel’s flag, ownership, beneficial control, commercial management, cargo origin and crew nationality may involve different jurisdictions and legal relationships. These characteristics are relevant to investigation, but none independently establishes that a state directed a particular act. Even evidence that a crew deliberately damaged a cable does not automatically establish that the act was conducted under government instructions or constituted a military operation. The Eagle S case illustrates the importance of maintaining separate analytical conclusions concerning physical cause, individual criminal responsibility and state involvement. The Finnish investigation and prosecution developed evidence concerning the vessel’s movements and alleged conduct. That record must not be converted into an unqualified finding of Russian state-directed sabotage simply because the vessel departed from Russia or was publicly associated with wider concerns over maritime activity. Establishing state responsibility requires evidence capable of connecting the relevant conduct to the state under the applicable rules of attribution. The absence of such evidence in the public record does not prove that no such relationship existed, but it limits the conclusions a responsible assessment can draw. The consequence is operationally significant. Governments may possess sufficient grounds to increase maritime surveillance or protect infrastructure before an investigation establishes criminal responsibility. They may also possess reasonable grounds to investigate possible hostile interference without being entitled to present the case publicly as a proven state attack. A disciplined response framework must preserve these distinctions because incorrect attribution can intensify diplomatic disputes, undermine prosecution and distort the assessment of future threats. Incident Attribution: From Physical Observation to Legal Responsibility The investigation of cable damage should be divided into distinct evidentiary questions. First, whether an identifiable cable fault occurred and when service degradation began. Second, whether technical evidence establishes the physical mechanism responsible. Third, whether reliable observations connect particular maritime activity to the damaged segment. Fourth, whether the conduct satisfies the requirements of a domestic offence or another applicable legal prohibition. Fifth, whether sufficient evidence establishes that the act was directed, controlled or otherwise attributable to a state. These stages should not be collapsed into a single conclusion because the evidence necessary for each is different. Environmental Events and the Strategic Problem of Correlated Failure Natural hazards deserve separate consideration because they can damage several cable systems without deliberate interference. Seismic activity and submarine landslides may affect geographically concentrated sections of infrastructure, creating simultaneous or near-simultaneous faults. Taiwan’s Ministry of Digital Affairs reported that seismic events in late 2025 affected six international submarine cable systems. This is evidence of correlated physical exposure, although the number of damaged systems does not by itself establish the proportion of total national bandwidth that became unavailable. MODA Releases 2025 Submarine Cable Damage Analysis Report — Taiwan Ministry of Digital Affairs — Apr 2026 . The operational importance of correlated damage is that restoration requirements can arise simultaneously. Different cable operators may need specialist vessels, technical crews and replacement components within the same period. Some repairs may require a different technical configuration or access to particular equipment, while geographical conditions may affect the time necessary for physical intervention. Under normal commercial circumstances, maintenance arrangements are designed to manage faults according to established procedures. When several systems are damaged together, the assumptions behind routine scheduling may become less reliable. The critical issue is the relationship between available resources and concurrent repair demand rather than the existence of a single especially difficult fault. Environmental damage also complicates security assessment. A naturally occurring event may already have reduced spare transmission capacity before a separate maritime incident takes place. In such circumstances, the consequences of the subsequent incident may be greater than they would have been under normal network conditions. This does not mean that every sequence of faults represents a coordinated campaign. It means that the cumulative condition of the network must be incorporated into security decisions. An incident’s strategic importance depends partly on the state of the infrastructure before the incident occurred. Strategic Concentration and the Limits of Geographic Threat Analysis Maritime geography affects exposure through the interaction of cable routes, coastal infrastructure, shipping patterns and available alternative connections. Constrained corridors may contain multiple systems serving different destinations, while remote oceanic routes may have fewer nearby hazards but more difficult logistical conditions. Neither configuration can be classified as categorically safer without examining the physical network and relevant operational constraints. The security significance of a corridor depends on at least four distinct relationships. The first is the concentration of infrastructure: how many independent systems occupy the relevant area. The second is the concentration of demand: how much essential communications traffic relies on those systems. The third is the availability of alternatives: whether other routes can accommodate affected services. The fourth is restoration accessibility: whether repair operations can be carried out under the prevailing maritime conditions. These variables may point in different directions. A heavily used corridor may possess extensive alternative capacity, while an apparently less important route may constitute the only practical international connection for a particular community. For institutional planning, the relevant objective is not to construct a speculative ranking of maritime locations according to hypothetical attack opportunities. It is to establish which critical services depend on particular infrastructure configurations and whether their continuity requirements remain satisfied after plausible categories of accident, environmental event or security-related disruption. The ITU’s 2026 recommendations reinforce this approach by calling for risk identification, improved monitoring, route diversity and enhanced preparedness rather than treating cable protection as a purely military mission. International Advisory Body on Submarine Cable Resilience: Final Report — International Telecommunication Union — Jul 2026 . The Limits of Maritime Monitoring Maritime domain awareness is necessary for cable protection but does not provide complete knowledge of underwater activity. Information derived from vessel identification systems, coastal monitoring, maritime patrols and other surveillance resources may help reconstruct movements or identify unusual behaviour. However, the absence of a particular electronic vessel signal does not independently demonstrate hostile intent, and the presence of a vessel near a cable does not establish that physical contact occurred. At the same time, reliance on voluntary or commercially available vessel information may produce incomplete observations of the relevant maritime environment. Effective monitoring therefore requires integration rather than dependence on a single data source. Telecommunications operators possess technical information concerning network status; maritime authorities possess information concerning shipping activity; law-enforcement institutions can collect admissible evidence; and military organisations may possess additional situational awareness within their lawful responsibilities. The challenge is developing coordination arrangements that permit rapid incident assessment while respecting confidentiality, legal competence and the protection of commercially sensitive information. The effectiveness of a monitoring programme should be assessed through observable outcomes: the ability to identify an actual fault, determine whether an incident requires intervention, preserve relevant evidence and support restoration. The number of surveillance assets deployed is not a sufficient performance measure. A sophisticated monitoring system that does not generate actionable decisions may provide less operational value than a smaller, well-integrated system linked to clear response responsibilities. Chapter 2 — Key Judgments The available record establishes that accidental human activity remains the dominant cause of routine submarine telecommunications cable faults. Environmental hazards can nevertheless produce multiple concurrent disruptions, while documented criminal investigations and official military observations demonstrate that deliberate interference and undersea security competition require separate institutional attention. These realities are not contradictory: an infrastructure system can experience mostly accidental faults while remaining vulnerable to intentional disruption. The Finnish Eagle S proceedings demonstrate the importance of distinguishing physical reconstruction, criminal allegations, financial damage and legal jurisdiction. Taiwan’s official reporting demonstrates the coexistence of nearshore human-related damage and offshore geological risks. The British and NATO records establish heightened concern about undersea military activity and the resulting expansion of monitoring initiatives. Collectively, these records support a security framework based on evidence, maritime cooperation, realistic restoration requirements and calibrated attribution. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would change materially if competent judicial or official investigations established additional confirmed cases of coordinated state-directed cable interference, or if improved reporting demonstrated that observed incidents were predominantly attributable to previously unrecognised technical or environmental mechanisms. More comprehensive operator data showing restoration demand, simultaneous fault frequency and actual service degradation would also permit a more precise assessment of how routine damage and hostile activity interact. Open Official Record The principal outstanding records concern the final judicial disposition and any subsequent appeals in major cable-damage proceedings; official post-incident technical assessments identifying physical causes; harmonised international reporting of concurrent submarine faults; and operational evidence connecting maritime surveillance to verified reductions in damage or restoration time. These records would improve attribution and effectiveness assessments without requiring speculative conclusions about hostile intent. Chapter 3 — Legal Jurisdiction, Sovereignty and the Protection of Submarine Infrastructure During Armed Conflict Principal Strategic Judgment The legal architecture governing submarine telecommunications infrastructure is characterised by an important asymmetry: international law recognises extensive freedoms to lay and maintain submarine cables, but authority to investigate interference, protect infrastructure, regulate vessels and conduct repair operations varies substantially according to maritime location, flag-state jurisdiction, national legislation and the existence of armed conflict. The resulting legal framework does not establish a single international authority responsible for submarine communications continuity. Instead, it distributes rights and obligations among coastal states, flag states, cable operators, repair contractors and, where relevant, parties to armed conflict. Consequently, the principal legal vulnerability is not a complete absence of protection, but the possibility that several competent authorities possess overlapping responsibilities while none has sufficient unilateral power to organise and secure an entire restoration operation. The foundational instrument is the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), adopted in 1982, which establishes maritime zones and regulates rights relating to navigation, submarine cables and continental-shelf activities. The applicable legal position differs between internal waters, territorial seas, exclusive economic zones, continental shelves and high-seas areas. During armed conflict, those rules must be considered alongside the applicable law of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, military necessity, proportionality and precautions in attack. Domestic criminal legislation, licensing arrangements, insurance contracts and the legal status of ships introduce additional considerations. The international framework therefore provides essential legal foundations without automatically resolving the administrative, operational or security requirements of emergency restoration. United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and Its Implementing Agreements — United Nations Office of Legal Affairs — 2025 . Sovereignty and Jurisdiction Across Maritime Zones The legal treatment of submarine cables depends principally on the distinction between coastal-state sovereignty and the specific rights established for other states within maritime zones. Under UNCLOS Article 2, coastal-state sovereignty extends over the territorial sea, its seabed and subsoil, subject to the Convention and other rules of international law. Article 3 permits a territorial sea extending to a maximum of 12 nautical miles from the applicable baselines. These provisions establish a comparatively strong jurisdictional position for coastal states in areas close to shore, where cables enter national territory and connect with terrestrial infrastructure. Nevertheless, coastal sovereignty is not unlimited; it operates within the rights and obligations established by international law, including applicable navigational rights. Beyond the territorial sea, the legal position changes. The exclusive economic zone extends no farther than 200 nautical miles from the applicable baselines under Article 57. Within that zone, the coastal state enjoys specified sovereign rights and jurisdiction, principally concerning natural resources and certain associated activities. It does not acquire the same comprehensive territorial sovereignty that applies within the territorial sea. Article 58 expressly preserves, subject to the Convention, the rights of other states relating to navigation and the laying of submarine cables and pipelines. On the continental shelf, Article 79 recognises the entitlement of all states to lay submarine cables and limits the circumstances in which the coastal state may impede their laying or maintenance. These provisions are central to the international character of submarine telecommunications infrastructure because many cable routes traverse maritime areas in which no single coastal state possesses comprehensive territorial authority. UNCLOS, Part II, Articles 2–3 — United Nations ; UNCLOS, Part V, Articles 56–58 — United Nations ; UNCLOS, Part VI, Article 79 — United Nations . The distinction has considerable operational consequences. A state may possess important security interests in a submarine cable crossing its exclusive economic zone without enjoying an unrestricted right to regulate every foreign vessel conducting activities in that zone. Similarly, the freedom to lay or maintain a cable does not automatically eliminate the practical requirement to comply with applicable domestic laws governing ports, customs, immigration, environmental protection and other matters within national competence. Repair operations may involve several legal regimes during a single mission: a vessel may depart from a foreign port, traverse international waters, enter a coastal state’s territorial sea, conduct technical work within an exclusive economic zone and require personnel or equipment to cross a national border. Each stage may involve different authorities and legal requirements. The Legal Distinction Between Submarine Cables and Pipelines UNCLOS Article 79 contains a distinction that is frequently overlooked in general discussions of undersea infrastructure. The provision addresses both submarine cables and pipelines, but does not apply identical restrictions to every aspect of their installation. Article 79(3) establishes that the delineation of the course for laying pipelines on the continental shelf is subject to coastal-state consent. That wording does not establish an equivalent general consent requirement for the course of telecommunications cables. Article 79(4), however, preserves coastal-state authority over cables and pipelines entering national territory or territorial seas and over specified infrastructure associated with exploitation of continental-shelf resources. This distinction matters because communications cables, electricity interconnectors and energy pipelines may share maritime environments while remaining subject to different technical and legal considerations. A government seeking to strengthen undersea infrastructure security cannot assume that an authority governing pipelines automatically applies in precisely the same way to telecommunications cables. Nor can a government assume that the absence of a general continental-shelf route-consent requirement eliminates other lawful regulatory powers. The correct legal assessment must identify the particular infrastructure, maritime zone, activity and applicable legal provision. UNCLOS, Article 79 — United Nations . The European Union’s submarine cable security framework encompasses both telecommunications and electricity cables, reflecting the common strategic concern that disruption to undersea infrastructure can affect essential economic functions. However, the legal and industrial requirements of protecting these assets remain different. Telecommunications systems carry digital information, while electricity interconnectors transmit electrical power, and pipelines may carry energy commodities. Their operational vulnerabilities and restoration requirements should therefore not be merged merely because they are located underwater. Submarine Cable Security Toolbox and Cable Projects of European Interest — European Commission — Feb 2026 . International Obligations Concerning Cable Damage UNCLOS Articles 112–115 establish several important protections and responsibilities relating to submarine cables beyond the continental shelf and to the conduct of states and persons subject to their jurisdiction. Article 112 recognises the right of all states to lay submarine cables and pipelines on the seabed of the high seas beyond the continental shelf. Article 113 requires states to adopt laws and regulations making certain deliberate or culpably negligent breaking or injury of submarine cables punishable when the relevant conditions are satisfied. Article 114 addresses responsibility for repair costs where an operator laying or repairing its own cable damages another cable or pipeline. Article 115 concerns indemnification where shipowners sacrifice anchors, nets or fishing equipment to avoid damaging submarine infrastructure after taking the required precautions. These provisions demonstrate that the international framework addresses both the protection of communications and the interaction between cables and ordinary maritime activity. It does not, however, establish a comprehensive international criminal court for every submarine cable incident, nor does it remove the need to determine which state possesses jurisdiction over the vessel or persons concerned. The existence of a substantive legal obligation to criminalise particular conduct is distinct from the competence of a national court to prosecute a particular defendant. UNCLOS, Part VII, Articles 112–115 — United Nations . The distinction becomes particularly consequential when a vessel is registered in one jurisdiction, its crew members possess different nationalities, the alleged conduct occurs beyond territorial waters and the consequences are experienced in another state. In such circumstances, legal proceedings may require careful analysis of flag-state jurisdiction, territorial effects, applicable criminal legislation and international restrictions on enforcement powers. The relevant rules cannot be reduced to the proposition that a coastal state automatically possesses criminal jurisdiction whenever infrastructure connected to its territory is damaged outside territorial waters. The Eagle S Litigation: A Significant 2026 Development in Maritime Criminal Jurisdiction The Finnish Eagle S proceedings provide a particularly important example of these legal questions because the jurisdictional issue developed through successive judicial decisions. On 3 October 2025, the Helsinki District Court ruled that it lacked jurisdiction to examine criminal charges arising from the alleged cable damage outside Finnish territorial waters. The case was appealed, and on 27 August 2026, the Helsinki Court of Appeal reversed that conclusion and returned the case to the District Court for examination. This development materially changes the legal assessment compared with accounts that stop at the October 2025 ruling. In decision HelHO:2026:9, the Court of Appeal concluded that Finnish authorities possessed jurisdiction because the alleged offences had produced legally relevant consequences in Finland. It also determined that the central conduct described in the charges did not constitute a maritime navigation incident of the type addressed by the relevant UNCLOS restriction. The court therefore considered that the Convention did not prevent Finnish criminal jurisdiction in the circumstances before it. This was a ruling concerning jurisdiction, not a final determination that the accused had committed the alleged offences. HelHO:2026:9, Judgment of 27 August 2026 — Helsinki Court of Appeal . The importance of this decision extends beyond the particular vessel because it demonstrates how the interpretation of maritime jurisdiction can affect the ability of coastal states to prosecute alleged interference with infrastructure situated outside territorial waters. The legal significance nevertheless remains bounded. It is a decision of a national appellate court concerning particular facts, domestic law and the interpretation of applicable international rules. It cannot be presented as a universal resolution of criminal jurisdiction over all submarine cable incidents. Nor should it be treated as automatically granting other states the same enforcement powers in every maritime zone.
