A national court’s competence to hear charges does not by itself determine the legality of every coercive measure undertaken at sea. Similarly, an investigation that collects compelling physical evidence does not automatically establish the criminal intent required for conviction. Effective maritime-security policy must therefore integrate competent legal advice before operational interventions and preserve evidentiary standards throughout subsequent proceedings. Flag-State Jurisdiction and the Limits of Coastal Enforcement The flag state occupies a central position in the international legal framework governing vessels operating beyond territorial waters. UNCLOS Articles 91–94 address nationality, status and flag-state duties, while Article 92 provides the general principle of exclusive flag-state jurisdiction on the high seas, subject to exceptions established by international treaties or the Convention. These rules are essential to maritime legal order but can complicate investigations involving infrastructure connected to other states. A ship may lawfully navigate through international waters while being subject to the administrative and disciplinary authority of its flag state, even when its activities affect infrastructure owned by companies established elsewhere. The coastal state’s response must therefore be based on an identified legal authority rather than a general assertion that the infrastructure is economically important. Depending on the circumstances, relevant grounds may arise from territorial jurisdiction, the effects of conduct, specific treaty provisions, applicable national legislation, flag-state consent or other recognised bases of authority. The assessment must also distinguish enforcement jurisdiction from prescriptive jurisdiction: the power to apply criminal law to certain conduct does not necessarily establish an unrestricted right to board, arrest or seize a foreign vessel outside territorial waters. The Eagle S litigation demonstrates the practical importance of these distinctions. The Court of Appeal’s recognition of jurisdiction to hear the charges cannot be generalised into an unlimited coastal-state power to enforce criminal law throughout an exclusive economic zone. The legal basis of any particular maritime operation must still be assessed according to the location, facts, applicable legislation and international obligations. UNCLOS, Part VII, Articles 91–94 — United Nations ; HelHO:2026:9 — Helsinki Court of Appeal — Aug 2026 . Wartime Legal Status of Submarine Telecommunications Cables When an armed conflict exists, submarine telecommunications infrastructure must be assessed under the applicable rules governing military objectives and civilian objects. The central principle is distinction: attacks may be directed against military objectives, but civilian objects must not be made the object of attack. Article 52 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions defines military objectives, insofar as objects are concerned, by reference to their nature, location, purpose or use and the definite military advantage that their destruction, capture or neutralisation would offer in the circumstances prevailing at the time. This definition is particularly important for submarine communications because commercial networks may carry traffic used by civilian organisations, government institutions and military authorities. Nevertheless, the existence of some military communications does not automatically establish that an entire geographically extensive cable network constitutes a lawful military objective. A legally competent assessment must consider the relevant object, its actual contribution to military action and the anticipated military advantage of attacking it. Where a cable system performs mixed civilian and military functions, the determination may be complex, especially because the consequences of its destruction may extend far beyond the immediate military use identified. Additional Protocol I, Article 52 — International Committee of the Red Cross Treaty Database — 1977 . The legal consequences also depend on treaty participation and customary international humanitarian law. Not every state is bound by every provision of Additional Protocol I as treaty law, although core principles concerning distinction, military objectives and the protection of civilians are also reflected in customary international humanitarian law. A national legal analysis must therefore identify which instruments bind the relevant parties and which rules apply independently as customary law. It would be incorrect to present a treaty provision as universally binding in precisely the same form without examining the parties’ legal positions. Military Necessity, Proportionality and Civilian Consequences Even where a submarine cable or related infrastructure qualifies as a military objective, the legality of an attack does not follow automatically. The customary rule of proportionality prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. The obligation to take feasible precautions in attack further requires those planning or deciding upon attacks to verify targets and take appropriate measures to avoid or minimise incidental civilian harm. These principles apply to military operations affecting communications infrastructure just as they apply to other objects, although the assessment may involve distinctive technical and systemic challenges. Customary International Humanitarian Law, Rule 14: Proportionality in Attack — International Committee of the Red Cross ; Additional Protocol I, Article 57: Precautions in Attack — International Committee of the Red Cross . The potential consequences of submarine cable disruption require particular attention because the infrastructure may support many civilian services that are geographically distant from the place of physical damage. A cable segment situated offshore may support financial communications, public administration, healthcare-related data exchange, industrial activity and other essential functions. The legal significance of these effects depends on their foreseeability, causal relationship to the contemplated attack and the applicable interpretation of incidental civilian harm. It would be inappropriate either to ignore reasonably foreseeable indirect consequences or to assert that every economically adverse effect automatically constitutes a legally relevant proportionality violation. The complexity of such assessments reinforces the need for technical information about network dependence and alternative routes. A state assessing military operations near communications infrastructure must distinguish the physical object under consideration from the services it supports and the civilian consequences of its interruption. This is particularly difficult where infrastructure ownership and network operation are divided among multiple commercial entities. The legal analysis cannot be separated from technical knowledge of the infrastructure’s actual use. Civilian Cable Repair Vessels and the Law of Naval Warfare Repair vessels present a distinct legal problem because their ordinary function is commercial infrastructure maintenance, but their activities may acquire military significance during armed conflict. A vessel repairing a civilian telecommunications system does not become a military objective simply because it operates in a conflict-affected maritime region. Its status depends on the applicable law and the circumstances of its use. Conversely, a vessel’s commercial ownership or civilian crew does not confer unconditional immunity if its activities satisfy the legal criteria applicable to military objectives. The central legal question is whether the vessel, by its nature, location, purpose or use, makes an effective contribution to military action and whether its neutralisation would offer a definite military advantage under the circumstances. A repair vessel engaged in restoring communications that substantially support military operations may require a more complex assessment than one working solely on civilian connectivity. Nevertheless, broad assumptions based on contractual relationships or the identity of the customer are inadequate substitutes for the actual legal test. The distinction is important because military support, contractual arrangements and technical activities may overlap without being identical. A related issue concerns naval escorts. The presence of military protection may be relevant to the operational and legal circumstances of a vessel, but escort alone should not be represented as universally or automatically converting every protected civilian ship into a lawful military objective. The analysis must consider the vessel’s own activities, the circumstances of the escort, the applicable law of naval warfare and the conduct of the parties. The protection of a repair vessel may also involve alternatives to close naval convoy, including maritime monitoring, coordination with coastal authorities and security arrangements designed to protect a wider operating area. Protection Arrangements and Their Legal Trade-Offs The operational need to protect repair vessels creates a relationship between security assistance and legal exposure. Governments may be asked to support commercial ships that cannot safely undertake repairs because of maritime threats, yet the form of assistance may affect the vessel’s operational conditions and the perception of its status. This is not a reason to deny protection categorically. It is a reason to design protection arrangements through prior legal and operational review rather than improvised decisions during an emergency. Domestic Emergency Powers and the Problem of Operational Coordination International law establishes important rights and constraints but does not create a comprehensive operational system for prioritising submarine cable restoration. Domestic legislation must therefore determine which national authorities can coordinate telecommunications operators, maritime institutions and other relevant actors during emergencies. The need for clarity becomes greater when cable damage affects essential services or requires public resources to support a commercially owned network. The United Kingdom’s October 2026 consultation is relevant because it explicitly addresses the modernisation of national legislation governing critical undersea infrastructure. The government’s proposals concern stronger security and resilience obligations and potential powers enabling authorities to intervene in particular circumstances. As of 5 November 2026, the consultation remains a policy and legislative process, not a completed statutory reform arising from the consultation itself. Its importance lies in the attempt to clarify the relationship between private infrastructure operation and national-security responsibilities. The European Union has pursued a complementary approach through coordinated risk assessment, security recommendations and investment programmes. The European Commission’s 2025 Action Plan on Cable Security established a framework addressing prevention, detection, response, recovery and deterrence, while the February 2026 Cable Security Toolbox and the list of Cable Projects of European Interest introduced further measures intended to reduce identified vulnerabilities. These instruments must be distinguished by legal character: a Commission recommendation, an action plan, a funding programme and a binding legislative obligation do not create identical enforceable duties. The Role of the International Telecommunication Union in Regulatory Coordination The ITU’s 2026 International Advisory Body recommendations provide a practical bridge between maritime law and telecommunications governance. The working group’s proposals include transparent permitting procedures, improvements to customs and cabotage arrangements where national law permits, pre-clearance of vessels and crews, and the designation of governmental single points of contact. These recommendations address administrative obstacles that can delay repair operations even when the physical resources required for restoration exist. Working Group 1 Recommendations: Timely Deployment and Repair — ITU and ICPC — Feb 2026 . The importance of a designated national point of contact is that it can reduce uncertainty concerning the authority responsible for coordinating permits and facilitating communications with operators. Such a mechanism would not displace the legal powers of other ministries or agencies, but it could improve coordination where several approvals are required. Similarly, pre-clearance arrangements and predictable regulatory procedures can reduce administrative uncertainty without requiring states to surrender substantive environmental, security or maritime jurisdiction. The recommendations are particularly relevant to multinational restoration operations. A vessel may possess the technical ability to repair a cable but still encounter delays when equipment importation, crew movement, port access or other regulatory requirements are unresolved. The ITU framework recognises that restoration capability depends on the compatibility of national procedures as well as the availability of ships and technical components. The Legal Position of Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom The European states most relevant to this assessment possess different maritime geographies and institutional responsibilities. Italy’s legal exposure is particularly associated with Mediterranean maritime activities, coastal infrastructure and international telecommunications connections. France’s responsibilities extend across metropolitan maritime regions and overseas territories, creating potentially diverse jurisdictional and operational requirements. Germany’s maritime interests include the Baltic and North Sea environments, while its dependence on European network integration creates legal and economic interests extending beyond infrastructure directly located in German waters. The United Kingdom operates outside the EU legal framework but remains bound by applicable international law and participates in NATO maritime-security structures. For each country, the legal assessment must identify national authorities competent to regulate telecommunications infrastructure, enforce maritime law, authorise port access and conduct security operations. It must also determine whether emergency powers are sufficient to coordinate essential-service restoration. These questions cannot be resolved through a generic assertion that all four states are subject to international maritime law. National legislation, administrative organisation and the distribution of competences differ, and practical restoration may involve infrastructure and vessels outside the jurisdiction of the state seeking to protect its communications. At the EU level, coordination is complicated by the distinction between European competence over relevant digital and internal-market matters and Member State responsibilities for national security, defence and particular maritime enforcement activities. The European Commission can develop policy instruments and administer funding within its competence, while national governments retain responsibilities that cannot simply be assumed by EU institutions. NATO adds a further institutional dimension because allied maritime security cooperation may support the protection of infrastructure without replacing national civil authorities or commercial maintenance arrangements. Legal Continuity During Armed Conflict and the Limits of Peacetime Assumptions A final distinction is necessary between the legal arrangements applicable during ordinary commercial operations and those that may become relevant during armed conflict. The peacetime law of the sea continues to provide an important background framework, but applicable rules of armed conflict may affect the rights, obligations and security conditions of vessels and infrastructure. These interactions must be analysed according to the particular circumstances rather than by assuming that peacetime commercial arrangements either remain entirely unaffected or automatically cease to apply. This distinction is especially important for neutral states and commercial operators. A repair vessel registered in a neutral state may operate under different legal and political conditions from a vessel controlled by a party to an armed conflict. The nature of the repair, the destination of the communications restored, the vessel’s conduct and its relationship with military forces may all require examination. It would be legally unsound to conclude that every repair operation supporting infrastructure used by a belligerent automatically constitutes direct participation in hostilities, just as it would be unsound to presume that a commercial label guarantees immunity regardless of actual military contribution. The law therefore imposes a requirement for factual precision. The legal status of an object cannot be determined solely by ownership, and the legality of an attack cannot be established exclusively through its possible contribution to military operations. Protection of civilian objects, proportionality and feasible precautions remain relevant, while the precise obligations depend on the applicable treaty and customary legal regime. Chapter 3 — Key Judgments The governing international legal framework provides substantial protections for submarine telecommunications infrastructure but distributes authority among states and institutions in ways that can complicate enforcement and emergency restoration. UNCLOS protects cable-laying and maintenance freedoms while recognising specific coastal-state rights, flag-state responsibilities and obligations concerning cable damage. These provisions do not create unlimited coastal jurisdiction throughout maritime zones, nor do they establish an international restoration authority capable of overriding national procedures. The Helsinki Court of Appeal’s 27 August 2026 decision in the Eagle S case is a significant development because it recognises Finnish criminal jurisdiction under the circumstances of the alleged incident, reversing an earlier restrictive interpretation. Its significance must not be overstated: it resolves a jurisdictional question at that procedural stage, not the ultimate criminal responsibility of the defendants or the universal application of the ruling to other maritime incidents. During armed conflict, commercial ownership does not automatically determine civilian protection or military-objective status. The applicable tests require examination of actual military contribution, definite military advantage and the continuing obligations of distinction, proportionality and precautions. The protection of repair vessels likewise requires case-specific assessment, particularly where military assistance is contemplated. The principal legal conclusion is that effective submarine cable resilience requires the alignment of international cable freedoms, national enforcement powers, emergency administrative procedures and the law governing maritime operations during armed conflict. Legal competence must be established before a crisis, rather than improvised after essential international communications have been disrupted. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would change materially if subsequent judicial decisions established a broader or narrower interpretation of national criminal jurisdiction over cable damage beyond territorial waters, if new binding international instruments clarified responsibilities for submarine infrastructure protection, or if national legislation created demonstrably effective emergency restoration powers. Developments in the law of naval warfare concerning commercial repair vessels and mixed civilian–military communications systems would also require careful examination. Open Official Record The consequential outstanding records include the ultimate judicial disposition of the Eagle S proceedings; authoritative national legislation defining submarine cable emergency powers; applicable bilateral and multinational repair-access arrangements; official rules governing maritime protection of civilian repair vessels; and completed legislative outcomes arising from the United Kingdom’s 2026 consultation. These documents are necessary to move from general international principles to a fully specified assessment of government authority and operational responsibility. Pillar I — Consolidated Strategic Assessment The three chapters establish a structural relationship among infrastructure geography, incident mechanisms and legal authority. Submarine telecommunications networks are international in physical design and economic function, but their protection remains dependent on geographically and institutionally differentiated arrangements. Their vulnerability arises partly from the concentration of transmission routes and supporting facilities, partly from maritime and environmental hazards, and partly from the difficulty of assigning responsibility when incidents involve foreign vessels or occur beyond territorial waters. The official record does not support the conclusion that the global network is inherently incapable of resisting disruption. It demonstrates that established commercial arrangements provide substantial ordinary resilience, that most routine faults arise from accidental activities and that governments and international organisations have introduced increasingly sophisticated security measures. It also establishes that the resilience of the system cannot be inferred from ordinary fault statistics, infrastructure counts or legal rights considered independently. The central strategic issue is the degree to which these elements remain effective when several incidents occur in different jurisdictions and when the conditions of armed conflict restrict maritime operations. A network may possess spare transmission capacity while lacking assured access to repair resources. A government may possess legal authority to investigate suspected wrongdoing without controlling the contractor required to restore a cable. A military organisation may be capable of detecting threatening maritime activity without possessing the legal or commercial authority to determine restoration priorities. These are different institutional and operational problems, and their solutions must be evaluated separately. Pillar I therefore establishes the foundation for the next analytical stage: determining whether the international cable maintenance and restoration system possesses sufficient industrial capacity, operational availability and legally coordinated authority to sustain essential communications under simultaneous disruption across several maritime theatres. Pillar II — Wartime Restoration, Industrial Capacity and the Strategic Economics of Infrastructure Continuity Chapter 4 — The Global Cable Repair System: Fleet Availability, Technical Capacity and Restoration Bottlenecks Principal Strategic Judgment The operational resilience of international submarine telecommunications infrastructure depends on a specialised maritime-industrial service whose capacity cannot be measured by the number of cable vessels formally registered, commercially advertised or associated with maintenance agreements. The decisive variable is the ability to assemble a technically compatible, legally authorised and operationally available repair capability at the required location within a period consistent with the continuity requirements of the affected communications network. This capability depends simultaneously on specialist vessels, trained crews, appropriate recovery and jointing equipment, compatible replacement materials, port infrastructure, maritime permissions, contractual mobilisation arrangements and the physical characteristics of the fault. These components form an interdependent restoration system in which the unavailability of one critical element can delay the entire operation, irrespective of the availability of the others. The international system has historically been organised to respond to geographically dispersed equipment failures and accidental damage under ordinary maritime conditions. This commercial model has enabled operators to maintain extensive global networks without financing a dedicated repair vessel for every cable system. Its economic efficiency, however, rests partly on the shared use of specialised assets. When several repairs compete for the same vessels, crews, technical equipment or replacement components, the allocation mechanisms that reduce commercial costs can become operational constraints. In wartime, this dependence may be amplified by restrictions on navigation, insurance, crew availability and access to particular maritime regions. The question is consequently not whether the global cable-maintenance industry possesses advanced capabilities—it demonstrably does—but whether its assets can be mobilised concurrently, across geographically separated operating areas, under conditions in which commercial assumptions about access and risk may no longer apply. The International Telecommunication Union’s July 2026 International Advisory Body report identifies increased repair times, insufficient regional resources and complex regulatory requirements among the major obstacles to submarine cable resilience. Its findings are consistent with the operational characteristics described in ITU-T G Supplement 41, the technical guidance governing the design of optical-fibre submarine cable systems. The latter explains that restoration requires identifying the fault, recovering the damaged section and replacing it using appropriate spare materials. It gives a typical mean time to repair of approximately one to three weeks, conditional on geographical location, depth, vessel availability, damage mechanism and weather. The interval is a technical reference estimate, not a guaranteed repair deadline or a reliable measure of restoration performance during armed conflict. The Operational Structure of a Submarine Cable Repair Mission A submarine cable restoration operation comprises successive technical and administrative stages whose duration depends on the characteristics of the affected system. The first is the identification and preliminary localisation of the fault through monitoring and testing performed by the relevant network operator. This determines whether the problem concerns submerged infrastructure, terminal transmission equipment or another part of the communications system. Once a marine repair is considered necessary, the operator or maintenance authority must identify a vessel capable of undertaking the work, confirm the availability of suitable equipment and materials, and arrange its deployment. The vessel must then reach the operating area, identify and recover the affected cable section, undertake the necessary replacement and jointing operations, return the repaired system to the seabed and support technical testing before restoration is declared complete. Although these activities form a recognisable operational sequence, their duration cannot be assumed to be uniform. Fault localisation may be complicated by the distance between cable landing stations and the damaged segment. The recovery process depends on seabed depth and local environmental conditions. The replacement operation requires components suited to the system concerned, while testing must establish that the repaired transmission path satisfies the necessary technical requirements. Weather can restrict maritime operations, and the availability of alternative telecommunications capacity may influence commercial decisions about the urgency of an intervention. Consequently, even an apparently straightforward cable fault can impose a restoration requirement extending beyond the repair work physically performed on the seabed. The distinction between time to restore service and time to complete physical repair is especially important. A network operator may restore customer connectivity through alternative routes before the damaged cable has been repaired. Conversely, completion of a physical cable repair does not necessarily establish that all previously affected services have recovered immediately, particularly where additional network reconfiguration is necessary. The two measurements describe different outcomes and must be reported independently. A government seeking to assess continuity of essential services should therefore require operational indicators for both the availability of communications and the condition of the damaged infrastructure. Maintenance Agreements and the Economics of Shared Repair Capacity The international maintenance model relies substantially on arrangements under which cable owners and operators obtain access to specialist repair services rather than maintaining entirely independent fleets. Regional maintenance agreements permit multiple cable systems to share maritime engineering assets, technical resources and operational support. This model reduces the capital burden borne by individual telecommunications operators, since a specialist vessel can serve several cable systems rather than remaining dedicated to a single route. The arrangement is economically rational where failures are sufficiently dispersed and repair demand remains compatible with available capacity. However, the relationship between a maintenance agreement and the immediate availability of a repair vessel must be interpreted carefully. Contractual participation may establish rights to request services, specify responsibilities and organise the sharing of costs, but it does not establish that a particular ship is permanently stationed near every participating cable. A vessel may already be engaged in another repair, carrying out installation work, undergoing maintenance or operating in a different geographical area. Its suitability may also depend on whether it carries appropriate equipment and materials for the affected cable system. Therefore, membership in an established maintenance arrangement should be considered evidence of a repair-service mechanism, not proof of immediate operational readiness. The ITU’s February 2026 recommendations recognise these problems and explicitly encourage governments to support the expansion of repair assets across different companies and countries, taking account of vessels and spare parts. The recommendations also support regional cooperation frameworks and the development of rapid-response capabilities for shallow-water incidents. These proposals indicate that the international policy discussion has moved beyond the narrow question of cable protection toward the availability, distribution and mobilisation of restoration resources. Specialist Vessel Categories and Actual Operational Capability The expression cable ship can conceal important differences between vessels designed for installation, maintenance and repair. Some vessels are equipped to undertake large-scale installation projects, transporting substantial quantities of new cable and operating along planned routes. Others are configured principally for maintenance and repair operations. Certain vessels may perform both functions, but their capability must be established through technical specifications rather than inferred from the general classification of the vessel. The relevant capabilities include cable storage arrangements, recovery and handling equipment, operational positioning systems, onboard jointing facilities, accommodation for specialist personnel, capacity to carry appropriate repair materials and suitability for the anticipated maritime environment. For deep-water operations, the ability to work effectively with cable at substantial depths becomes important. Nearshore interventions may require different equipment, particularly where access conditions make conventional deep-sea cable vessels unsuitable. The ITU’s recommendation to consider shallow-water rapid-response units reflects precisely this distinction. A nominal vessel inventory can therefore overstate effective global restoration capacity if it includes ships unsuitable for the relevant fault, unavailable because of existing commitments or unable to reach the operating area under current security conditions. Conversely, a vessel equipped for extensive installation work may represent an important reserve capability if it can be mobilised with the appropriate technical configuration. The relevant national-security assessment must identify the mission-compatible capacity of each vessel, not merely its classification or ownership. The Global Fleet Capacity Problem A reliable assessment of global repair capacity requires a consistent definition of the fleet being counted. An inventory may include vessels engaged in cable installation, dedicated maintenance ships, multipurpose vessels, ships undergoing construction and vessels technically capable of undertaking selected repair operations. These categories are not interchangeable. Counting every telecommunications cable vessel as an immediately deployable repair asset would overstate capacity, while counting only vessels permanently assigned to regional maintenance agreements could exclude assets capable of being redirected during emergencies. The available official record confirms that limited regional repair resources represent a recognised vulnerability. The ITU reported in February 2026 that vessel availability was restricted in certain regions and that repair initiation times had increased despite a relatively stable frequency of cable faults. Its April 2026 background assessment recorded more than 170 cable repairs worldwide during 2025, approximately equivalent to a reported average of 3.3 repairs per week when calculated over a 52-week year. This figure concerns documented repairs, not necessarily every physical fault occurring during that year. It cannot be used alone to infer the number of repair vessels required, because different incidents demand different quantities of vessel time and may involve different technical operations. Restoration Times: Technical Reference Values and Operational Reality The ITU-T technical reference of one to three weeks for mean repair time must be distinguished from the total duration of a national communications disruption. The figure describes a typical repair interval conditioned by technical and logistical circumstances; it is not a universal service-level guarantee. A repair operation can take longer because of vessel location, environmental conditions, equipment requirements or regulatory restrictions. Similarly, a communications outage can last less than the repair interval where operators successfully reroute traffic through alternative systems. The distinction becomes more important when several faults occur together. A single incident may require one mobilisation sequence, while additional incidents may require separate vessels, compatible materials and technical crews. If the necessary resources are shared, the second or subsequent repair may not begin immediately. Even where independent cable systems are damaged, their restoration requirements may compete for the same limited maritime assets. This creates a repair-queue problem whose consequences depend on vessel availability, service time and geographical distribution rather than the number of faults alone. A mathematically useful representation is to distinguish the arrival rate of repair requests, denoted by λ, from the effective completion capacity of the available repair system, denoted by μ. If repair demand persistently exceeds effective completion capacity, the outstanding repair workload will tend to increase. This is a general capacity constraint, not a calibrated prediction. The public institutional record does not establish a sufficiently consistent global dataset of repair arrivals, vessel operating hours, deployment times and mission compatibility to calculate a reliable wartime queue-growth rate. Qualified Personnel and the Limits of Expanding Fleet Numbers An additional vessel does not automatically provide an additional fully operational repair capability. Submarine telecommunications repair requires trained maritime personnel and specialist technical staff capable of handling cable recovery, jointing, optical transmission testing and associated marine engineering operations. These skills cannot necessarily be transferred immediately from conventional shipping or unrelated offshore industries. Technical qualification, practical experience with submerged systems and familiarity with the requirements of individual cable technologies are therefore integral elements of restoration capacity. Personnel availability also interacts with vessel deployment. A ship may be technically suitable and physically accessible but unable to undertake a particular operation without the required specialists. Commercial operators may maintain teams supporting several vessels, and individual repair missions can require expertise that is not available continuously at every location. Expanding the number of retained ships without ensuring the availability of qualified personnel could consequently generate nominal capacity that cannot be activated in practice. A government wishing to assess readiness should distinguish the number of qualified individuals, the number available for deployment, the number assigned to existing commitments and the number required for concurrent missions. The ITU’s recommendations concerning emergency response and regional cooperation imply the need to integrate human resources into preparedness planning. The relevant capability is a complete repair team supported by a suitable vessel and technical materials. In this context, personnel training is not a secondary administrative requirement but an industrial capability that may determine the speed at which additional restoration resources can be mobilised. Replacement Cable, Jointing Kits and Repeaters The technical materials required for submarine cable repair are not universally interchangeable. Individual submarine systems can differ in cable construction, optical characteristics, mechanical protection, repeater configuration, branching arrangements and other technical specifications. A repair contractor must therefore possess sufficiently accurate information about the damaged system and suitable replacement materials. Where the necessary components are unavailable locally, they may need to be transferred from an existing inventory or manufactured and transported to the repair location. ITU-T technical guidance identifies replacement of the damaged cable section as a central element of marine repair. This procedure requires both compatible cable and the ability to perform the appropriate jointing operations. The availability of a vessel alone is consequently insufficient if the relevant material inventory is incomplete. A spare cable section that cannot meet the necessary technical characteristics may not provide a viable substitute, while the unavailability of required components can delay operations even when the vessel and crew are ready. Repeaters introduce further technical requirements in long-distance systems. Their design and compatibility depend on the architecture of the particular cable system. The replacement of a component cannot be assumed to be possible using equipment intended for another manufacturer’s system without technical verification. These constraints create an important distinction between generic emergency supplies and validated repair inventories. The strategic value of a stockpile depends on the cable systems it can actually support. Ports, Shipyards and the European Modular Repair Model The European Union’s 2026 emergency repair programme introduces a useful alternative to relying exclusively on permanently dedicated repair vessels. Under the CEF-Digital Cable Repair Capacities initiative, public organisations with emergency-response responsibilities may seek funding for modular equipment that can be installed on suitably configured vessels. The second call, announced on 18 June 2026, provides €40 million and extends geographic coverage to the Mediterranean, Atlantic and EU outermost regions, following the earlier €20 million Baltic-focused call launched on 5 February 2026. The programme contains specific operational requirements. Applicants are expected to identify at least three vessels that are already configured, or will be configured, to receive the repair modules. The modules are to be located in ports or shipyards capable of installing them on a vessel within a maximum of three days after that vessel arrives at the relevant facility. This is a concrete requirement for equipment installation readiness, not a commitment to complete an offshore cable repair within three days. The total response also depends on vessel mobilisation, technical personnel, compatible replacement materials, maritime transit and the repair itself. CEF-Digital Second Call for Submarine Cable Repair Capacities — European Health and Digital Executive Agency — Jun 2026 . The programme is significant for three reasons. First, it attempts to separate the availability of specialist repair equipment from exclusive dependence on permanently dedicated cable ships. Second, it makes port and shipyard preparation an explicit part of emergency readiness. Third, it involves public organisations, including civil-protection authorities, coastguards and military navies, rather than relying solely on commercial telecommunications operators. Nevertheless, the modular model does not remove the need for engineering compatibility, vessel certification and trained personnel. A preconfigured commercial vessel may be suitable for a specified type of intervention without possessing the full capability of a purpose-built deep-water repair ship. The model should therefore be assessed through the number of modules delivered, the number of compatible vessels actually qualified, the readiness of installation facilities and the performance of practical exercises. Announced funding and application requirements are insufficient to establish that the programme has already delivered operational capacity across all intended sea basins. The United States: Retained Commercial Capability and the Limits of Budgetary Visibility The United States established the Cable Security Fleet under Chapter 532 of Title 46 of the United States Code. Section 53202 specifies a fleet of two vessels, privately owned and documented under the United States flag, operating under agreements intended to support national-security requirements. The statutory design preserves their use in commercial cable services while establishing arrangements for availability to the government. Section 53203 governs operating agreements, and the broader chapter defines the relevant national-security obligations and programme structure. The distinction between statutory capacity and operational availability is central. The existence of two vessels under an established programme does not establish that both can be mobilised simultaneously from favourable locations, that compatible equipment is available for every system or that the ships are free of commercial commitments at the moment of activation. Comparative Assessment: American Retention and European Modularity The US and European approaches address related problems through different institutional structures. The American system uses operating agreements to retain access to commercially active specialist vessels, while the European 2026 programme seeks to create adaptable repair equipment supported by preconfigured vessels and public emergency-response organisations. Neither architecture is sufficient to establish comprehensive restoration sovereignty independently. The US approach depends on the actual availability and deployment conditions of contracted ships. The European model depends on the successful procurement and certification of modules, the suitability of participating ships and the ability to assemble the necessary personnel and materials. A meaningful comparison must distinguish annual expenditure from multiyear investment commitments, retained vessels from modular equipment, and existing operational agreements from programmes still undergoing procurement. The American $10 million FY2026 allocation represents a documented annual programme appropriation. The European €60 million allocated across the two 2026 calls concerns funding opportunities for emergency repair capabilities. These figures cannot be converted into a direct measure of relative readiness without additional evidence concerning cost structures, actual assets delivered and operational performance. Chapter 4 — Key Judgments The international submarine cable repair industry possesses established technical competence, but the available official evidence does not support a reliable numerical estimate of the total repair capability immediately deployable during a simultaneous multi-region crisis. Commercial vessel inventories, regional maintenance arrangements and government funding figures describe different aspects of the system and should not be combined as though they measured a common operational quantity. The most consequential bottlenecks are the availability of technically compatible vessels, qualified personnel, suitable spare components, regulatory permissions and maritime access. Delays in any of these areas can prevent a repair operation from progressing, even where the physical cable fault is technically manageable. The European modular equipment initiative represents a concrete attempt to reduce dependence on permanently dedicated ships, while the American Cable Security Fleet provides a statutory mechanism for access to two privately operated vessels. The principal operational conclusion is that repair capacity must be measured through complete, deployable restoration missions rather than nominal vessel numbers. A useful readiness assessment requires confirmed resources, verified compatibility, defined mobilisation rights and realistic end-to-end restoration performance. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would change if authoritative vessel and maintenance records established that significant additional repair capacity can be mobilised rapidly across several regions without competing for personnel or equipment, or if official exercises demonstrated the ability to complete multiple simultaneous restoration operations under restricted maritime conditions. Evidence of persistent delays, vessel shortages or inadequate spare inventories would strengthen the conclusion that effective capacity is lower than nominal capacity suggests. Open Official Record The decisive outstanding information comprises the distribution and readiness of specialist vessels; the contents and mobilisation requirements of relevant maintenance agreements; validated inventories of compatible spare components; the availability of qualified repair personnel; actual deployment and repair durations; and performance results from completed emergency-response exercises. These records are needed to establish a credible operational baseline rather than relying on approximate fleet counts. Chapter 5 — Wartime Repair Under Contested Conditions: Military Protection, Insurance, Logistics and Government Authority Principal Strategic Judgment The transition from ordinary submarine cable maintenance to wartime restoration changes the operating conditions of the entire repair system. Commercial maintenance arrangements are generally organised around identifiable technical faults, contractually defined responsibilities, navigable maritime areas and the ability to obtain specialist resources through established markets. Armed conflict can disrupt these assumptions simultaneously. A repair vessel may remain physically available but be unable to obtain acceptable insurance, enter the affected waters, secure port services or assemble a crew willing and legally permitted to undertake the mission. The owner of the damaged cable may possess contractual rights to repair services while lacking the authority to compel military protection, alter national maritime restrictions or prioritise the restoration of essential government communications over other commercial requirements. Consequently, wartime restoration must be analysed as a combined civil–military operation requiring the coordination of distinct legal and operational authorities. The principal challenge is not simply to transfer commercial assets to military control. Such a transfer may create additional legal, contractual and security consequences without removing the underlying technical requirements. The necessary objective is to ensure that a competent authority can establish restoration priorities, identify suitable assets, secure lawful maritime access, allocate financial risks and coordinate protection while preserving clear responsibility for technical execution. An arrangement capable of performing these functions would represent a materially different level of preparedness from an ordinary maintenance contract or a maritime surveillance initiative. The Operational Transformation from Peacetime Maintenance to Wartime Restoration Under normal commercial conditions, restoration decisions are generally determined through contractual arrangements, technical urgency and the availability of alternative communications capacity. The consequences of a particular cable failure can be assessed in relation to the affected services and the economic interests of the parties responsible for the network. A wartime incident introduces additional considerations that cannot be reduced to private contractual obligations. A cable carrying essential government or military communications may receive priority despite limited commercial traffic. A highly utilised commercial network may require urgent restoration because its prolonged disruption would affect financial or public services. Another cable may be physically repairable but located in waters where maritime security conditions make immediate intervention unacceptable. These circumstances create a need for an explicit decision hierarchy. The authority responsible for establishing national restoration priorities may not own the cables concerned, while the organisations technically capable of conducting the work may be established abroad. Even where a government possesses statutory emergency powers, it must determine whether their exercise is operationally feasible and legally appropriate. A direction to repair infrastructure cannot create an available vessel, manufacture missing components or eliminate the physical risks faced by maritime personnel. Therefore, wartime restoration authority must be developed alongside industrial and logistical capacity. The UK government’s 22 October 2026 White Paper on Critical Undersea Infrastructure provides a particularly relevant institutional reference. The proposed national-security direction power would allow the Secretary of State, where necessary, to direct providers of submarine telecommunications infrastructure and providers of repair capabilities to undertake or refrain from specified actions. The White Paper expressly contemplates directions relating to the preservation of evidence, temporary reconfiguration or rerouting of traffic, prioritisation of essential connectivity and restoration work. Importantly, it recognises that government directions would need to account for technical feasibility, available vessels, personnel and safety constraints. As of 5 November 2026, these are proposals under consultation, not enacted powers arising from the White Paper. Critical Undersea Infrastructure Security and Resilience: Proposals for Modernising the UK’s Legislation — UK Government — Oct 2026 . The importance of this proposal lies in its attempt to address an institutional weakness that conventional telecommunications regulation may not fully resolve. Under ordinary circumstances, governments can cooperate with infrastructure operators through established emergency procedures and voluntary arrangements. During a severe national-security crisis, however, voluntary agreement may be insufficient to secure a particular outcome within the necessary period. An emergency direction power could provide a mechanism for prioritising public interests, but its utility would depend on clear thresholds, competent decision-making, safeguards and the actual capacity of the affected organisations to comply. Wartime Restoration as an Integrated Decision System A credible national restoration system requires decisions concerning technical feasibility, economic importance, maritime security and legal competence to be coordinated rather than taken independently. The first decision concerns whether the damaged infrastructure supports a function that cannot be adequately maintained through surviving routes. The second concerns whether the repair is technically possible with available vessels, personnel and components. The third concerns the maritime conditions under which the operation would be conducted. The fourth concerns which authority can approve, direct, finance or support the mission. The fifth concerns whether restoration should proceed immediately or whether another response—such as temporary rerouting, service prioritisation or additional maritime security—would provide a more acceptable balance of benefit and risk. These decisions are interdependent. A technically feasible operation may be delayed because the security risk is unacceptable. Conversely, a maritime environment considered sufficiently secure may not justify deployment if the required components are unavailable. A government may also determine that urgent rerouting offers a faster means of preserving essential services than physical repair, even where the cable must ultimately be restored. Effective emergency coordination should therefore distinguish the immediate continuity objective from the longer-term infrastructure restoration objective. Maritime War-Risk Insurance and the Commercial Availability of Repair Vessels Insurance is a critical component of maritime restoration because the willingness and ability of a shipowner to undertake a mission may depend on whether the risks associated with the operation are covered on acceptable terms. Conventional maritime insurance arrangements distinguish among several forms of exposure, while risks connected to war, hostile acts or designated high-risk areas may require specialised coverage. A deterioration in maritime security conditions can therefore affect a vessel’s commercial availability even when the ship remains technically capable of sailing. The United States maintains a federal Maritime War Risk Insurance programme administered through the Maritime Administration. Its stated objective is to provide war-risk insurance to US-flagged and foreign vessels when the Secretary of Transportation determines that adequate insurance for waterborne commerce cannot be obtained on reasonable commercial terms and conditions. This establishes an existing governmental instrument relevant to maritime operations under exceptional risk conditions. It does not establish that every submarine cable repair vessel automatically qualifies for coverage, that insurance will be issued for every conflict zone or that a particular crew can be compelled to undertake an unsafe operation. The existence of such a programme is strategically important because insurance market conditions may change more rapidly than physical vessel availability. A government could possess contractual access to a repair vessel while the commercial terms of the proposed mission become unacceptable to its owner or operator. Public insurance mechanisms may reduce a financial obstacle, but they cannot independently resolve navigational restrictions, the risk of attack or the absence of specialist personnel. Thus, insurance should be treated as one component of deployability rather than as a substitute for maritime security. The distinction between insurance for the vessel and protection of personnel is also important. The economic exposure of a shipowner may involve the hull, machinery, equipment, liabilities and interruption of commercial operations, while the interests and rights of crew members require separate consideration. Government-backed financial arrangements could address some of these risks, but the detailed terms of any intervention must be established through applicable law and contractual documentation. It would be unsound to assume that the presence of insurance automatically removes the legal, ethical or operational constraints associated with deploying civilian personnel in a conflict-affected area. Shipowners, Crews and Operational Risk Wartime restoration involves civilian maritime personnel whose employment conditions and safety cannot be treated as secondary to the technical urgency of a repair. Specialist cable vessels depend on experienced crews and technicians, and the loss or unavailability of these individuals may affect restoration capacity beyond a single mission. Operational planning must therefore account for personnel protection, contractual responsibilities, applicable labour requirements and the consequences of deployment into waters affected by military activity. The relevant question is not whether governments can eliminate every risk. Maritime operations inherently involve uncertainty, and emergency restoration may be necessary under difficult conditions. The institutional requirement is to establish a transparent decision process capable of weighing the importance of the communications function against the risks and practical constraints of the proposed intervention. Where crew participation is restricted by law or contract, a government cannot assume that a financial payment alone resolves the problem. For strategic readiness, a vessel should be considered deployable only when its physical condition, crew availability, insurance arrangements, legal permissions and operating-area conditions permit the intended mission. This definition is stricter than the commercial classification of a ship as operational or active, but it better reflects the actual requirements of restoration during hostilities. The Legal and Operational Consequences of Naval Protection Military protection may become necessary where threats to repair vessels prevent commercial operations from proceeding. Nevertheless, the decision to provide an escort or other security support requires a case-specific assessment of operational conditions, available naval assets, international law and the character of the repair activity. The legal distinction between civilian objects and military objectives remains relevant, as do the principles governing attacks and the protection of civilians. The presence of a naval escort should not automatically be equated with the loss of civilian protection, nor should commercial ownership be treated as an unconditional guarantee against lawful military action. The appropriate security arrangement may differ according to the mission. A repair vessel operating in a region where the main concern is interference by unidentified civilian vessels may benefit from maritime monitoring and coordination with coastal authorities. A mission facing credible threats associated with armed conflict may require more substantial protection, although the provision of close escort could impose additional military demands and require further legal assessment. In other circumstances, the security situation may make immediate repair unacceptable regardless of the resources available. The key requirement is that maritime protection be determined by the operational risk and lawful purpose of the mission. The integration of military resources should support the restoration objective without obscuring the technical responsibility of the repair contractor or creating unnecessary ambiguity over command and legal status. The Strategic Cost of Military Protection A naval escort consumes resources that may already be required for other operations. The use of frigates, patrol aircraft or other military assets to protect commercial repair activity can therefore create opportunity costs. During a regional conflict, governments may face competing demands for maritime security, protection of merchant shipping, military logistics and the defence of critical infrastructure. The decision to allocate military resources to a repair mission must consequently consider the expected benefit to essential communications and the effect on other authorised activities. This does not imply that cable restoration should receive a lower priority than conventional military missions. On the contrary, the continuity of communications may be essential to the operation of government and military systems. The relevant analytical requirement is to identify the relationship between the communications function being restored and the resources necessary to secure its restoration. Without this relationship, proposals for universal naval escorts risk becoming operationally unrealistic. Emergency Prioritisation of Competing Communications Functions A major disruption may force governments and network operators to distinguish among services that are all economically important but not equally urgent for national continuity. Military command communications, emergency public services, financial transaction systems and telecommunications networks supporting essential infrastructure may depend on different combinations of transmission routes. Restoration priorities should therefore be determined through an assessment of essential function, surviving capacity, likely duration of disruption and the consequences of further service degradation. A technically sound prioritisation system should not equate the commercial value of a cable with its strategic importance. A system carrying substantial commercial traffic may possess extensive alternatives, while a less commercially significant connection may support essential services in a location with limited redundancy. Likewise, the number of customers affected cannot be treated as the sole determinant of national-security priority. The relevant question concerns the consequences of continued disruption and the ability to mitigate those consequences by other means. The decision framework must also distinguish physical restoration from the allocation of remaining network capacity. In some circumstances, prioritising essential traffic over existing links may preserve critical services while marine repairs are delayed. In others, the network may lack sufficient alternative capacity, making physical repair more urgent. A competent emergency authority requires access to accurate information concerning both dimensions. Alliance Coordination and Cross-Border Restoration The multinational character of submarine telecommunications creates additional problems when a cable system connects several jurisdictions or passes through waters subject to different authorities. A repair operation may require diplomatic coordination, port access, equipment importation, permission to conduct marine work and cooperation between commercial operators established in different countries. During armed conflict, these requirements may become more difficult to satisfy, particularly if participating states differ in their legal positions or security assessments. The ITU’s 2026 recommendations address the peacetime foundations of this problem by encouraging transparent regulatory requirements, simplified customs procedures where permissible, pre-clearance of vessels and crews, and government-designated single points of contact. These proposals are operationally relevant to wartime readiness because administrative procedures developed before a crisis are more likely to remain usable when rapid mobilisation is necessary. However, a single point of contact is a coordination mechanism, not an independent authority empowered to override all national legal requirements. Within Europe, the Regional Cable Hubs and repair-capacity programmes provide potential foundations for coordinating information and resources across sea basins. NATO can contribute maritime situational awareness and authorised security activities, while Member States retain relevant national powers. The challenge is ensuring that these functions can be integrated without creating uncertainty about responsibility for decisions. A multinational arrangement should therefore specify the competent authority for approving a repair mission, the entity responsible for technical execution, the arrangements for maritime protection and the allocation of costs and liabilities. Chapter 5 — Key Judgments Wartime submarine cable restoration represents a distinct operational challenge that cannot be resolved solely by extending ordinary commercial maintenance procedures. The availability of ships, crews and technical materials must be considered together with maritime access, insurance, legal authority and the allocation of security resources. Government intervention powers can improve prioritisation and coordination, but they do not independently create deployable repair capacity. The United States possesses an existing statutory arrangement for access to retained commercial cable vessels and a federal maritime war-risk insurance programme. The United Kingdom has proposed additional powers to direct cable infrastructure and repair providers during serious national-security incidents. The European Union is developing regional coordination and modular emergency capabilities. These are materially different instruments whose effectiveness must be assessed according to legal status and operational performance. The principal judgment is that credible wartime readiness requires a pre-established civil–military restoration framework capable of converting technical resources and lawful authority into deployable missions under adverse conditions. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would be strengthened by official exercises demonstrating that maritime authorities, defence organisations, cable operators and insurers can mobilise and protect repair vessels during complex emergencies. It would also change if binding national legislation established clearer powers and responsibilities or if operational records demonstrated that existing commercial arrangements remain effective under severe access restrictions. Open Official Record The principal gaps concern the detailed terms of emergency vessel mobilisation agreements, the conditions under which government war-risk insurance can be activated for submarine cable repair missions, official maritime protection procedures, crew-safety arrangements, multinational command relationships and the performance of exercises involving concurrent restoration requirements. Chapter 6 — Industrial Sovereignty, Telecommunications Supply Chains and the Financial Consequences of Restoration Failure Principal Strategic Judgment Submarine cable restoration sovereignty ultimately depends on industrial capacity as much as maritime access. A government may possess the legal authority to prioritise an intervention and the financial resources to support it, yet remain unable to restore an essential communications link if compatible equipment cannot be manufactured, released from existing commitments, transported and installed within the required period. The principal industrial vulnerability is therefore not necessarily the absence of domestic cable production. It is the concentration of specialised manufacturing capabilities, the technical compatibility of equipment, the allocation of production capacity between new installations and maintenance, and the dependence of restoration on commercial supply chains whose priorities may not coincide with national-security requirements. The resulting economic problem has two dimensions. At the supply end, governments and telecommunications operators must determine whether sufficient industrial resources exist to repair important systems during concurrent disruptions. At the demand end, they must determine which essential economic activities would suffer from reduced international connectivity and how long those activities could operate through alternative communications arrangements. The relationship is potentially nonlinear: a short interruption affecting a highly redundant network may have limited consequences, whereas a prolonged reduction in capacity affecting a geographically concentrated market could disrupt several interconnected services. Neither effect can be quantified reliably through cable length, nominal transmission capacity or the number of affected systems alone. The European Commission’s Joint Research Centre estimated in August 2025 that the installation cost of submarine telecommunications cables generally ranged from approximately €25,000 to €45,000 per kilometre, compared with €1 million to €2 million per kilometre for submarine electricity cables. These figures refer to different infrastructure classes and should not be applied to emergency repairs without accounting for mobilisation, specialist components, operational complexity and the circumstances of the incident. Their importance is to demonstrate that submarine telecommunications and electricity infrastructure have materially different cost structures, even where they are both incorporated into public policies concerning critical undersea infrastructure. Subsea Cables: How Vulnerable Are They and Can We Protect Them? — European Commission Joint Research Centre — Aug 2025 . The Industrial Structure of Submarine Telecommunications Manufacturing A complete submarine telecommunications system requires several industrial capabilities that should be assessed separately: optical-fibre cable manufacturing, production of submerged transmission equipment, development of repeaters and associated components, engineering of integrated systems, marine installation, and technical maintenance. Some companies integrate several stages of this process, while others specialise in individual technologies. This creates a market in which the nationality of a cable manufacturer does not necessarily identify the origin of every component or the location of every critical engineering capability. The distinction matters for national-security procurement. A company may manufacture submarine cable in an allied country while relying on specialised components, intellectual property or subcontractors operating elsewhere. A system integrator may possess the technical knowledge necessary to design and install a cable without maintaining an independent industrial capacity to manufacture every replacement component. Conversely, an industrial group may own extensive cable production facilities without possessing all the specialised maritime resources required for emergency intervention. Industrial sovereignty should therefore be defined in operational terms. The relevant question is not whether every component is produced domestically, but whether essential technical capabilities and replacement materials can be obtained reliably under foreseeable restrictions. This may involve domestic manufacturing, allied industrial arrangements, qualified alternative suppliers, strategic inventories or a combination of these mechanisms. France: State Ownership and the Expansion of Submarine Telecommunications Production France provides a significant example of direct state participation in the submarine telecommunications industrial base. Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN) stated in March 2026 that it was 80% owned by the French State Investment Agency, the Agence des participations de l’État. The company reported more than 850,000 kilometres of submerged optical systems deployed worldwide, three European factories and an exclusive fleet of seven cable-laying vessels. These figures describe the company’s historical industrial activity and declared assets. The 850,000-kilometre figure is not the length of infrastructure currently owned by the French state, and the seven-vessel figure does not establish how many ships are immediately available for emergency repair. On 12 March 2026, ASN announced an investment programme of approximately €100 million over three years, from 2026 to 2028, to modernise its production facilities at Calais in France and Greenwich in the United Kingdom. The investment includes the renovation and expansion of facilities at Calais and the development of production infrastructure at Greenwich. ASN associated the programme with increasing demand for international bandwidth, cloud services and artificial-intelligence infrastructure. These are company-reported investment intentions; the announcement does not establish that the entire programme has already been completed or that its additional production capacity is available for emergency restoration. Alcatel Submarine Networks Invests in Its Industrial Production Facilities — Alcatel Submarine Networks — Mar 2026 . The French position is strategically important because state ownership provides a form of public influence over a major industrial participant. It does not, however, eliminate the need to distinguish corporate ownership from the legal authority to redirect commercial resources. A state-controlled company may possess obligations to customers, employees and contractual partners that must be addressed through the applicable legal framework. Its manufacturing and maritime assets may also be distributed across different jurisdictions, requiring cooperation with the relevant national authorities. The geographical distribution of ASN’s investment is particularly notable. Although the French state is the majority shareholder, the company is investing in industrial facilities located in both France and the United Kingdom. This demonstrates that industrial sovereignty may depend on cross-border production even where ownership is concentrated in a national public institution. The relevant resilience question is whether those facilities can support critical replacement production and how their capacity would be allocated during competing commercial and government requirements. Italy and Germany: Prysmian’s Expansion into Integrated Submarine Telecommunications A major development occurred on 13 October 2026, when Italian industrial group Prysmian announced completion of its acquisition of Xtera Topco Limited, a specialist in submarine telecommunications systems with UK and US operations. The acquisition was completed through a joint venture owned 80% by Prysmian and 20% by Fincantieri, with an announced enterprise value of $65 million. The combination brings Xtera’s proprietary repeater technology and telecommunications engineering capabilities together with Prysmian’s manufacturing and installation expertise. The transaction is important because it extends the industrial capabilities of an Italian-based group beyond conventional cable production into more integrated submarine telecommunications systems. It also introduces Fincantieri, an Italian shipbuilding and maritime-industrial group, into the ownership structure of the acquired telecommunications business. This combination may create opportunities for industrial coordination, but it does not prove that the joint venture possesses an independently deployable wartime cable repair fleet or that the transaction automatically establishes national control over every relevant technology. Those capabilities must be demonstrated through contracts, facilities, personnel and operational arrangements. Prysmian Completes Xtera Acquisition and Accelerates Expansion in Submarine Telecom — Prysmian — Oct 2026 . The same announcement identifies a concrete expansion of submarine telecommunications manufacturing in Germany. Prysmian stated that it was doubling production capacity at its Nordenham facility and seeking to recruit up to 300 additional employees. The company described Nordenham as an established industrial centre for submarine telecommunications cable production, with manufacturing activity dating to 1899. These developments make Germany an important part of the industrial geography of the Italian group’s expansion. Prysmian also reported that Xtera had been selected for the EXA Meridian transatlantic project, connecting New Jersey in the United States with Brean in the United Kingdom. The planned system is described as 6,552 kilometres in length, with 24 fibre pairs, more than 500 terabits per second of scalable capacity, and a target entry into service in 2029. These are announced project specifications and schedules, not verified operational capacity in November 2026. The cables are intended to be manufactured at Nordenham.
