The Historical Evolution of Fixed Naval Surveillance The development of fixed underwater military surveillance systems provides important evidence of the enduring strategic value of the seabed. The United States Navy traces the origins of its Sound Surveillance System (SOSUS) to the early Cold War, when underwater acoustic monitoring was developed to support submarine detection. The broader IUSS architecture subsequently integrated fixed systems with mobile and deployable surveillance capabilities. A US Navy account of the modernisation of its organisational structure records that the first SOSUS naval facility was commissioned in 1954 and that the later consolidation of surveillance processing produced the Naval Ocean Processing Facility structure. In October 2022, the Pacific facility was redesignated Theater Undersea Surveillance Command Pacific, reflecting the continuing development of underwater surveillance as an operational mission. The public record establishes institutional continuity and mission development, but it does not justify inferring that historical cable routes or surveillance configurations remain unchanged today. NOPF Whidbey Island Changes Name to Theater Undersea Surveillance Command Pacific — United States Navy — Oct 2022 . From a strategic perspective, the significance of this history lies in the distinction between underwater surveillance as a technical activity and surveillance as a complete military function. A fixed sensor network can contribute to persistent monitoring, but its operational value depends on data processing, command integration and appropriate communication with other military resources. Modern anti-submarine warfare involves combinations of fixed, mobile and deployable systems. It would therefore be incorrect to assume that loss of one fixed network necessarily renders a navy unable to detect submarines, just as it would be incorrect to assume that mobile systems automatically reproduce every function of a fixed installation. The strategic advantages of fixed infrastructure arise from its potential for persistent operation and integration with shore-based processing resources. Its limitations include the need to maintain physical components over long periods and the possibility that some systems are less readily repositioned than mobile surveillance assets. The appropriate defence-resilience question is whether essential surveillance functions can continue when individual components or supporting services are unavailable, rather than whether every element of the underwater network can be physically protected at all times. Military Communications and the Dependence on Commercial Infrastructure One of the most consequential characteristics of contemporary military communications is the coexistence of dedicated government systems and commercially provided connectivity. Military organisations may possess highly specialised communications resources, but they also conduct administrative, logistical, industrial and international support activities within economies whose digital infrastructure is predominantly privately owned. This creates dependencies that are not adequately represented by inventories of military communications equipment alone. The strategic issue is particularly important for states operating military installations abroad or supporting multinational deployments. A military command may retain secure communications capabilities while supporting organisations depend on broader civilian networks for procurement, personnel administration, maintenance coordination or exchanges with commercial suppliers. The consequences of a commercial cable interruption therefore depend on the precise functions affected and the available alternative arrangements. It would be inaccurate to conclude that commercial cable damage automatically disables military command-and-control systems. It would be equally inaccurate to conclude that military possession of dedicated communications means that commercial network disruption has no defence consequences. NATO’s 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements, published on 15 September 2026, explicitly connect civil communications resilience with continuity of government, support to military operations and other essential sectors. The requirements call for secure and reliable communications services, national risk assessments encompassing physical and digital vulnerabilities, and attention to cascading effects on civil support to armed forces. This establishes the civilian–military interdependence as an official Alliance planning concern rather than a purely theoretical proposition. 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements — North Atlantic Treaty Organization — Sep 2026 . A government assessing military continuity must consequently identify which essential functions depend on dedicated defence networks and which rely on external infrastructure. The relevant information includes service continuity arrangements, alternative transmission capabilities, electricity requirements and contractual relationships with providers. Sensitive routing information need not be published for a government to report credible aggregate readiness indicators. Nevertheless, operational claims should be supported by exercises and authoritative assessments rather than assurances based solely on network ownership. Defence Underwater Cable-Laying and Engineering Capabilities The existence of purpose-built naval cable vessels provides further evidence that undersea infrastructure is an established military engineering activity. The US Navy describes USNS Zeus (T-ARC 7) as the first cable-laying and repair ship designed and built specifically for the Navy. Its published mission included installation and maintenance of submarine cable systems, together with associated engineering and oceanographic tasks. The historical Navy fact file identifies the ship as delivered in 1984, with cable-handling equipment and specialised positioning capabilities. This source documents the engineering role of the vessel, but its historical description should not be treated as proof of its active status in November 2026. Cable Laying/Repair Ship, T-ARC — United States Navy, Military Sealift Command — Oct 2021 . Military cable-engineering capabilities are relevant to both the development of underwater systems and their maintenance. However, the technical equipment required for a particular military installation may differ from that used for commercial long-distance telecommunications repair. Vessel suitability depends on the system concerned, the engineering operation and the required personnel. A historical capability to lay submarine cables does not automatically establish the ability to restore a contemporary classified underwater surveillance system, particularly where specialised equipment or security clearances are required. The public record supports the existence of relevant military engineering expertise but does not provide a reconciled inventory of all current allied vessels capable of servicing dedicated defence underwater systems. This limitation matters because an assessment of military seabed readiness cannot simply add commercial repair fleets, naval oceanographic vessels and cable-installation ships together. Their missions and technical capabilities must be evaluated separately. The Military Value of Undersea Environmental Information Underwater surveillance systems do more than convey communications. They may contribute to the acquisition and processing of environmental information relevant to maritime operations. The US Navy’s IUSS mission explicitly includes the collection of acoustic, oceanographic and hydrographic information. Such information contributes to the understanding of underwater conditions and can support authorised naval operations. The strategic value arises from the integration of observations with the wider maritime operating picture, not from the existence of a particular underwater sensor in isolation. This distinction is important when examining the effects of infrastructure disruption. A reduction in the availability of underwater environmental data may affect the quality or timeliness of particular assessments without necessarily preventing all military operations. The operational impact would depend on the information lost, its relevance to current missions and the existence of other collection capabilities. Those factors cannot be quantified responsibly without authorised operational evidence. At the institutional level, however, the consequence is clear: governments should treat military sensor networks, their communications links and their supporting shore facilities as elements of an integrated capability requiring coordinated maintenance, cybersecurity and continuity arrangements. Protecting only the submerged portion of the system would leave unresolved risks associated with data processing, electricity and the transmission of information to authorised users. Intelligence Collection, Sovereignty and Public Attribution Underwater military activity presents a persistent challenge for open-source analysis because a large proportion of relevant operational information is legitimately withheld from public release. The existence of a naval programme, specialist vessel or publicly acknowledged reconnaissance mission does not establish the location of classified infrastructure or the full purpose of a particular deployment. Likewise, the observation of a foreign military vessel near critical undersea infrastructure does not automatically prove interference with a dedicated defence cable. The United Kingdom’s 9 April 2026 disclosure concerning Russian underwater activity is relevant because it explicitly identifies specialised Russian naval units associated with undersea infrastructure operations. The Ministry of Defence stated that British and allied forces monitored an Akula-class submarine and specialised units of Russia’s Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research, known as GUGI, in the High North. The government characterised the activity as a threat to critical undersea infrastructure and stated that the Russian vessels withdrew after the monitoring operation became overt. These are official British assessments of the observed activity, not a publicly verified record of completed cable destruction. UK Exposes Covert Russian Submarine Operation in and around UK Waters — UK Ministry of Defence — Apr 2026 . The episode demonstrates why the presence of specialised military underwater units must be analysed differently from ordinary commercial maritime incidents. A navy may possess legitimate reasons to collect oceanographic information or conduct submarine operations in international waters. At the same time, activities involving specialised undersea infrastructure capabilities can raise legitimate national-security concerns. The responsibility of the analyst is to distinguish the existence of a capability, the deployment of that capability, the officially assessed intention and any independently established hostile result. Failure to preserve these categories would exaggerate the evidence and undermine the credibility of the wider strategic assessment. Chapter 9 — Key Judgments Military submarine infrastructure includes dedicated communications systems, fixed underwater surveillance arrangements, sensor-to-shore transmission networks and facilities supporting naval operations. Public US Navy records establish the operational relevance of fixed and mobile surveillance systems, while NATO’s 2026 resilience requirements demonstrate that civilian communications continuity is also an explicit defence-planning concern. The principal strategic distinction is between interruption of a particular underwater asset and degradation of the military function that asset supports. A physically damaged cable does not automatically establish the loss of an entire military capability, because alternative systems and arrangements may exist. Conversely, the presence of dedicated defence networks does not eliminate dependence on commercial electricity, telecommunications and industrial services. A credible assessment must therefore examine complete defence functions, including their supporting infrastructure and continuity arrangements, without inventing details about classified deployments. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would become more precise if competent defence authorities released aggregate information concerning the redundancy, restoration preparedness and operational continuity of fixed undersea surveillance and communications systems. It would also change if official investigations demonstrated that the interruption of particular underwater military infrastructure had produced defined operational consequences. Open Official Record The principal gaps concern publicly releasable aggregate readiness assessments, military–civilian infrastructure dependencies, verified emergency engineering capabilities, completed continuity exercises and the formal arrangements governing the protection and restoration of relevant defence underwater infrastructure. Chapter 10 — Submarine Power Infrastructure: Military Energy Security, Offshore Electricity Systems and the Strategic Consequences of Interconnector Disruption Principal Strategic Judgment Submarine electricity infrastructure constitutes a separate strategic domain whose disruption can affect military readiness, civilian energy security and governmental continuity through mechanisms fundamentally different from those associated with fibre-optic telecommunications. A telecommunications cable transports information; a submarine power cable transmits electrical energy between generation facilities, electricity systems or specific installations. The loss of a communications route principally changes the availability and distribution of information, whereas the loss of an electricity connection can change the physical balance of generation, imports, reserves and consumption within the affected power system. The operational consequence depends on the role of the connection in the wider grid, the available replacement supply, the duration of the interruption and the ability of transmission system operators to maintain system stability. Military electricity dependence requires particularly careful analysis because most armed forces operate within national energy systems that are primarily civilian in ownership and management. Military installations may possess dedicated backup generation and other continuity arrangements, but the existence, endurance and operational suitability of those arrangements cannot be assumed without competent evidence. A submarine electricity interconnector may therefore have national-security importance even when it was constructed and financed for commercial electricity exchange. Its strategic value arises not necessarily from direct ownership by a defence ministry, but from its contribution to the availability of electricity supporting national economic activity, public services, military logistics and the broader industrial base. The European Commission’s Joint Research Centre distinguishes submarine telecommunications cables from submarine electricity cables in construction, function and cost. Its August 2025 analysis identifies typical submarine power-cable diameters of approximately 7–21 centimetres, compared with telecommunications cables reaching approximately 4–5 centimetres, depending on design and protection. The JRC reports average installation costs of approximately €1 million–€2 million per kilometre for submarine power cables, compared with around €25,000–€45,000 per kilometre for submarine telecommunications cables. These are broad infrastructure installation estimates, not standard costs for repairing a damaged system or replacing a specific high-voltage component. Subsea Cables: How Vulnerable Are They and Can We Protect Them? — European Commission Joint Research Centre — Aug 2025 . The Strategic Architecture of Submarine Electricity Transmission Submarine electricity infrastructure performs several distinct functions. Cross-border interconnectors permit electricity exchange between national or regional power systems. Offshore transmission connections transport electricity generated at sea to onshore grids. Certain island and remote-area connections supply electricity to communities or installations that would otherwise require greater reliance on local generation. Dedicated maritime or defence facilities may also require specialised electrical connections. These categories share some engineering characteristics but differ in scale, ownership, regulation and operational importance. A major cross-border interconnector is generally a component of the transmission system rather than an isolated supplier of electricity. Its value depends on the ability of two connected systems to exchange electricity when generation and demand conditions make such exchange beneficial. It can support security of supply, market integration and the use of different electricity-generation resources. Nevertheless, its rated transmission capacity does not mean that the entire amount is being transmitted continuously or that a disconnection necessarily causes an equivalent reduction in national electricity consumption. The distinction between megawatts (MW) and megawatt-hours (MWh) is essential. MW measures electrical power or transmission capacity at a particular moment, whereas MWh measures electricity transmitted or consumed over time. A 650 MW interconnector does not automatically deliver 650 MWh in every hour of operation, because actual flows depend on dispatch, availability and operating conditions. Nor does the loss of a 650 MW connection necessarily produce a 650 MW national electricity shortage. Other generation, imports, reserves or demand-response resources may compensate for the unavailable transfer capacity. These connections demonstrate the scale of submarine electricity infrastructure within north-western Europe. However, their capacities must not be aggregated and presented as firm electricity supply available to the United Kingdom at all times. Interconnectors can carry electricity in different directions, their availability varies, and their economic contribution depends on the conditions of the connected markets. Furthermore, a country may possess several nominally independent interconnectors while remaining exposed to common energy-market conditions or related terrestrial infrastructure constraints. The figures reveal a major difference between electricity and telecommunications restoration. A fibre-optic communications network may reroute information over another cable with suitable available capacity. Electricity transfers must instead be managed within the physical operating constraints of the interconnected power system. The availability of another transmission link is valuable, but the network must still maintain the necessary electrical conditions and supply-demand balance. This is why the consequences of losing a power interconnector cannot be inferred solely from its rated capacity or geographical position. EstLink 2: A Documented Test of Submarine Electricity Restoration The EstLink 2 incident provides a particularly important case because it establishes the real operational consequences of damage to a high-voltage submarine electricity connection. The link connects Finland and Estonia and has a transmission capacity of 650 MW. According to Fingrid, the total connection is approximately 170 kilometres long, comprising 145 kilometres of submarine cable, 14 kilometres of overhead line in Finland and 12 kilometres of underground cable in Estonia. These figures are rounded system descriptions and should not be interpreted as a precise engineering reconciliation of every component’s length. Fault in the EstLink 2 Electricity Transmission Connection Located in the Submarine Cable — Fingrid — Dec 2024 . On 25 December 2024, the connection disconnected from the electricity system. Fingrid subsequently confirmed that the fault was located in the submarine cable. At the time of the incident, the company stated that the failure had not endangered the Finnish electricity system, although it reduced cross-border transmission capability and could increase the risk of tighter supply conditions during prolonged periods of cold, low-wind weather. This distinction is significant because the loss of a large interconnector did not automatically produce a general electricity blackout. The actual restoration timeline is more informative than a simple statement that the cable had been damaged. Fingrid confirmed on 18 June 2025 that repairs had been completed and the system was expected to return to commercial use on 20 June 2025. The intervention involved replacement of approximately one kilometre of submarine cable, with actual offshore repair work performed during May and June. Fingrid later confirmed the 20 June restoration in its half-year report. The link was therefore unavailable for nearly six months, although the precise timing of physical repair activity was substantially shorter than the total period of unavailability. Electricity-System Sovereignty and the Baltic Synchronisation The Baltic States’ electricity integration provides an example of infrastructure decisions with direct geopolitical significance. On 9 February 2025, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania synchronised their electricity systems with the continental European network through Poland, ending their previous synchronous connection with the electricity system controlled by Russia and Belarus. The European Commission describes this as an important step in strengthening electricity-system independence, regional integration and energy security. Baltic Energy Market Interconnection Plan — European Commission . The distinction between electricity synchronisation and electricity trading is essential. Synchronisation concerns the operational relationship among power systems, including their frequency and associated control arrangements. Cross-border electricity trading concerns the exchange of electrical energy. A country may trade electricity with another system without surrendering control of its own grid frequency, depending on the technologies and network arrangements involved. The Baltic synchronisation project therefore addressed a deeper form of operational dependence than the availability of any single electricity interconnector. The European Commission reported that more than €1.2 billion in EU grants had supported the Baltic synchronisation programme and its associated infrastructure over the preceding period. This figure refers to a broad strategic electricity integration project, not expenditure devoted exclusively to protecting submarine cables. The synchronisation was intended to reduce dependence on the Russian and Belarusian electricity system while strengthening integration with continental Europe. It illustrates a wider form of infrastructure sovereignty in which strategic autonomy depends on control over essential system functions and not merely ownership of transmission assets. Commission, Baltic States and Poland Commit to Accelerated Baltic Grid Synchronisation — European Commission — Dec 2023 . The strategic consequence is that a state’s exposure to energy coercion cannot be assessed through submarine cables alone. It depends on generation capacity, electricity imports, transmission infrastructure, reserve resources, operational control and the arrangements linking the national grid to neighbouring systems. A disrupted submarine interconnector may reduce flexibility and market access without compromising the fundamental sovereignty of the national electricity system. Conversely, a state may possess substantial domestic generation while remaining exposed through operational dependencies or insufficient reserves under exceptional conditions. Military Installations and Civilian Electricity Dependence The availability of electricity is a foundational requirement for military operations, but the physical infrastructure supplying a military installation is not necessarily military-owned. Naval bases, air facilities, communications centres, logistics depots and defence-industrial establishments may draw electricity from the civilian grid while maintaining different forms of local backup generation. The operational significance of a submarine electricity interruption therefore depends on the affected installation’s relationship with the national grid and the endurance of its authorised continuity arrangements. The NATO 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements explicitly call for reliable energy supplies during crisis and conflict, taking account of industrial capacity, cross-border interconnections, supply-chain dependencies and the need to support military operations. They also require verified and exercised repair and restoration arrangements developed with infrastructure operators. This establishes electricity infrastructure resilience as an integral part of collective defence preparedness. 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements, Resilient Energy Supply — NATO — Sep 2026 . A national assessment should distinguish the loss of imported electricity from the loss of electricity to a particular military facility. The former changes the wider energy balance; the latter concerns the continuity of a specific installation. They may be connected but are not equivalent. A damaged international electricity link can alter national reserve margins or market prices without interrupting a naval base directly. Conversely, an installation may encounter local electricity problems while international interconnectors remain operational. The appropriate strategic evaluation must therefore include essential defence electricity demand, the availability of local alternatives, the reliability of the surrounding network and arrangements for restoring supply under exceptional conditions. Public reporting can assess aggregate readiness without revealing the precise endurance or technical configuration of individual sensitive installations. The Financial Consequences of Submarine Power-Cable Disruption The economic effects of submarine electricity infrastructure disruption differ from those associated with telecommunications because electricity availability is subject to physical system constraints and short-term balancing requirements. A reduced interconnector capacity can affect the ability of connected electricity markets to exchange power, potentially changing the use of local generation, reserves or other available connections. The consequences depend on electricity demand, weather, generation availability, market prices, network constraints and the duration of the outage. The EstLink 2 case demonstrates this distinction. Fingrid reported that the Finnish electricity system continued operating, while cross-border capacity was reduced by 650 MW. The absence of a general Finnish power failure does not mean the lost connection was economically irrelevant. The outage removed a source of transmission flexibility for an extended period and required a substantial physical restoration operation. However, a precise estimate of its total economic consequences would require verified price, dispatch and network data rather than simply multiplying the nominal capacity by the number of hours in the outage. Fingrid’s audited 2025 financial reporting states that the EstLink 2 repair represented a significant expense and that the company continued developing contingency measures with relevant energy-sector participants. The company reported €485.1 million in gross capital expenditure for 2025, but this figure covers the wider transmission business and must not be presented as the cost of the EstLink 2 repair. Fingrid Financial Statements Bulletin January–December 2025 — Fingrid — Mar 2026 . Chapter 10 — Key Judgments Submarine electricity infrastructure is strategically important to military readiness because the armed forces depend on reliable energy systems, including systems primarily operated for civilian purposes. The loss of an interconnector can affect electricity exchange and system flexibility without necessarily causing a national blackout. Its actual consequences depend on the characteristics of the wider electricity network and the availability of alternatives. The EstLink 2 case establishes that restoration of a high-voltage submarine connection may require several months even where the damaged section is comparatively limited. The Baltic electricity synchronisation demonstrates a separate geopolitical dimension: operational independence can depend on the architecture and control of the electricity system rather than on the availability of any particular cable. The central conclusion is that military energy resilience requires coordinated assessment of submarine transmission, onshore electricity infrastructure, national generation, operational control and the continuity of essential defence facilities. What Would Change the Assessment The assessment would change if official energy-system stress tests demonstrated materially greater or lower resilience to simultaneous interconnector outages, or if new operational records established different restoration requirements for high-voltage submarine systems. Verified information concerning the aggregate endurance of essential military electricity services would permit a more precise evaluation of defence continuity. Open Official Record The principal gaps concern comparable national interconnector contingency assessments, military-support electricity requirements, verified emergency equipment inventories, high-voltage repair capacity, restoration exercises and the financial consequences of prolonged loss of cross-border electricity transmission. Chapter 11 — State-Directed Seabed Warfare: Strategic Coercion, Hybrid Operations, Infrastructure Disruption and Escalation Principal Strategic Judgment The strategic significance of seabed infrastructure in interstate competition arises from its ability to connect military security with the economic and administrative continuity of a state. A government may depend on underwater assets for international communications, electricity exchange, maritime surveillance and the operation of strategically important facilities, while those assets remain distributed across international waters, foreign jurisdictions and privately owned systems. This creates opportunities for coercion and disruption that differ from conventional attacks on military installations: an incident affecting civilian infrastructure can generate national-security consequences, while uncertainty concerning responsibility may complicate diplomatic and military responses. The most important analytical distinction concerns the relationship between strategic purpose and documented conduct. States may possess the capability to undertake underwater reconnaissance or interfere with infrastructure, but the existence of such a capability does not establish that it has been employed against a specific target. Official allegations concerning hostile activity must be attributed to the governments making them, while criminal findings, physical engineering evidence and judicial determinations must retain their separate status. A defensible assessment of seabed warfare therefore examines strategic objectives, observable forms of coercion, defensive indicators and consequences without converting hypothetical operations into established historical events. The United Kingdom’s 2025 National Security Strategy explicitly identifies critical national infrastructure, including undersea cables and energy pipelines, as potential targets of hostile state activity. It further warns that states may use proxies, including criminal or other non-state organisations, complicating identification and accountability. The strategy associates infrastructure protection with a broader requirement to defend national sovereignty and reduce vulnerabilities arising from external dependence. These are official British strategic assessments, not proof of individual attacks. National Security Strategy 2025: Security for the British People in a Dangerous World — UK Government — Jun 2025 . The Strategic Purposes of Infrastructure Coercion The deliberate disruption or threatened disruption of undersea infrastructure can serve several distinct political and military purposes. One is coercive signalling: demonstrating the ability to impose costs on another state in order to influence its policy. Another is economic pressure, where the interruption of essential services may increase political and financial demands on the affected government. A third is the degradation of military-support functions, particularly where civilian electricity and communications networks contribute to the operation of defence institutions. A fourth concerns intelligence collection and strategic reconnaissance, which may support the broader assessment of a maritime operating environment without necessarily involving physical damage. These purposes must not be treated as automatically compatible. An operation intended to remain deniable may produce a different political effect from an openly announced coercive threat. A disruption of civilian services may create pressure on a government but could also strengthen public support for defensive measures or allied cooperation. Interference with an electricity interconnector may reduce market flexibility without achieving a politically significant loss of supply. Likewise, damage to a communications cable may produce little immediate economic effect if surviving networks have sufficient capacity. The outcome of infrastructure coercion therefore depends on the actual function interrupted, the ability of the affected state to compensate and the political interpretation of the event. The distinction between an intended strategic effect and a realised effect is particularly important. A hostile actor may seek to undermine confidence in national infrastructure, but public confidence may remain stable where services continue and authorities provide credible information. A state may hope to exploit uncertainty about responsibility, but an investigation may eventually identify the relevant conduct and support criminal or diplomatic measures. Conversely, the absence of definitive attribution may limit the proportionality and political feasibility of certain responses even when physical damage is undisputed. Russian Undersea Activity: Documented Capabilities and Official Allegations Russia is central to current European assessments of undersea infrastructure security because NATO and British authorities have publicly identified Russian activity as a significant concern. The United Kingdom’s April 2026 disclosure describes specialised Russian military units associated with GUGI and an operation involving a conventional attack submarine in the High North. The British government stated that these units possessed capabilities intended for underwater infrastructure reconnaissance and that such capabilities could be employed destructively during conflict. The account also described British and allied surveillance activity intended to expose and deter the operation. UK Exposes Covert Russian Submarine Operation — UK Ministry of Defence — Apr 2026 . This evidence supports the conclusion that British defence authorities consider Russian specialised undersea operations a credible national-security concern. It does not establish a complete public inventory of Russian equipment, deployment locations or operational plans. Nor does it prove that a particular military cable or energy interconnector was destroyed during the episode. The British account is an official institutional attribution of suspicious activity and assessed military capability, not a judicial determination concerning sabotage. The distinction is reinforced by the broader European record. In December 2024, following damage to electricity and communications cables in the Baltic, the European Commission and High Representative described a series of suspected attacks and identified concerns involving vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet. The statement called for stronger protective measures and potential sanctions while acknowledging an ongoing investigation. Its description of the suspected vessel’s commercial association should not be transformed into definitive proof of Russian state command over the incident. Joint Statement on the Investigation into Damaged Electricity and Data Cables in the Baltic Sea — European Commission and High Representative — Dec 2024 . The strategic importance of this record lies in the combination of physical infrastructure exposure, maritime intelligence concerns and the difficulty of attribution. Governments may need to improve protection and monitoring before a court establishes criminal responsibility or an intelligence authority makes an attributable finding of state direction. This creates a legitimate requirement for proportionate preventive action, but it does not justify presenting every incident involving a Russia-linked vessel as a completed Russian military operation. Physical Interference and Its Political Consequences Physical interference with undersea infrastructure can affect electricity and communications differently. The consequence of an interrupted telecommunications cable depends heavily on whether the required services can be transferred to other paths. The consequence of an electricity interconnector outage depends on the electrical system’s capacity to maintain supply, stability and cross-border exchange. The political objective of a hostile state may be similar in both cases—to impose uncertainty or economic costs—but the physical transmission mechanisms and the resilience of the affected systems differ. The EstLink 2 incident illustrates this distinction. The electricity link remained unavailable from December 2024 until June 2025, creating an extended reduction in cross-border capacity. However, Fingrid reported that the Finnish electricity system continued operating. The event therefore cannot be presented as proof that the loss of a large submarine electricity connection necessarily causes a national blackout. It does demonstrate that restoration may take months and that international electricity links can remain unavailable for substantial periods. EstLink 2 Returns to Commercial Use — Fingrid — Jun 2025 . This distinction limits the effectiveness of simplistic coercive assumptions. A state seeking to exert pressure through infrastructure disruption cannot reliably infer national consequences from cable capacity alone. The affected government may possess reserves, alternative connections, domestic generation or other arrangements that reduce the realised effect. Similarly, damage that creates significant repair expenditure may fail to produce the political outcome sought by the actor responsible. Cybersecurity and the Underwater Infrastructure Interface The cyber dimension of seabed security requires separate treatment because an underwater cable may remain physically intact while supporting systems become unavailable or compromised. Relevant risks can concern network management, associated shore facilities, communications services, electricity-system control environments and the digital systems used by operators and public authorities. The strategic consequence is that infrastructure continuity depends partly on cybersecurity outside the submerged cable itself. The United Kingdom’s October 2026 White Paper explicitly identifies cyber threats, physical sabotage and proxy activity among the risks relevant to critical undersea infrastructure. It also addresses the national-security implications of fibre-optic sensing technologies, recognising that systems capable of obtaining information from submarine cables may create security concerns if sensitive data are not appropriately governed. These are proposed policy and regulatory responses, not evidence of a particular successful cyberattack against a military underwater network. Critical Undersea Infrastructure Security and Resilience White Paper — UK Government — Oct 2026 . The European Commission similarly treats physical security and cybersecurity as interconnected dimensions of energy resilience. Its critical-infrastructure policy calls for cooperation across public and private sectors, integrated threat assessments, preparedness exercises and protection of essential energy networks. The practical implication is that a state should not equate seabed protection exclusively with naval patrols. The integrity of supporting digital systems and the ability to recover their operation are also necessary. Critical Infrastructure and Cybersecurity — European Commission, Directorate-General for Energy . Attribution Uncertainty as a Strategic Factor Uncertainty concerning responsibility can affect political decision-making independently from the technical severity of an incident. An infrastructure operator may identify the physical cause of a fault without knowing whether the conduct was accidental or deliberate. Maritime authorities may identify a vessel whose activities warrant investigation without possessing evidence of state direction. A government may possess intelligence supporting an assessment that cannot be fully disclosed publicly. These differences can complicate diplomatic responses and produce divergent interpretations among allies. Attribution uncertainty can also influence public confidence. Governments that present preliminary suspicions as established fact risk undermining credibility if later proceedings produce a different conclusion. Conversely, governments that wait for complete judicial certainty before undertaking proportionate defensive measures may leave infrastructure exposed to further disruption. The institutional response should therefore distinguish investigative thresholds, operational protection thresholds and thresholds for public attribution or international countermeasures. The December 2024 European institutional response demonstrates this distinction. The Commission and High Representative publicly identified a suspected attack and associated concerns, while Finnish authorities continued examining the events. The appropriate strategic interpretation is that the incident justified heightened attention to infrastructure security, while the ultimate attribution of responsibility required further evidence. This separation permits preventive action without prejudging legal outcomes. Regional Coercion and the Difference Between National and Alliance Exposure The effects of undersea infrastructure disruption depend on geography, international interdependence and the distribution of available alternatives. An interruption affecting an island electricity connection may have a different significance from the loss of a major cross-border interconnector. Similarly, an incident affecting a regional communications system may create a national emergency in one jurisdiction while generating comparatively minor congestion elsewhere. These differences make it inappropriate to assume that a hostile operation affecting one cable will impose uniform consequences across an alliance. The Baltic demonstrates the importance of regional interdependence. Several states share maritime infrastructure interests and participate in integrated electricity and communications markets. The European Commission’s Baltic synchronisation programme and NATO’s Baltic Sentry activity address different dimensions of this environment: energy-system independence and maritime-security awareness. Neither programme eliminates every possible infrastructure vulnerability, but both change the conditions under which a state could attempt to exert pressure. The Mediterranean presents a different institutional environment, involving EU and non-EU coastal states, international communications routes and potentially different legal and operational conditions for repairs. The Atlantic combines substantial transoceanic communications capacity with the strategic responsibilities of the United States, Canada and European allies. The Arctic presents challenges associated with maritime conditions and the monitoring of specialised undersea military activity. These environments require different contingency arrangements and should not be reduced to a single generic concept of seabed warfare. Escalation and International-Law Consequences Deliberate interference with infrastructure can generate consequences extending beyond the immediate physical damage. An incident attributed to a state may lead to diplomatic measures, criminal proceedings, sanctions, heightened military readiness or other lawful responses. The legal character of the event depends on the facts and applicable international law. Damage to infrastructure does not automatically constitute an armed attack within the meaning of Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, nor does every act of sabotage necessarily trigger collective defence under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. Those determinations require assessment of the nature, scale, effects and attribution of the conduct, together with the relevant legal and political procedures. The NATO Treaty provides for collective defence, while the Alliance’s contemporary resilience framework recognises infrastructure protection as an important element of security. However, the public record does not establish an automatic rule under which every submarine cable incident produces a specified military response. The Alliance must consider the evidence, the applicable law and the circumstances of the incident. 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements — NATO — Sep 2026 . The escalation problem is particularly important where responsibility remains contested. An excessive response based on incomplete evidence could intensify a confrontation without improving infrastructure security. An inadequate response to well-established hostile conduct could weaken deterrence and increase uncertainty about the protection of essential services. Effective policy therefore requires calibrated attribution, lawful defensive measures and communication among allies. Chapter 11 — Key Judgments State-directed seabed warfare should be understood as a potential instrument of strategic coercion affecting communications, energy security, maritime awareness and government continuity. Its effectiveness depends on the actual services disrupted, the resilience of the affected systems and the political response of the targeted state. The British and NATO records establish concern about specialised Russian undersea capabilities, while European investigations demonstrate the difficulty of determining responsibility for particular maritime incidents. These records support heightened preparedness but do not justify treating every cable fault as state-directed sabotage. The principal strategic conclusion is that infrastructure coercion derives much of its political significance from uncertainty and systemic dependence, yet neither deliberate damage nor threatening activity guarantees a successful coercive outcome. Strong redundancy, credible attribution procedures, rapid restoration and allied cooperation can reduce the leverage available to hostile actors. What Would Change the Assessment The judgment would change if authoritative investigations established additional cases of coordinated state-directed interference, if official operational assessments demonstrated that specific infrastructure disruptions had materially degraded defence functions, or if governments documented successful coercive outcomes linked to undersea infrastructure threats. Open Official Record The principal gaps concern completed criminal and official investigations, attributable evidence of state direction, publicly releasable assessments of military consequences, and reliable data distinguishing actual service disruption from physical infrastructure damage. Chapter 12 — Military Infrastructure Protection, Allied Defence Continuity and the 2027–2031 Seabed Security Architecture Principal Strategic Judgment The protection of military and dual-use submarine infrastructure must become an integral component of national defence continuity, rather than remain a specialised maritime-security activity conducted separately from telecommunications, electricity-system management and military operational planning. Undersea communications networks, military surveillance systems, cross-border electricity interconnectors and the shore-based infrastructure supporting them form a technologically diverse but strategically interconnected system. Their importance arises not simply from the possibility of physical damage, but from the dependence of governmental decision-making, military logistics, naval surveillance, industrial mobilisation and essential civilian services on resources that may be owned, operated and repaired by different public and private organisations. The principal strategic risk is consequently a failure of coordination between these organisations during a prolonged crisis, particularly when several infrastructure systems experience interruptions and military requirements compete with the needs of the civilian population. The principal policy objective for 2027–2031 should be to establish a demonstrable capacity to preserve essential defence functions while simultaneously protecting civilian continuity. This requires identifying critical dependencies, maintaining independent or alternative service arrangements, developing repair capabilities appropriate to the technologies concerned, and establishing legally authorised procedures for coordinating military and civilian priorities. The approach must distinguish dedicated defence systems from commercial infrastructure supporting defence activity; submarine telecommunications cables from high-voltage electricity transmission; and maritime surveillance from physical restoration. These capabilities are complementary, but they are not interchangeable. The most consequential recent institutional development is NATO’s 15 September 2026 revision of its Resilience Baseline Requirements. The Alliance explicitly connects national resilience with the execution of military plans, host-nation support, continuity of government, reliable energy supplies, civil communications and the restoration of essential infrastructure during crisis and conflict. The document requires attention to cascading failures, supply-chain dependencies, private-sector cooperation and the availability of repair resources. This establishes an authoritative basis for treating submarine infrastructure security as part of a wider defence-continuity problem rather than merely as a matter of naval patrols or commercial network maintenance. 2026 Resilience Baseline Requirements — North Atlantic Treaty Organization — Sep 2026 . The Strategic Transition from Asset Protection to Defence-Function Continuity The traditional protection of critical infrastructure often begins with the physical identification of installations, their operators and the threats to which they may be exposed. This remains necessary for submarine infrastructure, but it is insufficient for assessing military consequences because the same physical system may support different functions with different resilience requirements. An international telecommunications cable can transport commercial traffic while supporting communications needed by government departments, defence suppliers or authorised military users. An electricity interconnector can primarily serve an integrated civilian energy market while contributing to the availability of electricity for public institutions and military-support industries. A dedicated underwater surveillance system can depend on shore-based electricity, processing facilities and communications infrastructure that are not themselves situated on the seabed. The strategic unit of analysis must therefore be the essential function rather than the individual cable. A defence organisation requires certain information, energy and logistical capabilities to remain available under specified conditions. Those capabilities may be delivered through several independent assets or, in some circumstances, through assets sharing common supporting infrastructure. Determining whether a cable fault constitutes a significant military problem requires knowledge of this functional architecture. It cannot be inferred from cable capacity, length or ownership alone. This approach is directly supported by NATO’s revised baseline requirements. The Alliance identifies seven baseline areas encompassing continuity of government, energy, population movement, food and water, healthcare, communications and transport. Within these categories, the document establishes specific expectations concerning civil support to military operations. In its energy requirement, NATO calls for verified and exercised repair and restoration plans developed with infrastructure operators. In its communications requirement, it calls for reliable and secure services, regular risk assessments, supply-chain visibility and priority access supporting military requirements and societal resilience. These are operational objectives rather than a claim that all Allies already possess equivalent capabilities. The consequence is that submarine infrastructure preparedness must be incorporated into national continuity planning, while retaining the technical distinctions among the systems concerned. A defence continuity plan cannot assume that a commercial telecommunications provider can restore a dedicated military surveillance network. Nor can an electricity transmission operator be expected to resolve a defence communications failure outside its competence. The appropriate institutional response is to define the dependencies between these organisations, assign responsibility for maintaining them and establish tested alternatives where a critical function depends on resources vulnerable to interruption. The Seven NATO Resilience Requirements and Their Relationship to Undersea Infrastructure The September 2026 NATO framework provides a detailed institutional structure for understanding the indirect consequences of submarine infrastructure disruption. Its importance lies in connecting functions that are frequently examined independently. Electricity supply is relevant to military installations, but also to telecommunications, transport and healthcare. Communications are necessary for governmental coordination, yet they also support energy-system management and logistical activity. Transport is required to move military forces and commercial goods, while repair vessels and technical personnel may rely on ports and international travel arrangements. Consequently, the interruption of one infrastructure component can affect several resilience objectives without necessarily producing a complete failure of any individual sector. The Alliance’s requirements explicitly recognise the potential for combined crises, including physical attacks, cyber incidents, harmful economic dependencies and environmental hazards. They also recognise the need for more reliable restoration capabilities. This is a significant development because it places the repair of civilian infrastructure within the requirements of defence preparedness. Military Undersea Surveillance: Defence Protection Without Revealing Operational Configurations Dedicated military underwater surveillance infrastructure requires a protection framework different from that governing publicly operated commercial cable systems. Certain military sensor networks may be designed to support persistent maritime observation, the processing of underwater information and authorised reporting to naval commands. Their operational characteristics may be classified, and their effectiveness cannot be evaluated responsibly through public cable maps or assumptions about historical military infrastructure. Protection should instead be assessed according to the resilience of the military function. This involves the ability to identify an impairment, determine its operational significance, maintain essential information through authorised alternatives and conduct restoration where feasible. Such a framework does not require public disclosure of sensor positions, capabilities or technical vulnerabilities. Governments can assess and report aggregate preparedness while preserving sensitive operational information. The United States Navy’s official Integrated Undersea Surveillance System materials establish that fixed and mobile capabilities form part of a wider undersea surveillance mission. The institutional implication is that resilience depends on how these functions contribute collectively to maritime awareness. The loss of an individual fixed component may have limited consequences where alternative resources provide the required information, but that conclusion must be verified rather than assumed. Similarly, the availability of mobile platforms does not establish that every function of a fixed system can be replicated without constraints. The strategic protection requirements for dedicated military underwater infrastructure can be organised into five categories: continuity of mission-essential information; secure operation of associated processing and communications facilities; availability of authorised technical maintenance; resilience of supporting electricity and shore infrastructure; and clear institutional responsibility for restoration. These categories are relevant without identifying the precise locations or configurations of military installations. Maritime Security and the Actual Capabilities Demonstrated by NATO NATO’s Baltic Sentry activities provide a documented example of military capabilities supporting the protection of undersea infrastructure. In an official publication dated 26 October 2026, NATO described the contribution of Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 1 to maritime awareness and infrastructure inspection in the Baltic Sea. The activity involved naval vessels and underwater systems used to inspect maritime infrastructure and identify conditions warranting further assessment. The publication identifies participation by vessels and personnel from several Allies, including Germany, Finland, Lithuania, Poland and Portugal, demonstrating a multinational operational activity rather than a purely national initiative. Deterring Hybrid Threats at Sea — NATO — Oct 2026 . The significance of this capability is that equipment developed for one naval purpose can sometimes support additional authorised missions, including underwater inspection and the collection of information relevant to infrastructure protection. This can improve the use of existing military resources without necessarily requiring the acquisition of a separate platform for every function. Nevertheless, underwater inspection is not equivalent to submarine cable repair. Detecting a damaged segment or assessing suspicious activity does not establish the ability to manufacture a suitable replacement cable, perform specialist jointing or restore high-voltage electricity transmission. These activities require different industrial and engineering resources. NATO’s operational contribution should therefore be measured by its ability to improve situational awareness, support lawful maritime security and assist competent civilian authorities. The repair of commercial infrastructure remains dependent on the relevant operators and specialist contractors, except where military or public assets are specifically authorised and technically capable of performing the work. An important policy consequence is that governments should avoid double counting military platforms as restoration assets simply because they possess underwater inspection equipment. A mine-countermeasures vessel may be highly valuable for maritime assessment but unsuitable for repairing a deep-water optical cable. Its contribution to resilience lies in its actual mission capability, not its general proximity to the seabed-security problem. Defence Electricity Continuity and Submarine Power Systems The protection of submarine electricity cables is inseparable from wider national energy security. A military installation may depend on an electricity system incorporating domestic generation, terrestrial transmission, international interconnectors and local distribution networks. The contribution of a particular submarine interconnector depends on the broader electricity system’s configuration and available supply alternatives. Consequently, a security assessment should not equate the loss of nominal interconnector capacity with an equivalent reduction in electricity delivered to military facilities. The Baltic electricity transition demonstrates how strategic energy exposure can change through institutional and technical restructuring. On 9 February 2025, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania synchronised their electricity systems with the continental European network through Poland, ending their previous dependence on the Russian and Belarusian synchronous system. This did not remove every infrastructure risk or eliminate the need for electricity interconnectors. It changed an important aspect of operational control and reduced a strategic dependence identified by European authorities. Baltic Energy Market Interconnection Plan — European Commission . For military preparedness, the relevant lesson is that the protection of submarine power infrastructure must form part of a wider electricity-continuity strategy. The central questions concern the ability of the national grid to maintain essential supply, the availability of alternative generation and transmission, the resilience of distribution networks and the restoration arrangements applicable to particular high-voltage systems. These questions should be addressed through competent energy and defence authorities, supported by system operators and verified contingency exercises. The difference between telecommunications and electricity engineering must remain explicit. The replacement of an optical submarine cable and the restoration of a high-voltage direct-current interconnector require different equipment, engineering procedures and industrial components. A country possessing substantial telecommunications cable manufacturing cannot automatically be considered capable of repairing every high-voltage electricity system. Similarly, the presence of an offshore electricity installation vessel does not establish full compatibility with telecommunications repair. Joint assessment without technical conflation Allied Coordination: NATO, the European Union and National Sovereignty The institutional architecture of seabed security is necessarily multinational because military, energy and telecommunications systems cross national jurisdictions while remaining subject to different legal authorities. NATO’s role concerns collective defence, military planning and authorised security operations. The European Union can develop relevant common legislation, investment programmes and cross-border coordination within its competences. National governments retain responsibility for substantial aspects of maritime enforcement, defence operations, emergency authority and public-service continuity. Private operators possess engineering expertise and contractual rights essential to restoration. The challenge is not the absence of institutions, but the fragmentation of decision-making across institutions whose mandates overlap only partially. For example, NATO may possess maritime surveillance information relevant to a suspected incident, while a telecommunications operator possesses the technical records necessary to identify the affected system. An EU-funded regional coordination body may support information exchange, but a national authority may have to approve a repair vessel’s activities within its jurisdiction. The vessel itself may be privately owned and subject to contractual obligations determined by another company. The resulting response depends on decisions that must be coordinated without assuming that one institution possesses universal authority. The European Commission’s June 2026 announcement of €5.8 million for Baltic and Mediterranean Regional Cable Hubs and a €40 million call for repair capacity represents a concrete attempt to improve this architecture. The policy objective includes monitoring, detection and response to threats affecting critical undersea infrastructure. However, the funding of a regional hub does not establish an independent maritime command, nor does it give EU institutions automatic authority to direct national armed forces or foreign-flagged commercial vessels. The requirements specifically recognise the importance of aligning national civilian planning with allied military needs. This creates a basis for integrating seabed infrastructure continuity into defence plans without converting every civilian asset into a military installation.
